Could eating less protein slow ageing?

New Scientist July 31, 2026

Protein-rich products – from cereal to crisps to coffee – are all over supermarket shelves, but mounting evidence in non-human animals suggests that restricting our intake could slow ageing and extend lifespan. So, does that mean eating too much protein is harmful?

“We have this impression that dietary protein is sort of a universally good thing,” says Dudley Lamming at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. But according to the latest review of the evidence, “increasing dietary protein, beyond what’s needed, for sedentary individuals or animals leads to metabolic problems and can lead to shorter lifespan as well”, he says.

Your body changes as you age and so should your diet – here’s how

But others point out that nutritional studies in animals like mice and rats don’t readily translate to people, and a high protein intake has been linked to benefits in humans.

Advertisement

Lamming and his colleagues sifted through more than 300 studies, mostly in sedentary rodents, that explored how restricting protein intake to the minimum required to prevent deficiency affects ageing and lifespan.

In these studies, rodents generally either ate the equivalent of the minimum protein requirement recommended by US guidelines – 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight – or about double that. The latter is similar to the intake recently recommended by US dietary guidelines for optimal health, 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.

In one study, rats that ate around the minimum protein intake lived nearly 120 days, or more than 50 per cent, longer than those that ate about double that.

This may be because protein restriction increases levels of the hormone FGF21, says Lamming. In rodents, this acts on the brain, fat tissue and the liver to improve blood sugar levels and reduce the number of senescent cells. These cells, which accumulate with age, have stopped dividing and cause chronic inflammation.

Free newsletter

Restricting protein intake has also been shown to dampen the activity of a protein called mTORC1 in mice. mTORC1 ordinarily stimulates cell growth, but reducing its activity boosts cellular repair. “It essentially switches cells from a proliferative state, where they’re growing and engaging a lot of metabolism, to one where they’re dividing more slowly, if at all, and focusing on repair,” says Lamming. Studies suggest this cuts the risk of age-related conditions and extends lifespan in mice, he says.

All this suggests that the recent trend to up our protein intake is probably fine among people who exercise regularly, because they may need more protein to repair muscle damage, but eating more than is needed could cause harm in sedentary individuals, says Lamming.

But Donald Layman at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign points out that rodents vary hugely from people when it comes to protein metabolism. For instance, mTORC1 is activated by feeding, and while people tend to a have a few big meals a day, rodents graze more regularly. Protein restriction may therefore affect mTORC1 pathways differently between the different species, he says. We are also more exposed to factors that accelerate ageing, like infections and extreme heat, than lab animals, says Layman.

What’s more, the review does not include most of the studies in people that suggest that upping our protein intake beyond the minimum cuts our risk of frailty, he says.

Lamming says no studies were intentionally omitted. “We were focused on protein restriction, not the many studies looking at higher levels of protein intake,” he says. Beyond building muscle and preventing frailty, there is mixed evidence on whether a higher protein intake helps with ageing, says Lamming.

Why have so many people become fixated on protein? Donald Layman is one of the people behind the research showing the benefits of getting more protein in your diet, but he thinks things have gone too far and wants to set the record straight

For instance, one study linked this to a reduced risk of age-related muscle loss, or sarcopenia, among older twins in the UK. But the rates of sarcopenia were so low that the link is unreliable, says Elizabeth Williams at the University of Sheffield in the UK.

Still, some studies showed that restricting intake of certain amino acids – such as isoleucine and valine, which are highest in meat, fish and dairy – in mice has a similar effect to limiting overall protein intake, says Philip Atherton at the University of Nottingham, UK.

Atherton says he is planning a study to investigate whether drugs that deplete specific amino acids in people improve outcomes like blood sugar control, with results expected in the next few years.

Thousands of people in China have had banned Alzheimer’s surgery

New Scientist July 31, 2026

More than 2000 people in China are thought to have undergone an experimental surgery to treat Alzheimer’s disease, which allegedly helped a man with the condition who was bedbound walk again. The procedure – which involves connecting the lymphatic system to nearby veins to remove Alzheimer’s-associated proteins – has now been banned in the country.

“When I first heard of this treatment, I was shocked,” says Steven Proulx at the University of Bern in Switzerland. “There is basically no evidence supporting this.”

Inhaling high-dose CO2 clears Alzheimer’s proteins from the brain

But initial results from small safety trials in the US and Singapore, which were presented earlier this month at the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference in London, suggest the approach is safe for up to six months, with some signals of cognitive improvement.

Advertisement

An ongoing randomised trial is now comparing the surgery against a sham procedure, which should provide a clearer picture of its potential, but some have questioned the ethics of this and how helpful the trial will be.

The surgery, called deep cervical lymphovenous anastomosis (DCLVA), aims to enhance the drainage of brain waste via the lymphatic system, a network of vessels and nodes that collects waste from tissues to be broken down or removed from the body. The idea is that surgically attaching this network to nearby veins accelerates this process to more efficiently clear Alzheimer’s-related proteins like beta-amyloid and tau.

It was developed by Xie Qingping at Hangzhou Qiushi Hospital in China, based on a routine treatment for chronically swollen limbs. In 2024, Qingping – who didn’t respond to New Scientist’s requests for comment – and his colleagues reported in the journal Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery that they had conducted DCLVA on 50 people with Alzheimer’s disease. They also released a video of a man with Alzheimer’s who had been bedbound briskly walking eight months after the surgery.

Free newsletter

But some have concerns over the reliability of this case report. “A video from one patient I would not find trustworthy,” says Proulx, who added that the researchers didn’t assess for other improvements, such as changes to the man’s brain-imaging scans.

Still, the footage went viral in China, says Fan Fan at Augusta University in Georgia. By May 2025, thousands of people were estimated to have had the procedure in around 300 private and public hospitals across China.

Reports suggest that many of these were done by plastic surgeons, says Proulx, with fees ranging from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand Chinese yuan (thousands to tens of thousands of pounds).

But in June 2025, China’s National Health Commission banned the procedure outside of research settings, citing a lack of evidence on safety and effectiveness. The commission didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment. “It was appropriate for China to stop DCLVA from being offered for Alzheimer’s disease,” says Shiju Gu, who previously researched Alzheimer’s disease at Harvard University.

To date, about a dozen case reports and trials have reported doing DCLVA on people with moderate or severe Alzheimer’s. The US and Singaporean trials presented at the recent Alzheimer’s conference suggest it is safe over the short term. The Singaporean trial also found evidence of small cognitive improvements in two out of four of its participants.

These improvements aren’t necessarily trivial, says Jeff Iliff at the University of Washington in Seattle, but none of these trials was randomised or blinded.

“Based on the evidence currently available, I would describe DCLVA’s effectiveness as uncertain because the existing clinical studies in China have generally been uncontrolled, short term and methodologically limited, making it difficult to separate a real surgical effect from placebo effects, postoperative care or fluctuations in the patient’s condition,” says Gu.

It is also unclear whether any improvements were substantial enough for people or their families to notice them, says Per Kristian Eide at the University of Oslo in Norway.

A randomised controlled trial comparing DCLVA against sham surgery is now ongoing. Led by Hui-Sheng Chen at the General Hospital of Shenyang Military Region in China, who didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment, the trial is aiming to recruit 50 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s. Results are expected next year.

Despite previous trials being criticised for not having control groups, some have questioned the ethics of sham surgery. “The risks of any kind of surgery and the accompanying anaesthesia in an elderly and potentially frail population makes the performance of a ‘fake’ intervention very difficult to justify, despite the importance to the overall study,” says Iliff.

Eide, who shares these ethical concerns, also points out that the trial’s protocol says it will look for cognitive improvements four days after the surgery. “You wouldn’t expect any improvement in such a short time,” he says.

It has remained mysterious for millennia, but we’re finally uncovering the profound role the lymphatic system plays in everything from preventing dementia to fighting cancer

Yet the surgery could have one major advantage: it is a one-off intervention. That makes DCLVA worth pursuing, says Vincent Tay at Changi General Hospital, who is involved in the Singapore trial.

Treating Alzheimer’s generally focuses on relieving symptoms, but antibody therapies such as lecanemab that remove beta-amyloid clumps from the brain are approved in the US and the UK. But their questionable efficacy and high cost, partly due to being infused, mean they aren’t available through the UK’s health services. “The upside is this [surgery] is a one-time thing,” says Raag Airan at Stanford University in California.

So, could this procedure one day be routine in China again, and even around the world? “I’m paying close attention to results being published in this space, as is everyone working on this question,” says Iliff.

Wild deer costing Hawke’s Bay farmers tens of thousands of dollars - study

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

A herd of 100 deer can cost farmers more than $10,000 a year. Photo / Alan Gibson

By Alexa Cook of RNZ

A new study of Hawke’s Bay’s wild deer populations has found the problem is costing farmers tens of thousands of dollars.

The research, by primary sector economist Peter MacIntyre, reveals extensive pasture and crop losses from deer, as well as damage to native plantings and bush.

He said wild deer may be causing far greater economic damage to farms than landowners realise.

“There is good evidence from drone and helicopter thermal imaging that many landowners could have five to six times more deer than they think,” MacIntyre said.

“Once deer numbers grow from 50 to 100 and more, the economic damage gets significant, more so if they are getting 100% of their feed from your property.”

Porangahau farmer Sam Stoddart is all too familiar with the problem, with 8000 hectares of bush on his farm boundary.

“There’d be, at an estimate ... 800 plus deer right on our boundary, so a young kale crop will get pulled ... plucked out before it’s had time to establish,” Stoddart said.

He said if those 800 deer grazed on his land, they’d eat about the same as 1200 sheep, which could be making him $145,000 a year.

Instead, with hundreds of wild deer on his land, the farmer has paddocks he can’t put into higher value crops, winter grass that’s being chewed up and native plants that are disappearing.

He said wild deer populations have ballooned over the past 10 years.

“The numbers have just exploded.

“They were released as a bit of game for hunters but were never really controlled, I don’t think by DoC [Department of Conservation] or anything ... now it’s got to the stage where we need some sort of Government intervention.”

He’s one of 14 landowners MacIntyre talked to.

“It was a rather depressing story,” MacIntyre said.

“People had lost a lot of natives, people were losing forage crops.

“It was a pretty sobering story from everybody.”

The research was organised by Marie Taylor from Plant Hawke’s Bay and funded by the Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, the Joan Fernie Charitable Trust and the Pan Pac Environmental Trust.

During the study, a landowner who thought he had 50 deer on his property found nearly 300 with thermal imaging – and Taylor said this highlighted how huge the wild deer problem had become.

“Numbers have increased really exponentially,” she said.

“They are a real limiting factor for all things on-farm, including plantings; they’re also really totalling our biodiversity because they graze species by species, they take most palatable things out of the landscape first.

“Even though the canopy of the forest looks great, we are losing everything underneath.”

The study showed when 100 deer got half of their annual feed requirements from productive pasture, farmers lost more than $10,000 per year.

MacIntyre said over 10 years, using an 8.4% discount rate, that was more than $100,000 in lost value.

“If farmers are losing forage or won’t plant forage because of the likely damage, you can more than double the losses above.”

MacIntyre said new deer fences cost about $40,000 per kilometre and sustained shooting programmes were costly and required ongoing effort.

He calculated that electric fencing added to existing fences would be about $8000 per kilometre.

However, he said accounting for the losses from deer grazing, it became more economically viable to fence.

“If you try to ring-fence your farm it’s going to cost you quite a lot ... If you gang up with your neighbours and ring-fence off the problem area then it’s going to be a lot more cost effective for each farmer,” he said.

Taylor agreed.

“We need to work as catchment groups and put up deer fencing where we can defend the fence,” she said.

“I want to see people working together like they did with possum control areas – that was hugely successful in Hawke’s Bay.”

To achieve that, what is really needed is more funding for conservation and pest control, she said.

“There has been an uncontrolled invasion of feral deer into farmed land from the ranges in Hawke’s Bay with no co-ordinated control programmes and a consequent destruction of years of careful biodiversity planning, planting and management as well as economic loss to farmers.

“Unless DoC does its job properly this situation will only get worse with deer numbers increasing and environmental damage becoming even more significant and economic costs to farmers becoming unsustainable.”

DoC’s wild animals manager Mike Perry told RNZ that DoC actively managed deer in areas where they had the greatest impact on biodiversity, with about 200,000ha of deer management nationwide.

“We acknowledge that wild animal numbers are increasing,” Perry said.

“National monitoring shows ungulates – wild deer, goats, pigs, chamois and tahr – are present at approximately 83% of monitored sites on public conservation land, up from 63% in 2013.

“In response, DoC has significantly increased control efforts across the country in recent years through additional funding provided in Budget 2022, alongside more than $10 million received through the International Visitor Levy.”

DoC said deer management was carried out at several sites across Hawke’s Bay and surrounding areas, such as in the Ruahine Forest Park.

However, Perry said in Hawke’s Bay wild goats posed a greater ecological threat than deer in many conservation areas.

“DoC undertakes goat control across a range of sites in the region and is carrying out extensive work in the northeastern Ruahine Range with the goal of making that part of the park wild goat free.”

He said managing wild animals is a shared responsibility that extended beyond public conservation land.

“Iwi, landowners, hunters, councils, community groups and government agencies all have an important role to play in protecting biodiversity while ensuring sustainable management outcomes across the landscape.”

Professional firefighters reach 50 strikes with no plans to back down

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

Tony Adie said despite reaching the 50th strike, there were no plans to back down. Photo / Michaela Gower

It’s a milestone professional firefighters in Hastings never wanted to reach.

However, with their 50th strike done, they say they have no intention of backing down.

On Friday, firefighters once again spent an hour holding signs outside the Hastings Fire Station outlining the struggles they’re facing.

Career firefighters allege their employer, Fire and Emergency NZ, is providing them with failing equipment and not addressing workplace health and safety concerns.

Hawke’s Bay local secretary for the NZPFU, Tony Adie, said they had not had a pay rise since 2023 and had only been offered low-ball pay rises so far.

Nationally, there have been concerns from the NZ Professional Firefighter Union (NZPFU) that Fire and Emergency NZ is not employing sufficient career firefighters to maintain minimum crew levels.

In Hawke’s Bay, there are 75 career firefighters between the Napier and Hastings stations, a number Adie says is reasonable.

The NZ Professional Firefighters Union is also fighting to get occupational cancer risks faced by firefighters recognised.

Fire and Emergency NZ says it has been trying to get to the negotiating table, but has been stymied by the NZPFU.

It says the strikes are “reckless” and the union’s demands “not financially realistic”.

Career firefighters first went on strike in October 2025, with slogans painted on fire trucks from August to highlight “dire” concerns about the old and unreliable vehicles, markings that remain on the trucks.

Adie said the number of strikes wasn’t a good milestone to reach.

“It’s 50 strikes too many; at the end of the day it’s not a celebration, we shouldn’t be here at all.

“I worry every time we walk out there for an hour; I just hope nothing happens ... we have got a lot on our shoulders.”

He said any pay rise offer would need to include allowances and backdating to be accepted.

The NZPFU said trainee firefighters currently start on $56,500 and once on a fire station, earn $60,500.

A firefighter with at least four years’ experience and two more levels of qualifications has a base salary of $80,682.

Fire and Emergency NZ acting deputy national commander Ken Cooper said its most recent offer compared favourably with other public sector settlements.

Cooper said the offer would have delivered firefighters a 2.2% salary increase from December 1, 2025 and 2.2% from January 1, 2027, over a 24-month term to the end of November 2027.

Aide said NZPFU needed an offer worth discussing to call the strikes off.

He said he felt there had been “no real give and take” with Fire and Emergency NZ during the industrial action process.

Cooper said Fire and Emergency NZ remained committed to a fair and sustainable settlement.

“Most recently, the Employment Relations Authority [ERA] proposed both parties exchange their full revised bargaining positions at the same time, to help assess whether further facilitation is likely to assist.

“We agreed to this. The NZPFU did not.

“We continue to urge the NZPFU to call off these reckless strikes and engage with us and the ERA to try and come to a resolution so that their members can get the pay increases they deserve, and we can continue working together to keep communities safe.”

He said their offer would have come at a cost to Fire and Emergency NZ of roughly $50m over four years.

“By comparison, the NZPFU’s settlement proposal was for more than $130 million over the same period.

“That is not financially realistic at a time where we also have to keep investing in the trucks and equipment our people need to do their jobs safely.”

Cooper said advice for further strikes remained the same for the public.

“If there is a fire, get out early, stay out, then call 111.”

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

Lake Rotoiti residents are considering taking Rotorua Lakes Council to the High Court over its decision to approve a papakāinga housing development without public notification.

The council says the application did not meet the legal threshold for public notification and it is confident it followed the correct process.

Meanwhile, landowners have rejected the residents’ suggestion the project is the first stage of a much larger development.

The decision granted land-use consent for 28 papakāinga, or communal housing, units on Whangamoa Trust land opposite Ōtaramarae Marae on Whangamoa Drive.

The land is at the southern end of the Lake Rotoiti village off State Highway 33, near Ōkere Falls.

The consent was lodged in March last year and approved in December.

It allows for the construction of the 28 units, along with a playground, basketball court, parking, stormwater infrastructure and a community building.

Tim Manning, the spokesman for the Rotoiti residents’ group, said the community was not opposed to papakāinga development, but believed it should have had an opportunity to participate in the consent process.

“It’s not a not-in-my-backyard thing,” Manning said.

“It’s just let’s do it properly. If you’re going to do it, let’s notify it.”

Manning said about 85 residents supported the group’s campaign.

“The community have said to me, have one more go at trying to get the trust to have a big hui and talk to us. If that works, good. If not, we’ll go down the judicial review route.”

A legal letter sent to the council by lawyers representing the residents said the community had “good grounds for a judicial review”.

The letter argued the combined effects of future stages may not have been fully assessed, claiming the current consent was the first stage for a larger proposal. It said the council’s District Plan provided for up to 70 owners’ sites on the land.

Residents also raised concerns about traffic, environmental and cultural impacts.

Manning said residents believed they had twice been denied the opportunity to participate – first when the planning framework was established more than a decade ago, and again when the first stage of the papakāinga was approved on a non-notified basis.

He said a final letter appealing for “meaningful community consultation” was to be sent to the council and the trust next week. If this failed, he said the residents “will proceed” with legal proceedings.

Whangamoa Trust chairman James Schuster said the development was intended to provide housing for owners of the Māori land block and their whānau, not a wider residential subdivision.

“We’re just using a small corner up by the marae,” Schuster said.

“So that people from the marae can come back and live by there.”

Schuster rejected suggestions the development was the first stage of a much larger project.

“We’re not looking to develop the rest of the block,” he said.

“We’ve got quite a big farm area that is no longer in use, but there are no big development plans for any new suburbs.”

Schuster said the trust consulted leaseholders before lodging the application but the rest of the notification process was left in the council’s hands.

He could not give a timeline on the development.

The council’s destination development manager Jean-Paul Gaston said residents were not advised of the consent decision because the application was processed on a non-notified basis.

The council referred Local Democracy Reporting to the planner’s report, which found the proposal’s adverse effects would be less than minor and public notification was therefore not required.

The report also considered district planning provisions at the location that allow for residential builds, as well as potential tourism accommodation.

Gaston rejected suggestions the council should have assessed a larger development proposal and said the council can only consider the application in front of it.

“No application has been received for a bigger dwelling development area.”

A separate resource consent application to Bay of Plenty Regional Council for associated earthworks, stormwater discharges and wetland modifications was on hold.

Regional council consents manager Ella Tennent said the assessment had taken longer than expected due to “information gaps” in the original application, requiring further details from the applicant and its consultants.

She said further information had been requested on ecology, erosion and sediment control, stormwater, geotechnical matters, cultural considerations, planning compliance and contaminated land.

“At this stage, it is difficult to provide a reliable timeframe for a decision,” she said.

The council needed more information before it could determine whether neighbouring owners or other parties were affected.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

For the fourth time, Chris Brazendale needs his fence fixed after a car crashed into it.

Brazendale’s family has lived on the corner of a “very busy” roundabout at the intersection of Waihi, Otūmoetai and Cambridge Rds in Judea for 16 years.

He said crashes at the roundabout were “a regular thing”.

“It’s kind of a worry.”

The most recent incident on Tuesday last week involved two vehicles, one of which ended up on a transformer box, causing a power outage.

“My wife and I were home, and we heard the initial bang and then the second one a split second later of the car hitting the fence,” Brazendale said.

He said a vehicle hit the fence in about the same spot last year, causing minor damage.

Brazendale said in 2016, a young motorist took out the fence at the other end of the house by the garage, narrowly missing vehicles parked in the driveway.

In 2013, a motorist hit the fence and power box, causing a power outage.

And in 2012, a motorist crashed at roughly the same spot as last week’s incident – but went through the fence and into the back yard.

Brazendale said his insurance covered all repair costs, but the incidents made him feel unsafe.

His house was about 3m from the fence.

He said he worried a car might hit the house, or worse – one of his three boys or his wife, Koralee.

She had talked about moving because of the frequent accidents, he said.

Brazendale suspected drivers were entering the roundabout too quickly and not seeing other vehicles.

He said visibility was not great when approaching the roundabout, up the hill on Otūmoetai Rd.

He estimated there were accidents on the roundabout once a month, and told Local Democracy Reporting he wanted something done about it.

He said there was one incident at the house on the other side of the roundabout, where a motorist drove up the bank and through the fence.

“A few years ago, a chap got knocked off his bike and had to be taken to hospital. I was at work that time but my wife remembers it.”

In 2019, Brazendale asked the Tauranga City Council to help make the intersection safer.

He said the council changed the road layout to a one-lane approach, but he did not believe it made a difference.

Brazendale believed speed bumps or traffic lights would be the best solution.

Neighbour Dan Allen-Gordon said his family had attended many accidents in 25 years living near the roundabout.

He said his wife’s car was written off five years ago when a car crashed into it about 50 metres from the roundabout.

“We were out of pocket around $6000 as we had to replace the car that was written off.”

He said it happened early in the morning and a neighbour tried to get the vehicle’s occupants to stay, but they ran off, leaving behind bottles and a car smelling of alcohol.

“There have been many accidents at the roundabout, even after work was done to make it larger.”

He said a steel light pole at the entrance from Otūmoetai Rd had been taken down twice by cars.

In his opinion, the solution would be an intersection with lights.

Tauranga City Council transport strategy and assurance manager Karen Hay said the council recently undertook a high-level review of the intersection using recent crash data.

“The outcome was that further investigation was needed into potential minor improvements, such as line marking and signage.”

The investigation was expected to be completed by the end of August.

She said there had been 54 crashes at the roundabout in the six years since improvements were made in 2019, including 13 that resulted in injuries.

Police referred Local Democracy Reporting questions about crashes at the roundabout to be considered through an Official Information Act process.

Asked if police had spoken to the council about safety at the roundabout, Western Bay of Plenty road policing manager Senior Sergeant Wayne Hunter said police regularly worked with partner agencies to try to make sure roads were as safe as possible.

He said motorists approaching intersections should ensure they followed the road signs and checked it was clear before proceeding.

Ayla Yeoman is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based in Tauranga. She holds a Bachelor of Arts majoring in communications, politics and international relations from the University of Auckland, and has been a journalist since 2022.

Pakūranga College mourns maths teacher Dr David Hofman

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

Pakūranga College teacher Dr Dave Hofman died after a battle with cancer. Photo / Pakūranga College

An East Auckland school community is grieving the sudden death of one of its veteran teachers.

Pakūranga College announced the death of Dr David Hofman in a Facebook post on Monday afternoon, saying he had died over the weekend after a “brave, private battle with cancer”.

Hofman, a longstanding member of the maths faculty, was remembered by the college as a devoted and genuine educator who strove to make maths accessible to students.

“Dr Hofman was kind, incredibly intelligent, and had a wonderfully quirky sense of humour!” it wrote.

“He built genuine relationships with students; he cared deeply about them, and they absolutely loved being taught by him.

“His sense of humour was appreciated by staff and students alike.”

Despite undergoing treatment, Hofman remained committed to teaching.

Encouraged by colleagues last week to take some time off for himself, he said: “I need to be at school. I need that mental stimulation. I can’t let my students down.”

The school said his response captured the essence of his character.

“He cared deeply about his students and about this place.

“He truly enjoyed coming to work and being a humble, humorous, and hard-working member of the Pakūranga College whānau.”

Hofman’s classes inspired and made maths “accessible” to “countless students”, the school wrote.

Several of Hofman’s students wrote tributes that were shared online by the school.

“Dr Hofman for the win!” one remarked.

“He made sure we had a clear understanding of each topic,” another student wrote, adding Hofman would also stop to ask how students were doing when he saw them around school.

Others credited Hofman with helping them achieve better grades, saying he used “various techniques” and a “patient approach” to explain difficult concepts and always made time to help confused students.

His humour and approachable nature were also touched on.

“I want to show appreciation for Dr Hofman’s fun/funny personality and the way he teaches and builds relationships with students,” one wrote.

The school’s message was signed off with the traditional Jewish blessing “Zichrono Livrachah”, which means, “may his memory be a blessing”.

Whakatāne jewellery robbery: Three arrested, stolen property recovered

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

Police deployed road spikes in an attempt to stop a vehicle believed to be involved in the crime. Photo / NZME

Three people have been arrested following an aggravated robbery at a Whakatāne jewellery store on Monday afternoon.

Police were called to a business on The Strand at about 3.40pm after three masked offenders entered the store and fled with stolen property.

Eastern Bay of Plenty area commander Inspector Nicky Cooney said staff managed to escape through a rear door and were unharmed during the incident.

Armed police responded as a precaution, but the offenders had fled in a stolen vehicle before officers arrived.

Cooney said police immediately launched a search, aided by information from members of the public who quickly reported details of the getaway vehicle.

“Information about the alleged offenders’ vehicle was provided to Whakatāne Police almost immediately after the robbery, and that was crucial in helping direct resources to locate those involved,” Cooney said.

The vehicle was later spotted by Murupara police on State Highway 38, triggering a co-ordinated response involving officers from across the Bay of Plenty.

Police deployed road spikes and positioned patrol units ahead of the vehicle. It was successfully spiked and brought to a stop near a busy roundabout.

Three of the four alleged offenders were arrested at the scene.

Police also recovered property believed to have been stolen during the robbery, with several items of evidential value.

The alleged offenders, aged 16, 18 and 19, are due to appear in Rotorua Youth Court today charged with aggravated robbery.

Cooney praised the efforts of officers and the public, saying the arrests highlighted the value of timely information and co-ordinated policing.

“The quick-thinking actions of people who contacted police immediately after the robbery, combined with the efforts of staff and officers across the district, were instrumental in achieving a safe outcome,” she said.

She also acknowledged Whakatāne staff who identified the vehicle, the Murupara officers who located it and Rotorua police who provided tactical support during the pursuit.

Police inquiries are continuing and further arrests have not been ruled out.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Police via 105, online or by quoting file number 260803/7537. Information can also be provided anonymously through Crime Stoppers on 0800 555 111.

National Party Deputy leader Nicola Willis defended her leader this morning, saying Christopher Luxon’s decision to apologise for remarks made to Rotorua businesses would not cause another round of leadership speculation.

“We have a very capable Prime Minister leading the country in what are challenging times, making the decisions to ensure we are moving forward,” Willis told the Mike Hosking Breakfast on Newstalk ZB.

Luxon apologised on Monday after last week describing a business community’s concerns as taking a “negative view” and saying they should be acting like an “adult”. He said there was a “parent-child mentality” between government and business.

Willis said Luxon’s apology did him credit by acknowledging an error.

“I think this is about his integrity, which is that, yes, he stands by his philosophy, but equally where he thinks he’s caused offence he’s going to fess up and apologise – good on him.”

Asked by host Mike Hosking whether she gave Luxon an “ear bashing” at Monday morning’s Cabinet meeting, Willis said: “No, there was no ear bashing at Cabinet.

“It’s the mark of the man, as the Rotorua Mayor has reflected this morning. He was simply sorry that his comments hadn’t acknowledged the challenge that many small businesses face that sit outside their control, and he wanted to be clear and he understands that.

“Equally it remains his position and the Government’s position that the way through New Zealand’s economic challenges is not to be subsidising businesses – that’s long been our position.”

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell, who has previously run as a National candidate, told RNZ that there was no need for Luxon to apologise.

“I don’t think it’s a time for our leaders in New Zealand to be soft. We need to know the truth. We need to be honest, and we need to set a pathway forward,” Tapsell said.

National MPs are arriving at Parliament this morning for their caucus meeting, which occurs every Tuesday morning when Parliament is sitting.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said he supported the Prime Minister, and that Luxon himself had made clear that “the words didn’t come out quite right” at the Rotorua event.

“The words didn’t come out quite right and obviously we’re hugely supportive of small businesses up and down the country,” Goldsmith said.

Goldsmith said Luxon was right to apologise.

“The words that came out gave the impression that we don’t support small businesses – of course we do.

“These things happen.”

Simeon Brown, the National campaign chair, repeatedly said Luxon had apologised for the remarks when asked what he thought of them.

He said that was the “end of the matter”, but, when the Herald pushed back, saying some businesses may believe those comments reflect how Luxon thinks about them, Brown said no one backs small business more than National.

Brown questioned Labour’s commitment to business, saying that while the political party may be posting a lot on social media, they hadn’t explained how they would fund their promises. He also asked whether they would keep the Government’s Investment Boost scheme.

“So it might be all well and good for Labour to get on their Facebook pages and make all sorts of high and mighty remarks, but the real question is, will they keep it or will they axe it?”

Brown said he fully backed Luxon and denied the comments had hurt the National leader’s relationship with business.

He also said there would be no leadership challenge.

Defence Minister Chris Penk said there was no chatter over the weekend about a leadership change.

Penk said everyone can occasionally misspeak.

“Every person is capable of misspeaking – we’ve all done it. In this case, he didn’t mean to come across in the way some had said that he did.”

Grant McCallum, National’s Northland MP, also said he supported the Prime Minister.

Asked what small businesses in Northland would think of Luxon’s remarks, McCallum said they would be “delighted we are building a new highway, $3.5 billion worth of investment – it’s going to transform Northland”.

“Of course I support the Prime Minister,” McCallum said.

Suze Redmayne, the party’s junior whip, said Luxon’s actions showed he supported small business, noting he regularly visited businesses.

West Coast-Tasman MP Maureen Pugh said she had not seen Luxon’s remarks about small business because she had left her phone for “three days” and had been unable to read the news.

List MP Nancy Lu said the Prime Minister was right to apologise but that the party “backed small businesses” with policies like Investment Boost.

Hamilton East MP Ryan Hamilton said the Prime Minister’s remarks were “pretty straight down the middle, but he’s apologised for them nonetheless”.

MPs were also asked whether they believed remarks made by Foreign Minister Winston Peters about Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan were racist.

Xu-Nan was born in China but has lived in New Zealand since 1994. Peters unloaded on Xu-Nan in the debating chamber last week telling him to “go back” to his “own country”.

National Party Junior Whip Suze Redmayne was asked three times whether Peters’ remarks were racist. Initially, she did not respond, but when asked whether her constituents might want to hear her view on the comments, Redmayne said “yeah, I’d agree they were racist comments”.

Asked whether it was okay for Peters to stay in Cabinet, Redmayne said “it’s not my Cabinet”.

Pugh said Peters’ remarks were “very ill-conceived”.

Lu, asked about Peters’ comments, said she believed they were racist.

Commerce Minister Cameron Brewer said “the Prime Minister has made clear, those comments were racist and we’ve just got to move on”.

Hamilton said that it was close enough to the election that “voters will make their own minds up” about Peters’ comments.

At least 10 police staff face criminal charges after anti-corruption investigation

New Zealand Herald August 03, 2026

As of May, there were about 40 staff under investigation by the police's anti-corruption unit. Photo / RNZ, Richard Tindiller

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

A police staff member accused of kidnapping and sexual offending is among at least 10 staff facing criminal charges following investigations by the police’s anti-corruption unit, RNZ can reveal.

Other staff are before the courts charged with firearms trafficking-related offending, drug supply, and another staffer is charged with assault, blackmail, threats and damage.

As of May, there were about 40 staff under investigation by the unit.

The National Integrity Unit (NIU) was established in 2020, with then-Police Commissioner Mike Bush saying it had been created to “bolster Police’s capability in protecting against the risk of corruption and, where appropriate, investigating corruption within New Zealand Police”.

In May, RNZ requested under the Official Information Act the total number of cases investigated by the NIU since it was established, as well as the total number of active cases.

The information – which was initially due in June – was provided to RNZ on Friday.

In the response, director of integrity and conduct Detective Superintendent Kylie Schaare said the NIU received information from a wide variety of sources, much of it often incomplete or unverified.

“Each piece of information is recorded as a ‘matter’ and undergoes preliminary assessment. A matter may be progressed to a criminal investigation where it can be corroborated or expanded or, it may be closed as having no substance or insufficient merit.”

From January 2020 to May 2026, 117 “matters” had progressed to investigations, with no further action taken by the NIU.

“This generally reflects cases where there is no evidence of criminal offending or there is insufficient evidence for a prosecution.

“However, this does not preclude action being taken by other Police work groups, such as employment investigations or preventative interventions at a district level.”

During the same time period, 22 prosecutions have commenced following NIU investigations.

Of those, 12 are no longer before the courts. This includes one staffer being convicted for cocaine supply, corrupt use of official information and computer access offending. Three staff have been convicted for accessing a computer system for a dishonest purpose.

There were 10 staff before the courts as of May following NIU investigations.

This group includes a staffer facing “multiple serious offences” including firearms, violence, kidnapping and sexual offending. One staff member is charged with firearms trafficking-related offending, while another is charged with assault, blackmail, threats and damage.

Other charges faced by other staff include Passport Act offences, drug supply and obtaining by deception.

There were 39 active NIU investigations underway as of May 11.

RNZ asked police for further information on the cases before the courts.

A spokesperson replied: “As the matter is before the court, we are unable to provide any further information or comment in relation to the active criminal proceedings”.

RNZ earlier requested under the Official Information Act the total number of police staff under investigation, both criminal and employment as well as how long they had been under investigation for.

Figures released reveal that as of June 18 there were 271 open investigations involving 325 police employees. One hundred and nine are listed as an employment process only, the rest involve both employment and criminal matters.

Seven of the investigations had been open for more than 1000 days, including two staff who had been under investigation for 1542 days. Nearly 30 investigations were older than 500 days.

Allegations included perjury, manual use of force, such as striking, kicking or restraining, conflict of interest, drugs/alcohol and disgraceful behaviour.

There were 33 staff under investigation for sexual misconduct. Six of those had been going on for more than 500 days.

In response to questions about the figures, NZ Police acting chief operating officer Leigh MacDonald said allegations of sexual misconduct were taken seriously, regardless of who was involved.

“The message is clear – nobody is above the law or the standards expected of police employees.

“Every member of police’s more than 16,000 staff is expected to act with integrity and professionalism and will be held to account where misconduct is established.”

Police did not believe the figures indicated a widespread issue across the organisation, MacDonald said.

“The number of staff linked to these allegations represents a very small proportion of the police workforce. At the same time, it is important that people feel able to raise concerns, and that those concerns are listened to and assessed or investigated appropriately.”

- RNZ

Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month

Sydney Morning Herald August 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street.

Sophie, Standing ThereMeg MasonFourth Estate, $34.99, out nowSorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques.

BlackbirdingRyan ButtaSimon & Schuster, $36.99, out nowThe term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking.

Time Travel for BeginnersJaclyn MoriartyUltimo, $34.99, out nowJaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.”

Screw NiceAmy RemeikisHachette, $34.99, out nowPolitical analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”

Now, AutonomyMax EastonGiramondo, $32.95, out nowIf you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria.

Nuclear ArchipelagoElizabeth TynanNewSouth, $39.99, out nowThe third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”.

MineAdam OustonTransit Lounge, $$34.99, out nowDon’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide.

The HurtCatherine de Saint PhalleTransit Lounge, $32.99, out nowWhen she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”.

Realms of GoldA. J. MackinnonBlack Inc., $36.99, out August 4Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A. J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice.

Eye of the NeedleChristopher RajaText, $34.99, out August 4The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

HeresiesRichard FlanaganPenguin, $36.99, out August 4The Booker winner has never been shy about voicing his opinions, whether in print or on stage at writers festivals or elsewhere. He’s always enlivening − even if you disagree with him. This collection of pieces, published in a variety of outlets, ranges over the past 10 years or so. While Flanagan says that “writing, at its best, exists beyond morality and politics”, he takes a strongly moral position, whether he’s writing about cancel culture, Manus Island, Jillian Segal’s antisemitism report, free speech or salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour.

Alice’s DreamingTom GriffithsBlack Inc., $36.99, out August 11Historian Tom Griffiths tells the story of the writer Alice Duncan-Kemp, who was born on a station in Queensland in 1901. Her father died early and her mother stayed on the property, with Alice and her sisters finding friends among the Mithaka people and guidance from a remarkable Indigenous man, Moses Yoolpee, and others. There is some ambiguity about the source of her knowledge and the veracity of some of her writing, but nevertheless, writes Griffiths, she “participated in the most profound and important of Australian conversations” between Indigenous individuals and curious newcomers.

Three ShocksGeorge MegalogenisPenguin, $36.99, out August 18In the decade between the GFC and the pandemic, Australia became a majority migrant nation, saw the feminisation of the economy, and found that the interests of both its greatest ally and, separately, its largest trading partner, were no longer complementary to its own, says political scientist George Megalogenis. In the final of his detailed and characteristically accessible trilogy examining Australia’s diverse citizenry and place in the world, Megalogenis stresses the need for connection between city and country and, indeed, all Australians.

The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

Melbourne’s worst-kept secret: Behind the celebrity trappings, Ralph Carr was known simply as ‘The Rug’

Sydney Morning Herald August 04, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The conviction of veteran artist and sports manager Ralph Carr for rape was one of Melbourne’s worst-kept secrets.

What was also well known to many who had crossed paths with the celebrity manager was that Carr was a small man with an enormous ego, prone to bullying and manipulative behaviour.

He loved to surround himself with the trappings of success and the famous, but was difficult to work with and chaotic.

One former staffer went so far as to describe Carr as “revolting” and “a master manipulator”.

Carr’s conviction, and the lifting of a near three-year suppression order, has opened the floodgates for many in the music and sporting worlds who have long held a dim view of the man they dubbed “The Rug”.

One woman, who worked at Ralph Carr Management in the mid-2010s while in her early 20s, described her tenure there as “an awful and confusing time”, saying she and other staff experienced “outrageous bullying” from him.

“I saw some pretty terrible things,” she told this masthead while asking to speak anonymously to protect her employment. “None of it was nice … his behaviour was revolting.”

The former employee said news that Carr, 66, had been found guilty by a jury of one count of sexual assault and two counts of rape would trigger uncomfortable and difficult memories for many women.

“The past 24 hours have been very confronting,” she said. “There is the sexual predator side, but also the toxic work culture.

“This is about a pattern of behaviour. There are multiple women with stories about things that have gone on.”

Carr continues to strenuously deny he committed any crime, and his lawyer, Dermot Dann, KC, told the County Court on Monday his client planned to appeal against the verdict.

Carr’s Instagram account is filled with photos of his famous and wealthy friends and clients.

In one image, the twice-married and twice-divorced father of three is smiling arm-in-arm with country rock star Keith Urban. In others, he poses with supermodel Miranda Kerr, shares a drink with Molly Meldrum, and another with Nine entertainment reporter Richard Wilkins.

Then there’s Carr at the Brownlow Medal night with Dustin Martin, the champion Richmond footballer who was his prized celebrity management client.

Carr had been the man behind the AFL great when Martin was part of three premiership wins with the Tigers and won the 2017 Brownlow Medal.

The pair were more than just manager and client. They were close friends and business associates, having invested together in several, multimillion-dollar commercial properties in Melbourne.

However, like Carr’s freedom that relationship is now in tatters.

In a statement, Martin said he was “shocked to learn of the outcome of the court proceedings”.

“I had no knowledge whatsoever of the conduct that led to these convictions,” the footy great said.

“My thoughts are with those affected. Effective immediately, I have ended my professional relationship with my former manager. As this is a legal matter, I will not be making any further comment.”

While Martin was Carr’s sporting ace in the pack, over the years he also represented a who’s who of stars from across the music industry – including his ex-wife, Tina Arena, former Noiseworks frontman Jon Stevens, Kate Ceberano, Bonnie Anderson, Vanessa Amorosi and Rick Price. He also represented actor Madeleine West, magician Cosentino, Wilkins and singer Mark Vincent who ended up fighting with Carr in the County Court over money.

Carr also worked with Priscilla Presley when she visited Australia on a speaking tour, escorting her to Flemington for the Melbourne Cup.

Famously, Carr married former Young Talent Time star Tina Arena in 1995. The couple divorced a little over four years later in what was a messy split.

He had been her manager from 1992, with Arena later describing the union in memoirs and interviews as more of a complex business dynamic than a traditional romantic connection.

They no longer speak, with Arena reporting that the marriage left her financially devastated and reduced her net worth to zero after years of work.

In the AFL, Carr made a splash running his Richmond-based agency, Ralph Carr Management Sport. He was a Carlton Football Club director, serving on the board from December 2006 until October 2008, and remains a fanatical supporter of the Blues.

His official player agent accreditation, through the AFL Players Association, was likely to be revoked following his conviction, said a fellow player agent, speaking anonymously to talk freely.

Carr enjoyed prominence when it came to hardball, headline-grabbing contract negotiations.

One industry source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the colourful Carr had brought a “Hollywood” vibe to the managerial role, befitting his background in the entertainment industry. He was also dubbed “The Rug” in some circles, because of the distinct black toupee which he still sported in court.

Ralph Carr unmasked as man found guilty of rape

Prominent entertainment and sports agent Ralph Carr has been unmasked as the man who was convicted of raping a younger woman in his own home in Victoria.

Carr played the “media game” with a flourish, although, at times, it could seem chaotic, generating regular headlines. The industry source described him as staunch in his determination to deliver for his clients when fronting club powerbrokers, even if that ultimately left them in an uncomfortable situation with their employers.

He had stints managing former Tigers Shai Bolton, Daniel Rioli and Mabior Chol earlier in their careers.

While Carr’s stubbornness often paid dividends for his clients, even as recently as last year his ability to irritate was also on show.

Carr endured the wrath of AFL headquarters when he all but broke the news that Snoop Dogg would perform at the grand final – going public with a none-too-subtle post on his LinkedIn page 12 days before the league made its announcement.

“Representing Snoop Dogg for his visit to Australia”, read the post, which was deleted shortly after. “I am looking for brand alinement (sic) and corporate opportunities ...”

On former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire’s podcast, Eddie and Jimmy, McGuire said the AFL had been unimpressed with Carr, the latter having “had his nose severely pulled by the AFL saying: ‘Our announcement, dickhead, not yours’.”

McGuire added: “They weren’t happy that he was suddenly sending out to every person in the media that this was a done deal. That went down like a lead balloon.”

Carr, who is awaiting sentencing, looks to have been preparing financially for a change in his circumstances for some time.

As his rape trial unfolded, the mortgage on at least one property owned by him in Richmond was adjusted, while another property in Abbotsford to which he is linked was listed for sale with a $2.5 million price tag.

In the week before the guilty verdict was handed down, Carr also took out a fresh mortgage on a property that he had purchased in West Melbourne in 2021 for $4.1 million.

On the day of the jury verdict, Carr remained a director of 16 corporate vehicles. Under corporations law, only individuals with criminal convictions involving dishonesty are automatically disqualified from being a company director. This means Carr may not need to resign these roles, although his fast and fashionable universe is certainly changed forever.

Alongside his rock star-aligned lifestyle, Carr also professes a profound faith. His Instagram grid is interspersed with images and graphics featuring the crucifix, love hearts and words including “Jesus saves” and “Jesus equals love”.

“Each day is a gift and every breath is a reminder of God’s grace,” one post reads.

“From the time I was a child, I’ve carried deep faith in my heart – one that has guided me through every season of life and will never leave me,” says another from mid-last year.

On Monday, Wilkins, who said he hadn’t had anything to do with Carr for many years, summed up the thoughts of many in the entertainment industry: “I am obviously appalled ... my thoughts are with the victim.”

US states sue Trump administration over new tariffs on 60 trading partners

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 21:34:28 GMT

Coalition of 25 states ask the US Court of International Trade to halt tariffs, calling them unlawful

Trump imposes fresh tariffs on dozens of trading partners

A coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration on Monday over new tariffs pegged at 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the supreme court in February.

The states are asking the US Court of International Trade to halt the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid.

According to the states involved in the action, tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union imposed last month account for 99.4% of US imports. The Trump administration officials have charged that the countries have not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor.

“After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs,” New York attorney general Letitia James said in a statement.

“No matter how the administration tries to justify it, the law and our Constitution are clear that the president does not have the power to impose sweeping tariffs on whatever countries he wants,” James added.

In addition to New York, the states joining the action are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

The new tariffs went into effect in July after “Liberation Day” tariffs were ruled unconstitutional in February and a new set of temporary tariffs expired.

The latest proposal for tariffs uses Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a federal law meant to target countries that use forced labor. The new tariffs affect major trading partners including Canada, Japan, Norway, Taiwan and China.

The lawsuit follows a separate suit filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of two US small businesses who argue that Trump exceeded his executive authority with the new tariffs.

“The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said. “A foreign country’s failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed. Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President’s first term, and they remain so now.”

The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, and the state attorney general argue that the administration’s tariffs based on “a supposed investigation into countries’ efforts to combat forced labor do not satisfy the requirements of Section 301”, they said in a statement.

They said that the administration is using “forced labor” as an excuse to continue its policy of indiscriminately enacting damaging tariffs on a wide range of countries that lead to higher prices for their constituents.

“President Trump’s illegal tariffs are nothing more than a tax on hardworking families, driving up the cost of groceries, household essentials, building materials, and countless everyday goods that New Yorkers rely on,” Hochul said. “The Supreme Court has made it clear that this administration cannot ignore the law to impose sweeping tariffs.”

Rapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PM

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 21:30:03 GMT

Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October

Rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from early release plans to ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.

The prime minister said on Tuesday that he will delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales by a month until October.

But he will still allow domestic abusers and killers to go free including two men jailed for their role in the death of PC Andrew Harper.

The decision will put the lives of women and girls “at risk” and has “let down” serving police officers, a watchdog and a pressure group have warned.

It follows the suspension of Keir Starmer’s plans to release up to 6,000 offenders from prison early in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.

Burnham suspended the scheme in his second week as PM after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.

In a statement, Burnham said: “I asked for an urgent review of the prisoner release scheme. I fully understand the anger, anxiety and distress that’s been caused. I’ve heard that loud and clear. That’s why we’re making significant changes: offenders who have been sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences will be excluded from the changes.”

The Ministry of Justice has declined to release the numbers of prisoners who will no longer be freed as a result of Burnham’s intervention.

It has also declined to say when its own internal modelling predicts that prisons will be full again, and if there are already plans for further early release schemes.

The domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, said the decision to exclude those who have abused their partners was “wrong” and “puts victims’ lives at risk”.

“As I told the lord chancellor just last week, the danger perpetrators pose to their victim should not be underestimated. These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.

“Measures that will keep domestic abuse victims safe still appear to be an afterthought.”

Andrea Simon, the London victim’s commissioner said the failure was concerning, given a shortage of probation officers with experience of handling complex offenders.

“This will alarm many survivors of abuse that are desperately concerned about their safety, particularly when there are real challenges in delivering tougher community supervision,” she said.

An early release scheme in 2024 included specific protections for victims of domestic abuse.

Victims’ groups had objected to the proposal for 6,000 people to be freed early from September under the new Sentencing Act. Debbie Adlam, the mother of the police officer Andrew Harper, said last month that the proposed inclusion of two of her son’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – was “another letdown” for their family.

Prisoners serving longer sentences of four years or more would be eligible for release at the halfway point of their term, rather than at two-thirds as had previously been the case.

The changes were due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of less than 575 days, going up to prisoners jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June next year.

The government has said that, after listening to victims’ concerns, rapists and child sexual offenders will not be eligible for the sentencing changes.

Prisoners serving time for some sexual or violent offences where the automatic release stage is set at two-thirds will become eligible for release at the halfway point, provided they have not committed serious breaches of prison rules.

This applies to Bowers and Cole, two of Harper’s killers who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter. Henry Long, the main perpetrator, will not be subject to early release.

Tiff Lynch, national chair of the Police Federation, said: “Allowing those who take an officer’s life to be released earlier to save the prison system from collapsing gravely risks undermining not only public safety but public confidence, causing real distress to bereaved families and sending entirely the wrong message about the value we place on those who protect us. The government must urgently rethink this decision.”

The Ministry of Justice also announced a £10m package for victim support and said the new justice secretary Alex Norris would look at reviewing “outdated” Imprisonment for Public Protection [IPP] sentences.

Other community measures will be put in place to protect victims of crime including tougher periods of supervision and restriction zones for offenders, Burnham said.

“I wanted to go even further as I know there will still be concerns about other offenders having their sentence shortened. But it’s not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing, which would put public safety at much greater risk,” Burnham said.

The announcement follows days of wrangling inside the Ministry of Justice and No 10 over how to calm public anger while still ensuring that the criminal justice system does not seize up.

Prisons have become a major point of political contention, with Labour blaming the Conservatives for creating the overcrowding crisis by increasing sentences while failing to build enough jails.

Responding to Burnham’s announcement, the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said: “Labour whipped their MPs to vote to let rapists, paedophiles, and grooming gang perpetrators out of prison early.

“Now they admit the Conservative campaign to stop this was right – this is a victory for victims.

“But their U-turn doesn’t go far enough. Some child sex offenders and killers, like those responsible for the death of PC Harper, will still be released early. And the trauma of victims being told their abusers may be released can’t be undone.

“One of Andy Burnham’s first acts as prime minister will be to let thousands of criminals – including killers and paedophiles – out early.”

Celebrity Hunted review – if this lot can outwit our national security, we’re all in trouble

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 21:00:03 GMT

This near-hour of frothing wildness, in aid of Stand Up to Cancer, is utter chaos – interspersed with awareness-raising videos full of dignity and grace

If it’s early August, it must be Celebrity Hunted’s annual series in aid of the charity Stand Up to Cancer. The dozen famouses must evade capture for two weeks, which is a shorter time than civilians are required to manage it. Is it because celebrity schedules are fuller or their brains emptier? By the end of the first couple of episodes, I know which way I’m leaning.

The contestants, working in six pairs, include Britain’s last vaudevillian Brian Conley (“I’m like a coiled sponge!”) and his daughter Lucy (“Dad! Stop being funny”), TV property presenter siblings – a sort of hyphenate from hell – Scarlette and Stuart Douglas, plus comedians Jen Brister and Laura Smyth. In a game where predictability is the greatest – well, predictor – of failure, they may have the best plan. “I’m just not going to take my HRT for a week and let’s see what happens,” says Jen.

At Hunter HQ, Ray Howard (whose every feature still suggests thrillingly that only this gainful and well-publicised employment is keeping him from laying waste to everyone within a 50-mile radius, and I for one am going into hiding the minute he is forced to retire) has gathered his team about him. As ever, it comprises ex-police and military types, counter-terrorist dooberries, cyberwhatsits, analysts and profilers. The last two are vital because no one else is qualified to say things such as: “They will be using the networks they have,” “They could be hiding in plain sight,” or, if operating at peak performance levels, “They may have gone out the back way.” These all-seeing gods direct the “ground hunters” as to where best they might cut the fugitives off at the pass, and they do it expertly badly.

No matter how dim a prey may be – and God love the brace of children from Love Island, Chris and Toby, who dutifully tap in and out at the end of their Transport for London journeys and show HQ exactly where they are – the predator can be counted on to be dimmer, for at least as long as the producer needs them to be.

The Douglases go on a live morning news programme to promote their new show but – oh, they are whisked away in a taxi just in time to avoid capture!

Jen appears at a well-advertised gig in Brighton (“Jen is appearing at a well-advertised gig in Brighton!” announces one analyst, pretty much) but happens to have 400 Jen masks ready-printed (though not ready-strung with the necessary elastic) for the audience, to confuse any pursuers.

Brian calls his friend and member of “the Prat Pack” Joe Pasquale on a phone he knows is tapped and gives him the time and address at which to collect him and Lucy. “Sometimes it’s gruelling and analytical work,” grins Howard’s right-hand man Dr Steve Hersee. “And sometimes they just tell you exactly where they are.” The Conleys still escape, though. This is where you find yourself hoping fervently that it is all exactly as staged as it looks. Because if the people in charge of our national safety and security can be outwitted by Joe Pasquale, we are all in much worse shape than we ever suspected.

There are occasional outbreaks of competence, such as when one of the hunter team triangulates a phone belonging to the driver of the cab taken by ex-soldier and presenter JJ Chalmers and disability advocate Sophie Morgan and a phone it called during the journey. This gives them the name of the person who provided the fugitives with a switch in transport and thus the identity of the new vehicle. This is briefly reassuring, until you get to thinking about how widely and deeply we are all surveilled on the regular and how much information any bad actor at any time could get on us all … So it’s a good thing that Strictly Come Dancing stars Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu are on hand to distract us by attending Craig Revel Horwood’s gold-spangled 60th birthday bash on the grounds that Amy really, really wants to go and the hunters “can’t dictate what we do for the next two weeks! I’ve given up so much already!” But don’t worry – it’s still too early in the series for them to get caught and they are soon wading across a stream to freedom.

At the end of each near-hour of frothing wildness, however, you are dropped into an ice bath of reality. Each episode ends with a story told by someone with cancer – or, in some cases, by those who have survived them. Unlike what has gone before, these are told simply and stripped of any kind of manipulation. They speak of unbounded love and unfathomable loss and they break your heart. They are there to raise awareness and money, and do so with dignity and grace. The rest? Utter chaos, in the service of good.

Celebrity Hunted is on Channel 4
