Benjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defence

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 20:58:25 GMT

Benjamin Nygren was quickly back on the goal trail as Celtic began the defence of their Premiership title with a 1-0 home win over Dundee. Before the game, Celtic fans cheered as the captain, Callum McGregor, unfurled the flag which confirmed again a 14th title win in 15 seasons.

It was all a bit flat in a first half with Martin O’Neill’s side struggling to get into their stride as the visitors posed problems. However, the Sweden midfielder Nygren, so prolific last season with 21 goals, struck with a close-range header in the 52nd minute and the goal proved enough to keep the three points in Glasgow as a new season got up and running for the champions.

Celtic supporters continue to call for new recruits to the squad but Camilo Durán, the Colombian striker signed from Qarabag reportedly for £5.5m, and Kasper Høgh, the Denmark forward who cost a club-record £11m plus add-ons from Bodø/Glimt, made their debuts.

Alistair Johnston and Arne Engels, both attracting transfer interest, also started for the champions while the Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman came in for his debut.

Høgh fired wide in the ninth minute after being set up by Nygren, then the Dane redirected an effort from Nygren past a post. Moments later at the other end, as the ball bounced around Celtic’s penalty area, Dundee’s Charlie Reilly hit the side netting with a shot from 12 yards.

Steven Pressley’s well-drilled outfit were finding joy with the high ball, either crosses or throw-ins and in the 33rd minute defender Owen Bevan got his head to the ball in the box but the Celtic goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo gathered comfortably.

Five minutes later, Engels missed the best chance of the match to that point, unmarked in the visitors’ box, he headed a cross from Kieran Tierney past a post, before the Celtic left-back drew a fine save from Goodman with a close-range drive.

The home side faltered at the start of the second half but when Tierney curled in a cross from the left, Nygren headed past Goodman from inside the box and the growing anxiety subsided.

Celtic will face LASK in the Champions League playoffs.

Martin O’Neill’s side were drawn out first against the Austrian champions. The Linz-based club won the Austrian Bundesliga for the second time last season, finishing two points ahead of the defending champions Sturm Graz.

The Hoops avoided a potential rematch with Kairat Almaty, who knocked Celtic out on penalties at the same stage last season following a goalless 210 minutes of action.

The first leg will take place on 18/19 August, with the second leg the following week. PA Media

O’Neill’s side probed with more purpose, the fans got more excited and the noise levels increased while Dundee’s attacks were more sporadic and less convincing, although the pace of Joe Bevan was cause for concern for the Parkhead defence. In the 67th minute Goodman threw himself down to his right to save a long-distance drive from forward Yang Hyun-jun.

Celtic remained in control but as the second goal refused to arrive and the clock ticked on, some nerves returned. In the 82nd minute, Sinisalo pulled off a terrific save from the Dundee substitute Ashley Hay’s glancing header.

Høgh missed another chance when he slid a shot past a post from six yards before McGregor cracked the upright with an effort from inside Dundee’s penalty area; James Forrest bent the rebound wide of the target.

Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:36:44 GMT

Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing

Greek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill a Scottish charity worker found dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month.

Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted.

On Sunday the suspect, identified as Sharif Ahmadzai, was accused of intentional homicide after three days of questioning. He will appear before an investigating magistrate to be formally charged on Wednesday.

George Kalliakmanis, the honorary president of the police officers’ association in Athens, told the Guardian the homicide division was now intent on discovering the motive behind “the murder” because the Afghan was continuing to deny any role in it, although he had confessed to hiding Ross in a suitcase.

“He has admitted to carrying her body in a trolley to the site. Police have CCTV footage of him doing this on the night of 16 July. He has also confessed to withdrawing €10,000 from ATMs using credit cards that belonged to her. But he has denied murder which police do not believe,” Kalliakmanis said.

The Afghan, a professional boxer in the lightweight division, is believed to have arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee at the height of Europe’s migration crisis 10 years ago.

He has been quoted as telling police he discovered Ross’s lifeless body in the first floor flat of an apartment block he helped manage in Exarchia, a bohemian district in downtown Athens popular among leftists, foreigners and NGOs.

Ahmadzai, who married a US citizen and devout Christian, Alaina Hall, in 2023, had keys to the flat where their own refugee solidarity group, Love Every Nation, regularly met.

Investigators have confirmed that Ross, a friend of Hall’s with similar volunteering experience and religious views, had moved to the apartment on 10 July after staying with Greek friends and arriving the capital from Edinburgh on 26 June.

Her last telephone call was made from her mobile phone on the night of 15 July – three days before her body was discovered by a homeless man in an abandoned building in Kypseli, about two miles away.

Two possible scenarios in the run up to Ross’s death were being studied, police said. “We believe there was a confrontation,” said one source. “But that was spurred by Ross discovering the Afghan rummaging through her things and stealing her credit cards, or was it a case of sexual assault or the Briton spurning his advances?”

Forensic scientists believe Ross was “likely asphyxiated” after an initial on-site postmortem, which showed there were no evident signs of injuries on her body. However, the autopsy was also deemed inconclusive because of advanced decay.

Further toxicological tests and analysis of vital organs are expected to determine the exact cause of death in the coming days.

Hall, who met Ahmadzai on Lesbos, is widely described as having played a “significant role” in the investigation.

After allegedly becoming suspicious of Ahmadzai’s movements – and newfound wealth, the result of making cash withdrawals with Ross’s credit cards – she reportedly contacted the police, handed over cash he had given her and moved into a hotel.

Adding to the mystery that has engulfed the inquiry, Ross’s phone was used for several days after her death, with text messages sent to family and friends. The messages were described as “deliberately misleading” by police, who believe they were sent in a bid to delay Ross being declared missing. One spoke of her “need to be alone”.

“The Afghan’s partner was very helpful,” said Kalliakmanis. “From the day the victim was identified the investigation faced several challenges but thanks to the homicide division being so thorough they cracked it.”

Police, who collaborated with the UK’s National Crime Agency and the Scottish service, combed through CCTV footage from cameras in the area where the suitcase was found and from banks where cash withdrawals were made before identifying the suspect.

Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:36:44 GMT

US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.

Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme.

“The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.”

Trump reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran. “This is the last chance for them to sign a good document.”

Iran has been in discussions with Oman about the creation of a temporary route through the strait that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday.

Esmail Baghaei denied claims by Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” he said.

Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly.

It is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes.

On Monday, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media.

“They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’. They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, the Strait of Hormuz will be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our ‘Blockade’.”

A middle route through the strait would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over its routes and future management, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services.

One proposal is to create a joint Omani-Iranian company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries.

Unlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq.

Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Tehran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes.

Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route.”

He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides.

Baghaedi said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait.

Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers.

In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.”

However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”.

The Saudis’ intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East.

ICE detainee reveals video of drinking water apparently contaminated with worm-like creatures

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:35:20 GMT

‘Disturbing’ footage shared by California detainee surfaces amid wider complaints about conditions in ICE detention

Attorneys for a man detained in a California immigration detention center have released footage showing him holding up a bottle of water from inside the facility that appeared to be contaminated with worm-like creatures.

The footage came from a video call with Carlitos Ricardo Parias, a Los Angeles man who has been detained for months at the Adelanto Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, north-east of LA.

Margaret Hellerstein, one of Parias’s attorneys, shared the footage with the Guardian on Thursday and said it was filmed this week. The clip is brief and grainy, but shows him holding up a plastic bottle filled with water, which appeared to have small pests of some kind swimming inside.

Parias, in a statement shared by Hellerstein, described them as “worms” or some kind of “larvae”, though it’s unclear what exactly was in the bottle. He said the water was given to residents to drink.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to repeated questions about the video, with a spokesperson saying in an email that the facility gets its water from the city of Adelanto and provides the “the same water used by residents and businesses in the area”. Geo Group, the private prison company that runs the ICE facility, did not respond to inquiries.

The footage has surfaced weeks after a federal judge ordered ICE to ensure that people detained in Adelanto had “24-hour access to clean, potable drinking water”. The ruling was a response to a class-action lawsuit challenging “dangerous conditions” at Adelanto, with detained plaintiffs alleging they were denied sufficient food, clean drinking water and proper medical care.

Parias said in his statement that the contaminated water came from jugs that staff had given residents for drinking. He said he poured the water with the worms into a bottle to preserve it as evidence. He showed the bottle to a relative on a video call, which was shared with his attorneys.

“This is what they give us: contaminated water, water with larvae, water with little black worms, which is slowly killing each one of us who are detained here,” Parias said in his statement, which his lawyer translated from Spanish. “We need proper drinking water, better treatment.”

The exact source of the water in the footage was not clear, and it also was not clear how widely this water was distributed to residents in the detention center.

Parias is a TikTok creator known as Richard LA. He received national attention after he was shot by an ICE agent in October and then charged with assault. A federal judge dismissed the charge and he was transferred to ICE custody where he is facing removal.

“When I saw the video, I was horrified and disgusted. I felt sick to my stomach,” said Hellerstein. “This is video evidence. They can’t just sweep it under the rug.”

The footage has circulated widely among advocates and immigration attorneys in recent days.

Lawyers involved in the class-action case said they had seen the footage, but also had not heard direct accounts from other detained residents about the specific contaminant shown in the video.

“The video is very disturbing and we’re looking into it,” said Rebecca Brown, supervising attorney at Public Counsel, a public interest law firm that brought the lawsuit, alongside several other organizations. “Detained individuals have long complained about the quality of the water … We’ve heard of water being murky, tasting terrible, having unknown things in it.”

Carl Bergquist, counsel with the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, another group representing the class-action plaintiffs, said the footage was concerning and raised questions about whether the government was complying with the judge’s order to provide clean water.

The class-action lawsuit said the tap water at the facility was “discolored and tastes odd, raising serious concerns about its potability”, with lawyers writing: “The ‘drinking’ water provided in coolers often appears dirty and regularly runs out for hours at a time.”

The judge’s recent order called for consistent water access and improvements to other standards. In a filing challenging the judge’s order this week, lawyers for DHS said the drinking water had been “sampled and tested at various distribution points by an independent third party … and determined to be clean per Food and Drug Administration (FDA) standards”.

DHS has also argued in court that Geo Group as a contractor is responsible for the conditions of the facility. Geo Group is not a defendant in the lawsuit.

Charlton up for sale again as US owners look to cash in after three years

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:30:22 GMT

Owners led by Gabriel Brener paid £15m in 2023

Buyer would be the club’s fifth owner in six years

Charlton’s US owners have put the club up for sale just three years after taking over at the Valley. The ownership group is understood to have engaged Oakwell Sports Advisory to find what would be the club’s fifth owner in the past six years.

In a sales deck sent to potential investors, which has been seen by the Guardian, Oakwell describes Charlton as “the last remaining football club upside opportunity in London”. Oakwell also claims that Charlton would provide new owners with an opportunity for five to 10 times equity growth through promotion to the Premier League, commercial expansion and investment in women’s football.

Oakwell did the deal that led to the Bournemouth owner, Bill Foley, buying the Prem rugby club Exeter Chiefs this summer, and is helping the Rugby Football League to secure external investment.

Charlton’s location in south-east London is a plus, while the Valley is a modern stadium with a capacity of 27,000, but the club do not own the ground, which belongs to the hated former owner Roland Duchâtelet. Having considered looking at alternative sites, last year Charlton extended the lease on the Valley until 2040.

Charlton have repeatedly changed hands since the fans forced out Duchâtelet in 2020, when the club had three owners in quick succession. Duchâtelet sold Charlton to East Street Investments for just £1 in January 2020, but the consortium led initially by the former football agent Matt Southall collapsed amid in‑fighting and an acrimonious court case, with the club eventually bought by the Danish-American business Thomas Sandgaard later that year. In 2023, Sandgaard sold Charlton to a group of five US investors called Global Football Partners (GFP) led by Gabriel Brener via their UK subsidiary, SE7 Partners.

Under GFP, Charlton returned to the Championship for the first time in five years in 2025 by winning the League One playoff final at Wembley, while the women’s team were promoted to WSL1 last season.

More European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifies

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 19:24:32 GMT

FA no longer endorses Fifa president for re-election

Wales and Serbia join Finland in withdrawing backing

European countries began turning their backs on Gianni Infantino as moves intensified across the globe to end his crisis-hit tenure as Fifa president.

The Football Association was the highest-profile of several Uefa member associations to drop its support for Infantino’s proposed re-election next year. It will write to Fifa confirming it no longer endorses Infantino for a fourth term in charge after the intense controversy surrounding his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.

Wales and Serbia publicly confirmed that they had withdrawn their backing, following a lead taken by Finland last week. Along with the FA, those federations had all previously written letters in favour of Infantino prolonging his tenure but patience has run out across the continent. The Swedish Football Association, which was one of five European FAs not to write letters of support, issued a statement confirming it would oppose his candidature in the election in March.

The FA had previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the United Kingdom’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.

It is joined by the Football Association of Wales, which said in a statement: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Striking a similar tone, the Football Association of Serbia explained recent events had “seriously damaged the reputation and credibility of both Fifa and its president”, saying a withdrawal was “the only logical and rational step”.

In a sign that consensus may not be easy to achieve, the Swiss Football Association stopped short of abandoning its countryman. Instead it asked for “another personal exchange of views with the Fifa president” and said it would “continue to review the developments surrounding Fifa” before the leadership election.

More countries are, however, expected to withdraw their support for Infantino in what amounts to a vote of no confidence. The intended effect is for the embattled president to resign although some insiders are braced for a drawn-out process. While the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which runs the sport in North and Central America, have both strongly criticised Infantino there has been no move by any of their individual federations to call back letters in favour of his re-election.

Ensuring they do so may be critical to the ongoing efforts to remove Infantino quickly. There is acknowledgement in some parts of Europe that other continents should be seen taking the lead if enough of a groundswell for his departure is to be reached. Only 15 countries have publicly supported Infantino since he shelved the FFE project on Saturday but there is an appetite to form a broad coalition against his re-election quickly.

Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 18:45:20 GMT

Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP

A former neo-Nazi activist with convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP has been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election in Somerset.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine, the creator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district. He told the Guardian he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser.

“The branch and indeed party are fully aware of my past. Our chairman has been a vocal advocate and has supported me since I became a member of the party. I am very grateful for the support,” he said.

Bonehill-Paine, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights”, re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account that has gained a cult following.

While notably critical of Labour and Reform UK, its skits have cast the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, in a favourable light.

Rebecca Harris, the Conservative chief whip, was criticised earlier this year for reposting one video in which Badenoch and the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, were depicted as characters in the gangster film Scarface. This was after Bonehill-Paine had been revealed as the person behind the account.

Bonehill-Paine has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.

He was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting “vile” antisemitic material online ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.

In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at the then Labour MP Luciana Berger, who is Jewish, which included posting messages to his blog calling Berger a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.

He told the Guardian on Monday that his criminal convictions had been spent and that he held various Home Office counter-extremism certifications. He said he had spoken alongside MPs where he talked about his past and highlighted antisemitism faced by Britain’s Jewish community.

However, the Conservative party’s opponents on the right were quick to accuse the Tory leader of hypocrisy and being weak on claims to oppose antisemitism.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Kemi claims the Tories have changed and they will have a new generation of candidates – it’s now clear what calibre of candidates they will be. Kemi claims to support the fight against antisemitism yet selects a convicted antisemite Nazi as a candidate. The hypocrisy is breathtaking.”

The selection of Bonehill-Paine comes as Badenoch is accused of freezing out centrist Tories. Last month it emerged that all prospective Tory MPs must align with her pledge to scrap the 2050 net zero target and leave the European convention on human rights.

At the weekend, a young Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network. Cody Butler claimed in a public letter that he no longer believed there was a home for one nation conservatism in the party.

Badenoch told the BBC last week that she led “a brand new party full of new people” after it emerged that the former cabinet minister Grant Shapps had been rejected as a Tory parliamentary candidate.

The Conservative party has been approached for comment.

Sigrid Haugset stuns Tour de France Femmes favourites by storming to stage win

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 18:10:01 GMT

Norwegian breaks clear in stage three to take overall lead

Haugset: ‘I never thought it was possible, it’s unreal’

Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes, breaking away alone for 90km, to take the overall lead after winning stage three to Poligny.

“I never thought it was possible,” she said, after realising she had taken the biggest success of her career and the overall lead in the sport’s biggest race. “It’s unreal. I was so dizzy at the end. I know my boyfriend would be so angry at me for not celebrating, but I couldn’t. I could not lift my arms off the bike. It was impossible.”

Haugset’s spectacular solo effort surprised the peloton’s leading teams and on the eve of the 21km individual time trial, from Gevrey‑Chambertin to Dijon, she leads by 2min 2sec from Kim Le Court.

“I was thinking about all my teammates and everyone cheering from home, so I had to give it my all,” she said. “All done in the Norwegian champion’s jersey, too – it’s fantastic.

We had looked at this stage and it was the goal for this Tour. I told my father I’d get some flowers today. Tomorrow is the time trial, but I haven’t worked on it this year so I will just enjoy it.”

Haugset is the first Norwegian rider to wear the yellow jersey in the Tour Femmes. The 27-year-old’s lone effort began at the foot of the second‑category Col de la Savine and was marked by an intense pursuit from the former world road race champion Lotte Kopecky, winner of the points classification in all three Grand Tours.

“I thought Kopecky would catch me,” Haugset said. “I can’t believe that she didn’t, but I kept on. The team car was amazing, pushing me.”

Although, in what became an epic duel, Kopecky got as close as 10sec to Haugset, she was not able to find the power to finally close the gap and the Norwegian moved clear again to win the stage by almost a minute and a half.

Temperatures in the high 30s made it yet another suffocating and stifling day on the route, with the ever-present iced drinks and ice socks passed up to the riders throughout the 156km stage.

As the sweat-streaked Haugset held on to win, the first sparring match between the race favourites came on the Côte de Chaux‑Champagny, 25km from Poligny, where Le Court accelerated and temporarily left her rivals in disarray. But as the narrow climb went on, with brief tentative accelerations from Kasia Niewiadoma and Demi Vollering, the main contenders regrouped and with Tuesday’s potentially pivotal time trial looming large, a truce was called.

There is some uncertainty over how well the defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, will fare in the winding test through the Routes des Grand Crus, which includes the sharp climb of the Lacets de Marsannay.

“It’s a real challenge for me,” she said, acknowledging her lack of time‑trialling experience, certainly compared with Vollering and Le Court. The double Olympic gold medallist said she has spent several months working to improve her time trialling, but accepts that she will have to “limit the damage” against the clock.

“We made sure to put me in a more correct position on the time‑trial bike. We also set out to do quite a few aerodynamic tests on the track, and to try to find the fastest outfit.”

Even so, she appears to accept she will be on the back foot as the peloton heads into the Rhone valley on Wednesday. “It’s a possibility,” she said. “I don’t know how much time I will lose, but I will give my best to lose the least possible.”

Ferrand-Prévot is not the only rider worrying about time losses, after the pre-race favourite Vollering crashed early in stage three, on the climb of the Col de la Faucille. The 2023 winner remounted and was active later in the stage, but her team carried out medical checks on an injured knee on Monday evening.

Much of the south-east of France, which will host the summit finish to Mont Ventoux on Friday and the Côte d’Azur stages on Friday and Saturday, remains under elevated risk of wildfires.

While the climb of the Ventoux scheduled for stage seven is expected to remain intact, the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.

In a statement, the Vaucluse prefecture asked the Tour de France Femmes organisers to consider an alternative route. The prefecture is planning a risk assessment on Tuesday and has said that an “alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme”.

Apple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access data

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:35:44 GMT

The Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users

Apple has launched a new legal challenge against a UK government demand to access its customers’ highly encrypted data, a year after the Home Office agreed to abandon its previous request.

The US tech company launched the legal complaint last month at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), an independent court that has the power to investigate claims that the UK intelligence services have acted unlawfully.

The UK government had made a second request to Apple to grant it a “back door” to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users, according to an order issued by the court.

Britain backed down on its original demand for access to data from UK and US customers last year, after a heated transatlantic tussle over encryption between London and Washington.

UK authorities subsequently issued a new “technical capability notice” (TCN) to Apple that did not apply to American users.

Apple is seeking to challenge the British government’s powers to issue TCNs under the UK Investigatory Powers Act, according to the details of the new legal case first reported by the Financial Times.

The legislation compels companies to provide information to law enforcement agencies working on cases including terrorism and child sexual abuse. This can include forcing companies to provide the UK security services with access to customer data, even if such information is protected by secure encryption.

The court sent an order giving notice of the new Apple complaint to the human rights group Privacy International, which, alongside fellow campaigner Liberty, had previously launched a separate complaint against TCNs at the IPT.

Among the submissions made by the campaigners were requests for Apple’s claims to be held in public given the public interest in the matter, and a complaint “disputing the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of the purported Apple TCN and the legal regime underpinning TCNs in general”.

A case management hearing to discuss how the parallel complaints should be handled had been scheduled for next month, Privacy International said.

A spokesperson added: “We are happy to learn that Apple is once again challenging the UK’s regime of secret orders. While we don’t know the substance of Apple’s claim, if it relates to the previously reported orders aimed at undermining the security of Apple’s iCloud storage, then Apple’s claim, alongside ours and Liberty’s, is crucially important to preserving all of our privacy and security.”

Neither Apple nor the Home Office responded to requests for comment. Both are legally restricted from discussing TCNs.

The original TCN issued last year asked Apple for the right to see users’ encrypted data protected by its advanced data protection (ADP) programme in the event of a national security risk.

Apple said the removal of the tool – which not even it can access – would make users more vulnerable to data breaches from bad actors and other threats to customer privacy. Creating a “back door” would also mean all data was accessible by Apple, which it could be forced to share with law enforcement possessing a warrant.

As a result, Apple withdrew UK customers’ access to its ADP programme in January 2025.

The Home Office has maintained that the Investigatory Powers Act, under which such orders are issued, contains robust safeguards and is used only when absolutely necessary.

The Guardian view on events in Ceuta: chaos and tragedy are weaponised by the far right

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:30:00 GMT

Instead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro Sánchez

At least 72 people are believed to have died late last week, most of them drowned or crushed as they joined tens of thousands of others in attempting to swim from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Yet the scale of that human tragedy has barely registered, as Donald Trump has decried an “invasion” while European politicians exploit the crisis to serve their own agendas. If further evidence were needed of the way that the radical right increasingly distorts the terms of the migration debate in the EU, the last few days have furnished it.

More needs to be understood about the drivers behind a shocking episode. Misinformation on social media – orchestrated or otherwise – appears to have played a big part, following a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily turned back. Moroccan authorities seemingly did little to prevent the chaotic exodus, which echoed previous smaller incidents and focused international attention on a territory whose sovereignty Rabat contests. If there were online indications that such an incursion was a possibility, no alarm was sounded.

The Spanish government, distracted by the need to combat ongoing wildfires, was utterly unprepared. But the vast majority of the 60,000 or so who crossed into Ceuta returned voluntarily across the border within 48 hours, some having aired grievances to reporters at the lack of work, decent wages and prospects available to them at home. The dangerous recklessness of their actions underlined the pressure-cooker levels of frustration beyond Europe’s external borders, particularly among the young.

Subsequently, the response of leaders such as Italy’s Giorgia Meloni has been predictable but deeply dispiriting. In a performative overreaction, Ms Meloni sought to demonstrate her hard line on irregular migration by temporarily suspending Rome’s Schengen agreement with Madrid, though Ceuta has never been included in Schengen, and Italy and Spain share no border. Along with Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, she was also among 22 signatories to a letter sent to the European Commission, suggesting that the liberal migration policies of the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – which, again, have no application in Ceuta – are undermining Europe’s security.

Such posturing is largely intended for a domestic audience. Mr Merz, for example, faces a major challenge from the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in three imminent state elections, while Ms Meloni is dealing with the emergence of a new party that threatens her own right flank. The zeal of such forces to weaponise the immigration issue was shown by the speed with which the AfD’s leader, Alice Weidel, claimed that the “likely destination” for most of those entering Ceuta was Germany.

Hyperbolic rhetoric and finger-pointing will only undermine solidarity between European nations, and hamper attempts to deal effectively with the challenges of migration. It is impossible to cross from Ceuta into mainland Spain and the Schengen zone without passing through a checkpoint. It is also worth noting that the number of irregular border crossings into Europe in fact declined by 40% in the first half of 2026 compared with last year, partly as a result of better-coordinated preventive strategies. Instead of rounding on Mr Sánchez, mainstream European leaders should be pledging their cooperation in helping Spain to minimise the possibility of such a tragic incident ever happening again.

Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m gift

Nigel Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months before election, appearing to undermine previous claims

Nigel Farage has made his clearest admission that he was in talks to return to lead Reform UK months before the 2024 general election, casting fresh doubt on previous claims that he was not involved in politics when he received a £5m gift.

The admission will reopen questions about the nature of the gift – Farage has repeatedly insisted it was not linked to his political career since the Guardian first revealed it in April.

On Monday, Farage admitted he had struck a deal with the party’s then leader, Richard Tice, and the convicted fraudster George Cottrell to return to frontline politics. Labour said the claim “has blown a gaping hole in his excuse” about why he did not declare the gift.

Farage has previously said he did not need to declare the £5m from Christopher Harborne or benefits in kind from Cottrell because he was not in politics at the time they were received. He has said he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, just before the election.

Sources have previously told the Guardian that Farage told senior figures in Reform UK he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.

The news comes with Farage facing a reopened investigation into his conduct by the Commons standards commissioner should he, as expected, win the byelection in Clacton.

It caps a testing period for the Reform leader, who has seen his party’s average poll rating decline to its lowest level in 15 months – and his own rating with the public slip to its lowest since he returned to the role.

Meanwhile on Monday:

Senior naval figures and the French authorities dismissed Reform’s plans to use military vessels to stop small boats crossing the Channel, saying the proposals “lacked substance” and amounted to a “violation of maritime law and international law”.

Farage continued to face a challenge from Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party, with Lowe accusing him of lying over an exchange of messages between the pair about an offer to work together.

Parliament’s standards watchdog opened an investigation into Tice, now Reform’s deputy leader, which Tice said was over “whether I should have referenced my register of interests at the start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence”.

Farage, who last summer dominated much of the media cycle with a stream of interventions on immigration, attempted to reset the narrative on Monday morning with a news conference on the party’s proposals to use the Royal Navy in the Channel. But once again he was forced to answer multiple questions about the party’s finances.

He said: “I had no intention about returning to politics, or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if … I was to come back to that position.”

The Sunday Times reported that Farage had negotiated the deal in March and April 2024, which was said to have involved Reform agreeing to repay or write off more than £1m in loans to Tice’s company.

“You would be a bit of a mug if you were to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial,” Farage said.

“That was useful for me to know but it wasn’t a deal. It wasn’t an agreement. It was subject to if I came back. And if you want clarification on this, that came some time after the gift, which perhaps is the important point.”

After the comments admitting he had discussed a return as party leader, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared.

“Farage has desperately tried to distract from his catalogue of scandals. But the embattled Reform leader has run out of road and must come clean with the public. If he had done nothing wrong, he surely would have explained himself by now.

“With grubby pacts, police probes and support from a convicted fraudster, Reform are up to their neck in sleaze and they clearly think the rules don’t apply to them.”

Pressed later at the same Reform event about when he had started to think about returning in 2024 to frontline politics, Farage said he had been “bullied and bullied for months by lots of different people”.

He claimed he had been “60/40” in favour of going to America, where an exciting period potentially beckoned for him in his role as a GB News host covering US politics.

The Guardian view on funerals: the law must change following Robert Bush’s crimes

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:25:00 GMT

An undertaker’s trial has exposed a regulatory blind spot. The public, as well as trade bodies, should be involved in shaping reform

There are few more vulnerable moments in life than the days before and after the loss of a loved one. The rituals of farewell surrounding a funeral matter deeply. Hence the horrified public reaction to the crimes of Robert Bush in Hull. Bush was sentenced last week to 20 years in prison for 67 offences including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.

When his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Services, was searched, police found multiple bodies decomposing on racks. Bush had returned the wrong ashes to families, stolen money donated to charities and spent more than £42,000 on holidays over 12 years. In court, relatives revealed the distress caused; David Gorbutt, who scattered a stranger’s ashes in place of his wife’s, described feeling “abused”.

The Competition and Markets Authority proposed tighter regulation of the funeral industry in 2020. The independent inquiry into David Fuller – who abused the bodies of more than 100 women and girls in hospital mortuaries – included regulation of undertakers among its recommendations. Now, a year after that report was published, ministers have decided that they agree. New laws, which should be expected to include a licensing scheme, minimum standards and provision for inspections, are on the way.

This is the right call. It is a peculiar blind spot in UK law that a service as sensitive and essential as that provided by undertakers is unregulated; the Scottish government, recognising this, introduced its own system last year. And while Bush’s case is by far the most extreme of several recent ones, he is not the only undertaker to have been jailed. Last year, another funeral director, Amie Upton, was banned from NHS mortuaries and maternity wards in Leeds after the BBC uncovered complaints about Florrie’s Army, a baby-loss service that she set up. Ms Upton has not been charged with any crime. But the Labour MP Mark Sewards has argued, rightly, that his constituents’ disturbing experiences with Florrie’s Army point to the need for new laws.

An enhanced role for local government would be in keeping with the government’s devolution push, and would require funding. Trade organisations have proposed a model in which they would play a part alongside the Human Tissue Authority. But while all options should be looked at, regulation must not be mistaken for a panacea. As in other situations where a position of trust has been abused, opportunities to intervene in Hull appear to have been missed.

About 65% of the more than 500,000 funerals that take place in the UK each year are handled by small, independent businesses. Regulation must be protective of them as well as of families who want to prepare bodies for cremation or burial themselves. Undertakers do a difficult job; those paying for their services are often extremely vulnerable. The likely increase in the cost of funerals, following tighter regulation, must also be taken seriously. Many people already struggle to afford them. It is vital to find out what the public, as well as the industry, want.

It may be that laws concerning dead bodies require a wider review, as the Law Commission believes. But the priority must be to find an effective, proportionate way to prevent rogue operators from setting up funeral businesses, and to identify any who already have. Grieving people ought to be able to have confidence in those they entrust with the bodies of relatives.

AstraZeneca should stick to its winning formula. It doesn’t need a $400bn US mega-merger

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:22:28 GMT

The Anglo-Swedish drugmaker’s flirtation with a grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb is baffling

AstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firm

Sir Pascal Soriot, chief executive of AstraZeneca, starts with huge credit in the bank, obviously. His long tenure has been a triumph, starting with the against-the-odds victory over Pfizer’s charmless accountants in 2014.

The $39bn (£29bn) purchase of Alexion in 2021 looked a little over-priced at the time, but you could see how it sat well with Soriot’s sermons on the importance of backing science. The deal got AZ into the field of medicines for rare diseases, which should offer decades of growth.

A flirtation with a grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), by contrast, looks baffling. What’s the big idea here? Why bet the farm on a $400bn (£300bn) mega-merger? The first challenge would be how to rip out a few billions-worth of costs to justify the takeover premium. Soriot has normally viewed such corporate exercises as anti-patient. And why do it now?

In the absence of a statement by AZ – not even to confirm the basic accuracy of the FT’s initial report of talks with BMS – one must assume we’re in the territory of discussions that could end up being quietly ditched. One hopes that will be the outcome because the 67-year-old Soriot risks spoiling his legacy if a high-risk financial adventure goes wrong.

A calamity must be a possibility since the acquisition of a $133bn (£99bn) rival would inevitably come with a large helping of debt. “If there is one company that doesn’t need financial engineering it’s AZ in our view,” commented Jefferies’ analyst. Quite.

The only guarantee in buying BMS is that AZ would inherit the target’s patent cliff challenge that will see sales of its blockbuster Opdivo cancer treatment plunge between now and 2030. Expiries of major drugs can feel smaller if shared within a bigger group, so you can see why BMS would be minded to seek shelter, but it’s hard to understand why AZ would volunteer to pay for the umbrella.

The theoretical appeal, perhaps, is the prospect of building a market-beating global colossus in oncology, the field that is also AZ’s greatest strength. But Soriot’s strategy of supplementing AZ’s own development drugs with smart licensing and partnerships, especially in China, is a proven winner. Why mess with the formula? US competition regulators may also have something to say about two leading oncology franchises being welded into one. Approval would be a long, and probably distracting, process.

Plan A, by contrast, has the virtue of simplicity. It was only last week that Soriot said he was “absolutely confident” of hitting AZ’s 2030 target for annual revenues of $80bn despite the failure of a heart disease drug in late-stage trials. He gave a typically bullish performance: investors should know the drug business involves the odd hiccup in the labs, so put one blemish in the context of the “20 high-value readouts due over the next 18 months”.

The worry in the background is that Soriot’s enthusiasm for US risk-taking and innovation has somehow led to the conclusion that AZ needs to join the pharmaceutical establishment in the world’s largest market, never mind the fact that it is already investing $50bn in US research and development and manufacturing.

Last autumn, AZ “harmonised” its listing on the New York Stock Exchange to give it equal status with the ones in London and Stockholm. “A global listing for global investors in a global company,” the corporate spin declared, but you didn’t have to be overly cynical to see how a new listing structure would make US deal-making simpler.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

But not all US deals are alike. The thumping near-9% fall in AZ’s share price on Monday spoke volumes: shareholders of all stripes struggled to see the sense in a mega-deal with BMS.

Viewed through patriotic British eyes, one can worry about AZ’s transatlantic drift or applaud the unusual sight of a UK-based company (for now, at least) being in the driver’s seat. Either way, though, the commercial logic has to add up. This idea just looks wholly out of character for AZ. It is best dropped.
