The body snatchers: how a young Nigerian man was lured to London in an organ-trafficking plot

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 17:10:26 GMT

Daniel was working at a market in Lagos when he was given the chance to start anew in the UK. He had no idea what was expected of him in return

The summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now. Click here to order

Daniel arrived in Lagos for the first time in 2016. He had come from a village in Ebonyi, a state in south-eastern Nigeria. He was 15 years old, the eldest of nine siblings, and his parents were farmers. When he was a boy, his father became sick and Daniel started working to assist his family, helping to cut trees and clear land. A few years later, he decided to seek his fortune in Lagos.

In Nigeria’s commercial capital, Daniel spent his days in the open-air Ikotun Market, where thousands of people shop every day for everything from tomatoes and fabric to suitcases and electronics. He sold cellphone accessories out of a wheelbarrow under a wide umbrella, making less than £10 a day. After living with a relative, he moved into a room with friends, including a young man named Chukwudi, who also worked in the market. Daniel had grown up in the same village as Chukwudi. A photo from their early childhood shows the boys together, Daniel in a red sportswear shirt.

Daniel was short and slight, with an unassuming face and sleepy eyes. He was playful and liked to joke around, Chukwudi recalled, “not a troublemaker”. They often hung out with another friend from the market, Ben, who was older and carried himself like he was destined for better things. “Ben was living big boy life,” Chukwudi told me. “He was balling out, flexing; he can go and eat anything he like.”

One day in 2021, Ben disappeared from the market. He wouldn’t be in touch again until later that year, when he called Daniel and told him the good news: he had got a job in the UK. “Wow, God has done for you then?” Daniel said. Ben asked if Daniel was interested in working abroad. Ben sent his friends videos of himself dancing in London, living the good life. He had accomplished the dream: he had escaped the dim economic prospects offered by his home country and got out. (There is a Yoruba slang term for it: “japa”, or as one Lagosian put it to me, “It’s like running for your life.”) Daniel was interested in doing the same.

Soon after, Daniel received a call from a man named Obinna Obeta, who had got his number from Ben. Obeta said that he could help Daniel get to the UK, where he would provide him with accommodation and work. But first, he said, Daniel would need to go to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, to undergo some medical tests. Daniel wasn’t sure what to make of this, until he received the money for his trip to Abuja. “That is the day that I knew he was serious,” Daniel later told a court in London. He assumed the medical tests were part of the process for getting a visa.

In February 2022, Daniel said goodbye to Chukwudi at a bus station in Lagos and began his journey to Britain. He had never met Obeta in person. When later asked in court why he thought Obeta was helping him, he responded simply: “Because I think it’s from God.”

Obinna Obeta, the man who contacted Daniel, was a Nigerian radiologist who had moved to London to seek treatment for kidney failure. Nigeria suffers from high rates of kidney disease, but few have health insurance or can afford dialysis and medications. “Kidney disease treatment in Nigeria: people are just moving from here to the morgue. It’s traumatising honestly,” Obeta would later say. It was not until 2025 that Nigeria introduced comprehensive standards and guidelines for organ transplants, and only 2,000 or so kidney transplants have taken place there. Many Nigerians who have undergone organ transplants have done so abroad.

Even in countries with advanced healthcare systems, the wait time for a kidney can be long: two to three years, on average, in the UK, and up to five years or more in the US. According to the World Health Organization, organ transplant tourism – where patients travel abroad to purchase organs – accounts for at least 5% to 10% of transplants worldwide. Organ trafficking is believed to take place in about 50 countries, and it is one of the most under-reported forms of human trafficking. The UK considers moving people across international borders for the purpose of harvesting their organs a form of slavery, treating human beings as commodities to be bought and sold.

In July 2021, seven months before Daniel left for the UK, Obeta had undergone a successful kidney transplant at the Royal Free hospital in north London. It cost him £70,000. He used the services of a medical tourism company, run by a Nigerian doctor who was then an NHS consultant. The kidney donor was Daniel’s friend Ben, whom Obeta had falsely claimed was his cousin.

On the flight to London, Daniel knew none of this. Accompanied by a man and woman he had not met before, he had only a few possessions: some clothes, lotion and soap. No shoes besides the ones on his feet. It was his first time on a plane, and he slept for much of the flight. After landing, the man took Daniel to a house off the Old Kent Road in south London, where he met Obeta for the first time. Daniel was told he would sleep in the living room.

As Daniel would later testify, Obeta treated him like a “houseboy”. “Every day I wash plates, I wash toilet, I wash, I sweep,” he recalled. Daniel did not have any money and was reliant on Obeta for his meals. Even his passport was taken. There seemed to be no escape.

Across London, in Willesden Green, Sonia Ekweremadu was getting sicker. Less than two months before Daniel arrived in the UK, she had posted an end-of-year recap reel on her Instagram page. It showed her, a light-skinned 24-year-old woman, dancing, going out with friends, and lying in a hospital bed with a pink teddy bear. Her family home was in Abuja but she lived in London, having attended various private schools in England. With several family properties in Nigeria, as well as in the US and UAE, she had the privileged upbringing that is typical of a Nigerian politician’s children.

Sonia’s father was Ike Ekweremadu, one of the most prominent and powerful figures in Nigeria. Ike Ekweremadu had been elected to the Nigerian senate for a fifth consecutive term in 2019, and served as deputy president of the senate. His reputation extended beyond national borders, after his stint as speaker of the parliament of the Economic Community of West African States in the 2010s.

It was while Sonia was studying for her master’s degree in film at Newcastle University, in 2019, that she became sick. As she grew weaker, she had to drop out. A family friend eventually referred her to the Royal Free in Hampstead, which specialises in treating kidney disease. Sonia was diagnosed with FSGS nephrotic syndrome, a rare disease where kidney scarring leaks protein into the urine and causes bodily swelling. In August 2021, Sonia met with Peter Dupont, a consultant nephrologist at the Royal Free, who noted that she would require dialysis or a renal transplant. She received dialysis in a private patients’ unit on the top floor.

In September 2021, the court later heard, Sonia’s uncle, Isaac “Diwe” Ekweremadu, who is a doctor, called an old medical school classmate to talk about the transplant that he had at the Royal Free that year. Diwe wanted to know whether his niece might be able to have a similar operation. His former classmate was Obinna Obeta.

At the time, Obeta was in desperate need of money. As a non-UK resident, he still owed £27,000 to the Royal Free as part of the £70,000 he was paying for his kidney transplant. He also had to spend £1,600 every month on immunosuppressants, so his body wouldn’t reject the kidney, and other medications and tests. “It just kept increasing. Just kept increasing,” he later said of his debt. For an initial sum of just under £2,000, Obeta agreed to help find a kidney donor for Sonia. He referred the Ekweremadus to the medical concierge service he had used for his own transplant. Soon after, Obeta got in touch with the young man who had provided him with his kidney, Ben, to ask for help finding a donor. Through him, he found Daniel.

By November 2021, Ike Ekweremadu had a solution for his daughter. He forwarded a message to his wife: Diwe had found a donor who “matched very well”. The next step was to get the donor a passport and then a visa to the UK. Daniel had no idea that the following statement was written on his visa application:

“I wish to state on conclusion of this application that I would be donating an organ to my closest cousin (Sonia Chinonso Ekweremadu) in appreciation for her sacrifices towards me, my family, and our community. I’m willing to put my life on the line for her to live and continue her good service to humanity. Finally, I wish to state that I’ll be travelling in company with my uncle, Obinna. He has been a father‑figure since I lost my biological father.”

None of this was true: Sonia was not a relative of Daniel’s, nor was Obinna Obeta. He had never met them. His biological father was still alive. He had never discussed the prospect of organ donation with anyone.

Daniel arrived in London in February 2022. Before his arrival, Sonia’s doctor at the Royal Free had written a letter to the Nigerian doctor who ran the concierge service, stating that she was not responding well to treatments and agreeing that a transplant would be the “best way forward for her”. The family had informed the Royal Free that they had a candidate, telling them that Daniel was 19 and a distant cousin of Sonia’s. The doctor added in his letter that this prospective donor was younger than he would consider ideal and, because he was not a close relative, there could be difficulties gaining approval from the hospital and the UK Human Tissue Authority.

In the UK, kidney transplants are highly regulated. If the donor is alive, they have to go through extensive physical and psychological evaluations to make sure they are medically suitable and willing to donate. Once the surgical team approves the donation, the Human Tissue Authority must interview both the donor and the recipient to determine whether the donor has given consent and to ensure that no payment or coercion is involved.

According to the court transcript, Diwe told her parents that they should now say that Daniel was a first cousin of Sonia, not a distant one. He also later told them that there was a medical secretary at the hospital who would act as Daniel’s interpreter. For a fee of £1,500, she had agreed to coach Daniel on what to say during the interview he’d need to do for his kidney donation to be approved. She recommended that Daniel be at the hospital during Sonia’s dialysis treatments to show his firm commitment to his cousin’s health.

The week of Daniel’s arrival in London, Obeta took him to a west African restaurant on the Old Kent Road to have lunch with a young woman and an older woman. Daniel had no idea who they were, and testified that the women didn’t ask him any questions about himself. They seemed afraid of something, he said. At the end of the lunch, the group took a photo. The two women were Sonia and her mother, Beatrice Ekweremadu.

Later that week, Obeta took Daniel to the Royal Free, where he saw Sonia and Beatrice outside. Before Obeta began talking with them, he told Daniel to stand away so he could not hear. “Obinna would just tell me where to stay and he would go with them and they would start discussing. Like they was controlling me,” Daniel testified. He was confused to learn that he would be meeting with a doctor. “They said if the doctor ask me the school that I go, I should tell the doctor that I go to higher institution,” Daniel told the court. “If the doctor ask me who is Sonia, I should say that Sonia is my cousin. They give me many things to answer the doctor. I should tell the doctor that they not pay me.”

On 24 February 2022, Daniel went in for a meeting with Peter Dupont, the consultant nephrologist at the Royal Free, while Obeta waited outside. “He told me that I want to do a kidney transplant,” Daniel later recalled. “I was shocked because that is the first day that I hear about this kidney transplant.” Dupont asked him about his relationship to Sonia and what had motivated him to be a donor; about whether he was working or studying; and about what his parents did for a living.

Daniel gave the answers he had been coached to provide. In court, Dupont recalled that Daniel had been subdued: “We spoke for perhaps 15 or 20 minutes. His answers were very brief: single sentences, single words. He didn’t really appear to have any understanding of what it was that he was signing up for.” Dupont explained that there were dangers associated with the procedure, such as excess bleeding, infections and blood clots, and “a small risk of death”, as he wrote in his notes. Even if the operation went well, Daniel would have an increased risk of chronic kidney disease and end‑stage renal disease. He would require regular follow-ups for the rest of his life to monitor his kidney function, blood pressure and urine protein levels.

Noticing Daniel’s uneasiness, Dupont asked if he was scared to tell the Ekweremadus that he did not want to go ahead. Daniel said he did not want to donate his kidney. It was only when Dupont made clear that the operation would not happen that Daniel finally made eye contact, the doctor testified. “He was nervous that I would say or imply that the decision not to proceed was his fault. I assured him that confidentiality was paramount and the intended recipient would be told he was unsuitable.” He recalled Daniel saying about Obeta: “He had not told me anything about this. I would never have agreed to any of this. My body was not for sale.”

Afterward, Daniel told Obeta that he answered what questions he could, but there were some he could not. Obeta was angry. “He say that if I don’t do this – he used Igbo language to say this – if I don’t do this … I will find it difficult,” Daniel testified. (Obeta insisted to the court that he had discussed the kidney transplant with Daniel before the meeting.) Obeta also told Daniel that he had 1.2m naira, or about £2,000 then, for him if he went through with the operation.

At the end of March, the decision was taken out of their hands. The Royal Free formally ruled out the possibility of allowing Daniel’s transplant operation to go ahead.

Daniel was relieved, but he was still living in limbo. He was not allowed to leave the house, and spent much of his time with Obeta’s kids when he was not doing chores. A few weeks after the Royal Free declined to proceed with the operation, two people came to Obeta’s house to examine Daniel. They asked him to remove his clothes and applied pressure to his stomach. They still wanted to do the transplant, Daniel said, and Obeta told Daniel he had booked him a flight back to Nigeria. Daniel was unsure what they had planned for him. “That is when I start to become afraid because I don’t know what I am going to do. Because all the plans, everything they are doing is behind my back,” Daniel testified.

As Daniel later told Chukwudi, his childhood friend, he had been in a state of panic. “He was even crying, he don’t know what to do,” Chukwudi recalled. “Even me, when he was telling me everything, I was crying. I didn’t know what to do. Because if he comes back, he has nothing to do again. He has already sold his market [stock], he used the money to buy some clothes for his trip.”

In court, Daniel and Obeta’s accounts of what happened next differed in a few small ways. But the likeliest story is that on 2 or 3 May 2022, a friend of Obeta’s took Daniel to Heathrow airport for a flight back to Abuja. But Daniel decided he could not go back to Nigeria, where he feared he would be coerced into donating his kidney. Despite carrying little more than a used Samsung phone, AirPods, chargers and £27.90 in cash, he fled. He ended up walking around for three days, sleeping outside. He then ran into a stranger on Kingston Road in Staines, who gave him food and let him take a shower in his flat.

On 5 May, Daniel went to nearby Staines police station, where he told officers a story that was mostly fictional. He said he had been begging for money on the streets of Lagos before coming to London, and that he was an orphan with no family in Nigeria. He told officers that the man he had travelled with had promised him money, but that he couldn’t say what the money was for. He said he was only 15. (Daniel would later testify that he was trying to give the impression of being a vulnerable youth with nowhere to live in Lagos, so he wouldn’t be deported.)

According to Chukwudi, who spoke to Daniel not long after he went to the station, a Nigerian woman hosted Daniel at her home when the police released him into protective care. On the call, Daniel still sounded afraid about the attempted kidney transplant, but he said the Nigerian woman was taking him to church. He thought he might even get the chance to go to school.

With Daniel now gone, the Ekweremadus needed a new plan. After consulting with friends and colleagues, they decided on a new transplant location: Turkey. While the Ekweremadus maintain that Sonia had no knowledge of the plan to illegally get a kidney donor, she responded to her father’s WhatsApp messages that had photos of new potential donors. To one photo of two young Black men, Sonia wrote: “OK, that’s fine. Thank you. Are they still more to test?”

Her father told her: “Yes, but by the end of the week, I will decide who to proceed with. We will get it right this time.”

Sonia wrote back: “I trust you, daddy, thank you ❤️”. Then she added: “The dark one looks better, the light one looks like he’ll run away 😂😂😂”.

In June 2022, on Father’s Day, Sonia wrote to her father on the family group chat: “Happy Father’s Day, daddy, you mean the world to us … You are the best father in the world. I know lots of people say that about their fathers, but mine is really the best … I pray for long life and prosperity, to be able to see your grandchildren and great-grandchildren in Jesus’ name. Amen. I want to especially thank you for everything you’ve done and are doing regarding this transplant process. You and mummy have gone above and beyond for me, and it never goes unnoticed and unappreciated … I hope that one day I’ll be able to take care of you, and mummy, the way that you’ve taken care of us all these years (don’t worry, I haven’t forgotten your Range Rover gift).”

Ike replied: “I know you didn’t forget, sweetheart … I will spare nothing to ensure your good health and comfort. I have the support of mummy on this objective 100%. By the grace of God, you will be out of this challenge before the end of August. It’s a promise. Just be strong for all of us.”

Two days later, Ike and Beatrice Ekweremadu were arrested at Heathrow as they travelled back from Turkey. They were charged with conspiracy to commit human trafficking for the purpose of exploitation, specifically organ harvesting. The couple had at least £30,000 in cash on them. Sonia was arrested the same day at her home in London. Obeta was arrested the next month. Sonia’s uncle Diwe remained in Nigeria and was not extradited to the UK. (I was unable to reach Diwe for comment.)

It is extremely rare for a Nigerian politician of Ekweremadu’s status to face criminal charges. In the UK, the story was widely covered in the media, but in Nigeria, the case attracted a different level of interest, dominating the front pages of newspapers and sparking discussions on primetime TV news, as well as endless social media posts and WhatsApp messages across both Nigeria and the diaspora. One of Daniel’s uncles, Linus, who had given him a place to stay when he first came to Lagos, discovered his nephew’s story on social media like everyone else. “If I had known, I wouldn’t have allowed him to go,” Linus told me.

On 6 February 2023, the trial of Obinna Obeta and Ike, Beatrice and Sonia Ekweremadu began at the Old Bailey in London. All pleaded not guilty. Ike claimed that he thought Daniel was donating a kidney to his daughter out of kindness, and that he never agreed to pay him. He accused Obeta of scamming him out of money, and he argued that Daniel had lied to the police so that he could get asylum in the UK. “D was never exploited, D accepted and agreed, volunteered to help my daughter with this kidney and we believed him,” Ike told the court. “But looking back now it was obvious that he was scamming everybody, he just wanted to come to England and take refuge.”

Ike downplayed Daniel’s vulnerability. “Lagos is a place where you get wiser by the day for you to survive. So, even a young person in Lagos cannot be intimidated,” he said in court. “Because they are just streetwise.” When asked if he knew Daniel was selling phone accessories out of a wheelbarrow, he responded: “I didn’t know in particular but that’s also a big business, he’d make millions with that.”

Ike did admit to fabricating the familial relationship to Daniel. “That is what Dr Obeta advised us,” he said. “My daughter was sick, and somebody had told us what we would need to do, and we didn’t see any corruption in this; we didn’t corrupt anybody.” (Contacted before publication of this article, the Royal Free declined to comment. After publication, it sent the following statement: “We would like to pay tribute to the victim for his bravery in coming forward and sharing his experience. National guidance for the clinical assessment of living donor transplantation, which applies to both our NHS and private patients, was followed in this case and a decision taken not to go ahead with the procedure.”)

Both Ike and Beatrice kept saying during the trial that their lies to the Royal Free about Daniel’s identity were “not who we are” – they were just desperate to save their daughter’s life. “She was born premature, so we struggled to save her life from day one,” the former senator said. He refused to admit any guilt. When asked if he was the victim in all this, Ekweremadu said: “Yes.”

The trial shed more light on Obeta, who had obtained a UK medical visa for his own transplant and then stayed to work in the country illegally, getting a job as a cleaner during the pandemic. “It was amazing … I’ve never seen this kind of, you know, surgery skill,” Obeta told the court of his transplant experience. “I want to use this opportunity to thank the people of the UK for saving my life.”

On 23 March 2023, at the end of the six-week trial, Ike and Beatrice Ekweremadu were found guilty of organ trafficking. Ike was later sentenced to nine years and eight months; Beatrice to four and a half years. Sonia, who had also been charged with conspiracy to arrange organ harvesting, was acquitted. Obeta was convicted of organ trafficking and sentenced to 10 years. The Ekweremadu case was the first successful organ-trafficking conviction in the UK under the Modern Slavery Act.

After he testified in court via a video link in February 2023, Daniel vanished. The police had placed him in protective custody, and none of his family or friends in Nigeria knew where he was. He had told the court: “I have no one here [in the UK], no family or friends. I’m having to start my life again. I am wary of new people that come into my life now. My plan now is to work and to get an education and to play football.”

In Lagos, in 2024, I met a childhood friend of Daniel’s, Jeremiah Nwamkpuma. In a beige, shabby office upstairs from the stalls in Ikotun Market, we chatted over the noise of hawkers and shoppers. Nwamkpuma told me that he’d recently visited Daniel’s dad in the family village. “[He] asked me about Daniel. I’m telling him that I’m not hearing from him. He’s crying. Since Daniel left, he’s not heard from him,” Nwamkpuma said. “Tension is high in the family.”

The family was confused and hurt that Daniel had disappeared from their lives, even though they understood that he, too, was likely afraid. His parents were angry, Nwamkpuma said. They farmed cassava, plantain, yam and other crops, but had little money. When Daniel was selling cellphones, he would send money back home to help them. “We’re happy he’s saved, but there’s no proper communication,” Jeremiah Mbah, who is the pastor of a church Daniel occasionally attended, told me. “It’s as if he’s lost.”

For more than two years no one heard from Daniel, but then last year, he called from the UK. He reached Chukwudi, who was surprised and relieved. “He wanted to hear from me, and know how his parents are doing. I explained to him that his daddy is very sick, and that they needed him present. But he said there was no way for him to come. He was feeling bad,” Chukwudi told me. In court, Daniel had said that he was concerned about his safety if he returned home. Ekweremadu “has a lot of people that know him. In Nigeria, those people can do anything.” He asked Chukwudi to help with the cost of Daniel’s father’s care. “He told me that he was going to school. He sounded very good,” Chukwudi said.

Daniel’s father died last August. Nwamkpuma called him to let him know of the death. Daniel cried, Nwamkpuma recalled, but said that he still couldn’t come because of his studies; Nwamkpuma told him to stay.

Chukwudi, Nwamkpuma and Daniel’s family have tried to reach him since then, with no success.

After her parents were convicted, Sonia gave a short interview to the BBC. She looked poised, wearing understated gold jewellery, with her hair in braids. “It’s sad. It’s been really hard to really wrap my head around it,” she said. “I understand the conviction, personally I disagree with it. However, that’s from a very biased perspective as their daughter. I would obviously always, always back my parents. However, the law has taken its course, and we just have to now move forward as a family.” She admitted she was aware “to an extent” of her parents’ plan, but that she “didn’t really know anything leading up to it”. She added that she didn’t “feel anything” towards Daniel, but wished him “all the best”.

She was now in a precarious medical situation. “Either I stay on dialysis for the rest of my life, or I get a transplant; these are my two options,” she said. She had visited her parents in jail, and said they seemed calm. “I feel guilty,” she said, her voice breaking. “Because I feel like all this has happened because of me.” (Sonia declined to comment for this article, but on her Instagram, she often posts stories with bible verses and prayers, as well as photos with friends.)

The Ekweremadu case is still the only successful conviction for organ trafficking under the Modern Slavery Act in the UK. There is a simple reason that such convictions are rare, particularly in Nigeria, says Frank Tietie, a human rights lawyer: “Those who are involved are usually very powerful people, and they’re able to influence our justice system.” While Ike Ekweremadu remains in prison, Beatrice was released in January, after serving the custodial portion of her sentence. Upon her return to Nigeria, local media reported that she was greeted with celebrations in her home town of Mpu.

Late last year, in a sign of Ike’s continued status in his home country, Nigeria’s foreign minister met with officials at the UK Ministry of Justice to request that he be returned to Nigeria to serve out the rest of his sentence there. The UK rejected the request. Nigeria has arrested and charged several other people with organ trafficking, but the trials have lagged. As Tietie said: “So it’s still going on, largely unreported, largely unchecked.”

Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picks

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 16:54:39 GMT

Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks for Europe

Rookies Ramirez, Nadaud and Rhodes also selected

Leona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’s Solheim Cup team despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks named on Monday by Anna Nordqvist.

Maguire joins three rookies – Julia López Ramirez, Nastasia Nadaud and Mimi Rhodes – in completing the Europe side who will attempt to reclaim the trophy in the Netherlands next month.

A missed cut for Maguire in the Women’s British Open last week meant the 31-year-old had failed to play in the closing 36 holes of four from a possible five majors in 2026. In the one where she made the cut, the Women’s PGA Championship, Maguire tied 53rd. She started this week ranked 83rd in the world.

These numbers are striking for a player who was tipped for greatness at a young age. There is also the matter of the controversy that surrounded Maguire at the 2024 Solheim Cup when she admitted her limited play under the captain Suzann Pettersen proved a “bitter pill to swallow”. Maguire has enjoyed positive experiences in this arena in the past, however, having starred for Europe in the Solheim Cups of 2021 and 2023. The Irish golfer has also claimed eight and a half points from a dozen Solheim Cup matches.

“I would rather play alongside her than against her,” Nordqvist said of Maguire. “She is such a fierce competitor and will do anything for you on the team. I had the honour of playing with her in Spain [at the 2021 Solheim Cup]. Her matchplay record, as an amateur too, definitely helps. I’m excited to see what she can do.”

Maguire’s experience was clearly key to Nordqvist’s decision. Another blunt reality is that European options were not especially strong. “I love the Solheim Cup,” Maguire said. “It brings the best out of my game and I love being part of the team.”

Ramirez said she is “living the dream” after her maiden call-up. The 23-year-old from Málaga is yet to win a professional event. Nadaud did taste victory, at the Ladies European Tour event in Andalusia late last year. England’s Rhodes was the LET’s rookie of the year in 2025, when she won three times. Nordqvist hailed Rhodes as a “fierce competitor”.

Charley Hull, Esther Henseleit, Lottie Wood, Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Céline Boutier, Carlota Ciganda and Nanna Koerstz Madsen sealed Europe’s automatic berths. Albeit more than a month has to pass until the Solheim Cup gets under way at Bernardus Golf, Nordqvist will have high hopes for Henseleit. The German was beaten to the Women’s Open title in a playoff on Sunday by Shiho Kuwaki. In the second and defining extra hole at Royal Lytham and St Annes, Henseleit’s drive rebounded from the leg of a marshal and to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit had no idea what had transpired when watching from the tee.

“I thought it was further left to be honest,” Henseleit said. “It must have gotten some kind of bad bounce. At least I still had a shot and could kind of get a good angle going into the green. I didn’t have to take an unplayable or something. But, probably a bit unlucky there. That’s just links golf.”

Angel Yin and Jennifer Kupcho secured spots in the US Solheim Cup team at the Women’s Open conclusion. Nelly Korda had already done likewise. Angela Stanford, the US captain, will name three captain’s picks after their qualification period ends in late August.

Driver jailed for four years after faking brake failure on motorway

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 16:20:50 GMT

Nathan Owen drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph and lied to police it was malfunctioning and out of his control

A man who drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph on motorways falsely telling police the car was malfunctioning and out of his control has been jailed for four years and three months.

Nathan Owen fabricated not being able to brake in a “frighteningly stupid” ploy to avoid paying car finance, Liverpool crown court heard.

In a statement, Jaguar Land Rover UK (JLR) said the firm had spent an extra £50m in marketing to try to counter the publicity from the false allegations, which they said generated 180 pieces of adverse media coverage.

Owen, 33, collided with a police car 31 times as officers attempted to stop him after he phoned emergency services to tell them his vehicle was accelerating and there was nothing he could do.

He drove at speeds of up to 86mph on the M58, M57 and M62 in Merseyside for about 35 minutes, over a distance of about 38 miles, during the incident on 6 March 2024.

The Jaguar I-Pace eventually came to a stop near junction 12 of the M62 when the battery ran out.

Sentencing him, Judge Ian Unsworth KC said: “You set in train a course of conduct which caused a significant police traffic operation to be deployed, undoubted alarm to the public and very substantial loss and disruption to others.”

The judge said police officers placed themselves in danger because they believed they were dealing with a genuine emergency.

Addressing Owen, he added: “You, meanwhile, sought to profit from a lie.”

Police said that an extensive investigation with JLR revealed the car was functioning correctly and data showed that Owen did not press the brakes at any point.

He was arrested on 13 March and denied making it all up for financial gain. But police discovered Owen had a high level of personal debt and multiple missed payments on the vehicle finance.

Eric Lamb, prosecuting, said Owen, of Prestatyn, had about £5,000 left to pay to a car finance company and, on the day of the incident, attempted and failed to borrow money from a loan company.

Minutes after being turned down for the loan money he called 999 claiming his car would not brake and he had no control over the vehicle, which he said was accelerating.

Lamb said: “In fact, his car was stationary at the time of that call.”

Footage of the police pursuit of Owen was played in court, along with the audio from his 999 call, in which he was heard telling an operator he was “shaking” and the car had “gone crazy”.

When the car was eventually brought to a stop the brake lights could be seen turning on.

Owen contacted the finance company 40 minutes after the incident.

He was later paid £300 by the Sun and £500 by the Daily Mail for his story, the court heard.

Daniel Travers, defending, said Owen’s actions were “frighteningly stupid”.

Travers said Owen, who had no previous convictions and came from a “successful, stable family”, had been described by his father as a Walter Mitty character who “lives in a fantasy world”.

He added: “He had grand ideas and things just went wrong.”

Owen pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and two counts of fraud in June.

He was banned from driving for a period of five years after his release from custody.

‘A rug helps anchor all the pieces’: how to start decorating your home

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 16:00:22 GMT

Designers share tips on creating a space you love, from mixing eras and colors to not getting in your head

Home is where you sleep. It’s also where you eat, work, cry, laugh, socialize and celebrate. It is a spatial extension of the self – which can make home decorating daunting to some.

“People get in their heads about decorating their space,” says Drew Michael Scott, interior designer and founder of the lifestyle and decor brand Lone Fox. It can be hard to know where to start, what you can afford or accomplish, or if you’re getting it wrong.

“Decorating your home is not that serious, and it’s nothing to lose sleep over,” Scott says. “Your house is probably never going to look like it belongs in a magazine, and that’s OK. The goal should be to create a space you love, and that will look different for each person.”

Whether you’re moving into a new place, refreshing an old one, renting or buying, here are some tips from experts on how to start decorating your space.

If you’ve dated straight men who are in their 20s, you’ll know that some people don’t see the point in decorating.

But research has shown that the physical spaces we inhabit can have a profound impact on our mental wellbeing and productivity – one small study showed that curved rooms, for example, increased creative thinking, and research shows clutter can increase levels of stress and anxiety.

“Home is where you’re supposed to feel safe, happy and completely free,” says Imani Keal, content creator and interior decorator. “Loving your home is an extension of loving yourself.”

And if you feel safe, happy and completely free in an undecorated apartment, that’s fine too.

“If you don’t mind a blank space, don’t enjoy decorating and can’t afford to hire someone to do it for you, then live in your blank space,” says Scott.

Identify how you need your space to function. “It won’t matter how nice [a space] is if it’s not functional,” says Tara Pallay, interior designer and YouTuber.

Consider your day-to-day needs. Will your space need a lot of storage, comfortable seating or a workspace? Do you need to take other people’s needs into account, or a pet? Once you have the answers to the relevant questions, you can make a plan.

Be honest with yourself about how you live. “If you watch TV regularly, hiding a TV for the sake of aesthetics is stupid,” says Keal.

Think of how you want the space to feel. Once you’ve identified the function of a room, imagine how you want to feel in it, says Dani Klarić, interior designer and co-founder of the Euphoria Collective design group.

“Do you want your bedroom to feel romantic and calming? Do you want your living room to feel playful and energetic? Once you identify an emotion, the design decisions become much easier,” she says.

Start with the big stuff. The items and elements that take up the most space visually – a rug, sofa, paint color – play a major role in the look and feel of a room, so experts agree it’s good to start with them and go from there.

Scott recommends starting with a rug, because “a rug helps anchor all the pieces and helps determine the color scheme”.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Make it personal. Mood boards and inspiration pics are great, but if you hew to them too closely, “you can end up with a technically beautiful home that looks like a storefront with no soul”, says Keal.

Keal made a list of seven essential items you should include in a space when decorating: something you’ve made, something thrifted, something stolen (!), something gifted, something you saved for, something you’ve inherited and something you’ve earned.

Even if you don’t have all seven, choosing items you have a connection to will make it feel more personal and alive.

“If someone walks into your home and says: ‘This feels so you,’ then you’ve done it right,” says Klarić.

Let the space evolve. Too often, experts say, people feel pressure to finish a space quickly. But “the most beautiful homes are layered over time”, says Klarić. Buying everything all at once can make a space feel more like a showroom than a home.

And if you make a design decision and decide you hate it? “Change it,” says Keal. “It’s not a big deal. Paint over it, sell it on Facebook Marketplace and buy something else. We’re decorating, not doing brain surgery.”

More from How to start:

How to start meditating

How to start weightlifting

How to start budgeting

How to start running

How to start finding your personal style

Not sizing properly. “People struggle a lot with scale,” says Scott. “Rugs are often too small, curtains too short and couches too oversized.”

Other designers also bemoan undersized rugs. “The rug is almost always too small,” says Keal. “A 5’x7’ has no place in a living room.”

Focusing too much on trends. “The decorating process should be about cultivating personal style rather than trying to copy what’s popular,” says Pallay.

Following trends can also quickly leave a space feeling dated. “I always encourage people to mix eras, mix colors, and incorporate pieces that carry meaning,” says Klarić.

Vincent Pastore obituary

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:55:26 GMT

American actor best known for his role as Salvatore ‘Big Pussy’ Bonpensiero in the US TV crime drama series The Sopranos

The character actor Vincent Pastore, who has died aged 80, made Italian mobster roles his speciality, most notably playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero, one of the capos in The Sopranos. Although the character’s nickname came from his early career as a cat burglar, in a recent interview Pastore said the Soprano’s creator, David Chase, had written the part “for an actor who could play a tough guy but also could be sensitive. I saw Big Pussy as a man with a big heart.”

In the show, Pastore’s Pussy balanced the violent intensity of Tony Sirico’s Paulie Walnuts. “It was like sharing the camera with an elephant,” Pastore joked about the much smaller but intense actor.

One of The Sopranos’ most touching, if surreal, moments was centred on Pussy – and his demise. This came in the finale of series two, when Tony Soprano (played by James Gandolfini), in a fever dream while suffering food poisoning, realises who has been ratting the family out. Pussy, speaking to him as an eight-pound fish selling for four dollars a pound, confesses to Tony, and points out that the fish next to him are “sleeping”. As Pastore’s voice speaks, Tony says, “Don’t even say that,” as he realises agonisingly he will have to make Pussy sleep with the fishes too. The episode ends with Tony and two others (including a vengeful Paulie) shooting Pussy on Tony’s boat and tossing his body overboard.

Pastore himself was born in the Bronx, but grew up in what he described as the “true Italian” neighbourhood in the Westchester suburb of New Rochelle, in New York, where his father, John, was a school caretaker and his mother, Natalie (nee Santadonata), cooked part-time for the Italian men’s social club over which they lived. It was not a mob setting. “We saw bookies and loan sharks, but to play these parts you don’t rely on memories,” he said. “You use your own personality.”

After high school, during the Vietnam war, he enlisted in the US navy, then studied drama at the Westchester campus of Pace University. He worked as a bouncer in nightclubs, and as a limo driver, eventually buying his own club in New Rochelle. His first break came when he drove the actors Matt and Kevin Dillon, also from Westchester. They came to his club, saw him in local theatre, and were impressed. Kevin offered support, but as Pastore began to land roles, the actor Danny Aiello became his mentor.

In 1988 he made his film debut in the Canadian horror movie Black Roses. He played small parts in films, some of them very good, almost all of them involving crime. Between 1990 and 1995 he was in 15 movies, including an uncredited part in Sidney Lumet’s Q&A.

But the nature of his parts are reflected in his billing: “Man With Coat-rack” in Goodfellas, “Fat Tony” in Backstreet Dreams, “Tony Clams” in Who’s the Man, and “Copa Wiseguy” – from the Copacabana nightclub – in Carlito’s Way. His TV debut came in 1990, on the short-lived combined emergency services show H. E. L. P. with John Mahoney and Wesley Snipes. Like many New York actors, including other Sopranos cast members, he played in four episodes of Law and Order. Pastore’s breakthrough role came in a comedy crime vehicle, The Jerky Boys (1995), as Tony Scarboni, right-hand man to Alan Arkin’s crime boss, who is crossed by the eponymous comedians.

In 1996, he played a similar role in the HBO film Gotti, playing Angelo Ruggerio, the loyal No 2 to the New York crime boss John Gotti, played by Armand Assante, with whom he had worked on Q&A.

In 1997 he acted with Aiello in A Brooklyn State of Mind (with the future Sopranos cast member Jamie-Lynn Sigler), and in 1999 he was in the Hugh Grant comedy Mickey Blue Eyes.

The Sopranos debuted the same year, and in 2000 he won a Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding performance in an ensemble drama. Though Big Pussy was killed off at the end of season two, his career took new turns.

He had participated as a celebrity on the quiz comedy Hollywood Squares, but was soon in demand on the reality TV circuit. He was the host of Repo Men: Stealing for a Living, and lost 13kg on Celebrity Fit Club. He withdrew from Dancing With the Stars after a week, but his time on Celebrity Apprentice was marked by a feud with Piers Morgan. “Reality producers … to bring out the best or worst … place you in a bad improvisation scene with someone you genuinely don’t like,” he said.

In 2007 he made his Broadway debut in Chicago; the following year he also joined the cast of the daytime soap opera General Hospital. Pastore longed to do comedy; in 2009’s Oy Vey! My Son Is Gay! he was the father of the Italian boyfriend whose Jewish partner’s parents are more worried their son is with a non-Jewish boy than that he is gay.

Still he was landing roles such as “Don Vito Perspirino” in Pizza With Bullets (2010) or “Amadore Condimento” in Made in Chinatown (2021). He returned to Broadway in Woody Allen’s Bullets Over Broadway: The Musical in 2014, and that year led the Columbus Day parade in the Bronx.

He played recurring parts in Hawaii 5-0, Wu-Tang: An American Saga, and Gravesend, and had another leading role in the 2022 film The Black Caesar. He started a theatre company in 2021; his revival of the play Lamp Post Reunion starred Aiello. A new film, Bad News on the Doorstep, starring Chazz Palmintieri, Robert Davi, their sons Dante and Nick, respectively, and Sylvester Stallone’s daughter Sistine, has yet to be released.

Pastore lived alone in City Island in the Bronx. His marriage to Nancy Berke ended in divorce; he is survived by their daughter, Renee.

Vincent Dominic Pastore, actor, born 14 July 1946; died 1 August 2026

July was driest month in southern England since records began

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:44:20 GMT

England and Wales provisionally record driest July in nearly 200 years, Met Office says

July 2026 was the driest month in southern England since records began nearly 200 years ago, the Met Office has said.

England and Wales also provisionally recorded their driest July since records began in 1836. Wales had its joint warmest July on record for mean temperature, and England recorded its second warmest July.

The Met Office said the “remarkable conditions” this year came amid a summer marked by multiple heat records.

The heatwaves have been made more intense and more likely by the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis. The heatwave that affected western Europe at the end of June was the most severe and widespread ever.

July was the sixth consecutive month this year to have had above average mean temperatures, with only January so far experiencing mean temperatures below average.

Dr Amy Doherty, a science manager at the Met Office, said: “The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records.”

The Environment Agency said the conditions were affecting farmers, wildlife and the amount of water available for public and business use.

Half of England and the whole of Wales were last week declared to be officially in drought. In England, 40% of the population are under a hosepipe ban.

The National Farmers’ Union has warned the punishing drought could lead to shortages of certain foods in Britain.

A series of huge wildfires, supercharged by the climate crisis, has torched large parts of Europe this summer.

Greece is battling one of the worst seasons of wildfires of the past decade and in France, thousands of evacuees were allowed to return home or to holiday accommodation on Monday after the country’s largest wildfire on record.

Rivers in Europe are facing extremely low flows. The Danube’s water flow has fallen to 1,500 cubic metres a second in Romania, less than a third of its July average.

The Met Office said on Monday England had its driest July on record, with only 6.5mm of rainfall. That is only 10% of its long-term meteorological average for the month, and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

Wales has also had its driest July on record, with 9.3mm of rainfall – only 9% of its long-term meteorological average for the month.

Nineteen counties recorded less than (or equal to) 1mm of rainfall in July. These were: Berkshire, Dorset, East Riding of Yorkshire, East Sussex, Essex, Gloucestershire, Greater London, Herefordshire, Isle of Wight, Kent, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire, Nottinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Rutland, Surrey, Warwickshire and West Sussex.

The Environment Agency said last month water reserves “should be enough for the coming months until the next period of sustained rainfall”.

While rain is forecast for some parts of England, the Met Office said south-east England would continue to experience little rain.

Vampire-obsessed man detained after dumping animal corpses outside churches in New Forest

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:32:54 GMT

Benjamin Lewis, who believed drinking blood would prolong life, will be kept in hospital for treatment

A man fascinated with vampires and graveyards who apparently believed he would live for ever if he drank blood has been detained in hospital after being caught dumping animal corpses outside churches in a British forest.

Benjamin Lewis, 48, left the bodies of sheep and deer on the doorsteps of churches in the New Forest in Hampshire, frightening parishioners and upsetting farmers whose livestock he stole and slaughtered.

As part of the operation to trap Lewis, police officers carried out surveillance on ecclesiastical sites on significant dates in the satanic calendar.

Lewis was finally arrested after traces of his DNA were found on a lamb’s remains. He admitted causing religiously aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress and the theft of lambs.

During an earlier court appearance, Lewis, of Totton, Southampton, answered “Count Dracula” when asked to identify himself.

Judge William Mousley KC said he would be detained for treatment unless and until either a mental health tribunal or the justice secretary considered it safe for him to be released.

After his sentence, Lewis, who appeared via video link from hospital, apologised to his victims and said he bore no grudge towards the police who had caught him.

Speaking outside court, PC Jessica Surman of Hampshire police said it was the most unusual case she had worked on. “It’s one where you think you have reached the end of the bizarreness and then something else happens and throws a curveball into the mix.”

Lewis believed drinking blood would prolong his life, Surman said. “And if he drinks it enough he won’t go to hell, he won’t die and he will become a vampire.”

Police began investigating when dead animals – lambs stolen from farmers and deer killed on roads – started being found at churches.

Surman said police began to see a pattern in his offending. “We were almost able to predict when he was going to be striking.” They consulted satanic calendars, posting officers at churches on significant days.

People connected to the churches Lewis focused on were very concerned. “We have had people who were so upset and frightened by it, they couldn’t go to church,” Surman said. One woman was too scared to visit the church where her son was buried.

Laura Deuxberry, prosecuting, told Southampton crown court that lambs and deer were left by Lewis outside and inside churches, sometimes with an inverted cross nearby. A tarot card was also left near one.

A lamb was put on a cross on top of a church and a second close to a statue of Jesus’s mother, Mary. Another lamb was left in a church pulpit on a cross taken from the altar. On one occasion children saw what had happened and were very distressed.

One vicar said it made him angry – as if the “opposition” had left a signature. Another said: “It’s an insidious way to make a point.”

A church warden said she was “on edge” when she went to one of the churches Lewis targeted. She said he was trying to cause fear and unrest. A churchgoer said she felt someone was sending a “sadistic message”.

Deuxberry said one of the incidents centred on a community mental health facility close to Lewis’s home. A deer’s head and an inverted cross were left on the gates. The person who found the head said she was shocked and afterwards feared the culprit was watching her.

When police searched Lewis’s home they found sketches of vampires, notes about rituals and references to sucking blood.

Deuxberry said the offences he had been charged with took place between February and August last year but there had been concerns over him for a number of years.

The woods and heaths of the New Forest national park are the setting for all manner of tales of witches, pixies, cursed souls and rituals, and even today are a magnet for those fascinated by the otherworldly.

The village of Burley was the home of the “white witch” Sybil Leek, who wrote books on witchcraft and was famed for strolling around with her pet jackdaw.

But Lewis’s actions were quite different. Livestock owners that Lewis stole from were very disturbed. “It’s a terrible thing to do,” said Myra Noyce, one of the people Lewis took lambs from.

“It’s upset us all, made us feel very uncomfortable. This is a lovely part of the world and to think of someone going around doing something like that is horrible.”

Sarah Harrison, a New Forest farmer Lewis stole black lambs from, said: “It’s pretty awful – there are some silly people around. One of her lambs ended up outside St Peter’s church in the village of Bramshaw, another draped over a finger post. “I suppose it’s to do with his beliefs but it’s scared some people.”

In her victim personal statement, Harrison said she had been scared to walk alone at night and had thought about leaving the New Forest, though her family had lived there for generations. “I’m wondering what will it be next. When I hear a sound outside I think is that him.”

She said the lambs would have suffered when he cut their throat and he put the bodies on show as if they meant nothing. She said the incidents had put the flock on alert.

The consultant psychiatrist Dr Gauruv Malhan told the court Lewis had “complex mental health difficulties” and had recently been moved from a low- to medium-secure hospital.

He said at the age of 13 Lewis had left a dead frog on a cross in church and the psychiatrist said he feared he could harm humans as well as animals. In hospital he had assaulted other patients and attempted to assault Malhan when he visited him and had to be restrained.

Andrew Price, defending, said Lewis was sorry and recognised he had done wrong.

Lewis’s conviction is not his first brush with the law. In 2003 he was jailed for terrorising a vicar and his family near his home by claiming to be a vampire. He and another man made abusive and frightening phone calls, set off fireworks and posted obscene pictures on the church noticeboard.

Science funding cuts will harm Britain’s global standing

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:28:04 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial about the threat to research funding, including plans to close the Jodrell Bank Observatory

Your editorial rightly criticises the decision to cease funding the Lovell telescope from March 2028 (The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics, 31 July). There are additional reasons why this decision is so shortsighted. Modern astronomy is no longer simply physics. It brings together physics, chemistry, biology and computing to understand how the universe evolved and where we came from. The universe is an inexpensive laboratory in which we can study the interaction of physical, chemical and biological processes under conditions that can never be reproduced on Earth. Understanding how galaxies formed and evolved requires complementary observations across the radio, optical and infrared spectrum. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

As a PhD researcher at Jodrell Bank in the 1960s, I saw first-hand how its innovations transformed radio astronomy. Jodrell played a pioneering role in the development of long-baseline radio interferometry, which links separate telescopes together to create virtual telescopes thousands of miles across. Removing the Lovell telescope from this network would weaken its ability to produce pictures of the radio universe with a sharpness comparable to that achieved by billion-pound space observatories such as Hubble.

The Lovell telescope still plays a role in science diplomacy and it has long been a symbol of UK scientific leadership and hope. Ministers should think again. George Kildare MileyEmeritus professor of astronomy, Leiden University, the Netherlands

The shortsighted attitude to science funding goes back to Margaret Thatcher. In the late 1980s I was briefly the economic adviser to the chief scientist, working in the Cabinet Office. The policy was to rate research funding on objective criteria such as the number of peer-reviewed publications and citations, and also to focus funding on research expected to have economic benefits in the near term. It was assumed that, as an economist, I would be a primary advocate for this approach. I argued that there was no methodology for assessing which research would turn out to be economically beneficial. There still isn’t.

I also argued that the attempt to quantify research success by counting publications was leading to counterproductive effects – pressure to publish too much and too soon, multiple authors on every paper and a high-stress atmosphere that is fundamentally counterproductive to good research.

I also found myself the sole advocate in the Cabinet Office for supporting research for its own sake – to advance human knowledge. We are made far poorer culturally as well as economically if we close the spaces in which talented people are given the time and funding to follow wherever their creativity leads them. Mick FosterChelmsford, Essex

The UK Research and Innovation budget is expected to rise to £10bn by 2030. However, UKRI consists of research councils (which mostly fund fundamental science) plus Innovate UK. The latter funds only companies, and only its budget has risen. That for research councils has plummeted, by 40%-50% in real terms since 2011. As universities also grab a higher proportion of grants in “overheads”, the amount of actual science being funded is even lower. The flow of postdoctoral fellows needed to work in innovative industries is consequently being choked. Douglas KellOxford

Thank you for an excellent editorial on the devastating cuts to major projects and research facilities, announced in a year when UKRI received a record budget settlement. The Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) upgrade, a top priority of the European Strategy for Particle Physics, endorsed by Cern Council with UK support, has been particularly hard hit. The announced withdrawal of funding risks cutting off a generation of UK scientists from the future of one of Cern’s four flagship experiments.

The UK’s leadership in LHCb was built through decades of sustained investment. The UK should now reap the returns: graduates skilled in AI and data science; advances in semiconductors, materials and technology; students who are attracted to science by the opportunity to work at a world-leading laboratory; and, crucially, a reputation as a trusted partner capable of participating in and hosting major international projects.

Withdrawing previously secured funding has shocked international partners. It undermines UK leadership, drastically reduces opportunities for PhD students and postdocs, and damages technological development.

This investment represents less than 0.05% of the UK’s £10bn annual research budget. We hope that it will be swiftly restored. Paula CollinsLHCb deputy spokesperson, Cern

The buzz about fly infestations this summer

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:27:51 GMT

Readers respond to an article on the swarms of houseflies people are having to cope with in hot weather

My experience of flies is that during the past 20 years or so there has been a significant decline in numbers – Highland midges not included of course (‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies?, 30 July).

Memories of childhood summers in the 1950s and 60s are of endless sticky flytraps, typically placed near doorways in the house. Any foodstuffs left out on a counter would immediately attract a variety of coloured flies within seconds.

Summer picnics could be a constant tussle against flying insects, including wasps. Sandwiches, even wrapped, presented a challenge that flies and wasps couldn’t resist. Pints of beer would encourage wasps to take up swimming until they became intoxicated. The swarms of butterflies this year are a different matter – and delightful sight to see. Mal Jones Cardiff

While I do not diminish the efforts of the people behind Buglife and the expertise of Erica McAlister quoted in your article, as we do need insects, I found the ideas presented to ameliorate fly infestations quite out of touch with a large number of people suffering from this plague.

What about those of us who live in flats with no access to a garden to create a wildlife pond? Or those without the means to turn their outside space into a haven for wildlife? Placing a bucket on the veranda might work for those with the space, but those of us in flats must suffer without resolution. Jonathon MoloneyLeighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire

The best solution is to fit permanent insect screens to all windows and doors. It can be expensive, but it’s a one-off cost. A major benefit is that it allows windows to be open at night for ventilation, while still preventing insects, especially mosquitoes, from entering. A problem in the UK is that most windows open outwards, so while screens can easily be fixed to the outside frame of the inward-opening windows here in Switzerland, the same would not be true in the UK.

Let’s hope some smart, enterprising people can come up with a solution for UK windows. Dr Janet DawsonBennwil, Switzerland

Here in the French Basque Country, our house is next to a sheep farm where several hundred sheep are housed, largely indoors, and in the summer we are usually beset by dozens of flies indoors. We have several barn swallows’ nests in our barn, which I carefully protect, but despite the swallows’ best efforts, the number of flies has always been annoying – until this year when we have had very few flies. The (inhumane) fly papers hanging in the kitchen are almost bare of prey. My first reaction was one of relief, although this was relatively short-lived as it was not long before I saw the decline in the fly population as an indication of the enormous and worrying decline in the overall insect population. Phil RuslingSaint-Jean-le-Vieux, France

As a football-mad 10-year-old, I had the misfortune on the day of the final to be on our family summer holiday in the then sleepy village of Goathland, staying in a house with no TV.

Hope rose when my dad was invited to watch the final at a neighbour’s who had one of the few TVs in the village and he asked if he could bring his children. When the neighbour learned that there were seven of us, he not surprisingly drew the line at a still very generous three, but as the fourth in line I missed out.

Instead, I sat in the kitchen along with my mam and three younger sisters listening to the rarely mentioned but equally brilliant Brian Moore and Alan Clarke’s commentary on BBC radio. To this day, I still haven’t seen the match but nevertheless, like Garry, cherish my happy memories of it. Andrew KeeleyWarrington, Cheshire

The best way to protect NHS patients’ data

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:27:07 GMT

A genuinely competitive market would prevent any single company’s decisions from putting the system at risk, says Prof Erika Denton

Your article on the TPG/Optum UK deal, over the patient record system used by most GP practices in England, highlights a specific issue that is symptomatic of a much bigger problem (Alarm at NHS patient records being put under control of US private equity firm, 27 July). I’ve spent years working across the NHS, both in clinical radiology and in national policy roles, and this deal follows a pattern. Systems holding patients’ most sensitive data keep ending up with a small number of large suppliers.

The real opportunity now is to build on the progress already under way, so that ownership of any single system carries less risk regardless of who holds it. NHS England’s own steps, from guidance on AI-enabled tools to the health bill’s proposed provisions on the single patient record, point in the right direction. What should follow on from that is straightforward: data hosted in the UK, a clinician signing off before anything changes in a patient’s record, and an audit trail that regulators and patients can actually check.

The deeper opportunity is in the market itself. A genuinely competitive market needs suppliers working on open, standards-based systems, so that patient records aren’t trapped behind one vendor’s walls, and information is captured as structured, checkable data.

The NHS has already begun building accountability like this into how it works with suppliers, and there’s real value in going further, applying that same standard consistently to every supplier, wherever they are based, on open interoperability and clear governance. That’s what keeps any single company’s decisions from putting the whole system at risk. I’d rather see energy go into growing that choice, so that the NHS is never again this dependent on so few hands. Erika DentonHonorary professor of radiology, University of East Anglia; clinical adviser to AI care partner, Heidi

Yoga, kabaddi and the cut-price plan for Commonwealth Games survival

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:19:45 GMT

Glasgow proved that a streamlined programme could hold the key to reviving the prospects of a seemingly doomed event

How good are you at judging a sun salutation or scorpion pose? I ask because yoga is under consideration as a sport at the next Commonwealth Games in India. Less surprisingly, so is kabaddi. But if Amdavad 2030 really wants to find experts in landing seemingly impossible manoeuvres, or holding their breath in tricky situations, they should take the next flight to Scotland.

Let us be frank. Glasgow 2026 has saved the Commonwealth Games, at least for now. After Victoria pulled out in 2023, the event was in limbo. Some feared it would never find a way out. Then Glasgow stepped in, less a knight in shining armour, more one that was a little dented and rusty, to put on an event from scratch in barely 20 months.

It didn’t help that the BBC did not televise it, but that is not the Commonwealth Games’ fault. The BBC offered a derisory sum, which left organisers with little option but to go with Warner Bros Discovery. For many, it was out of sight, out of mind. But those in Glasgow will testify these were a fun Games, full of heart and surprise.

There were fears that few fans would show up. In the end, 434,000 of the 500,000 tickets were sold, putting the Games at 87% capacity. There were great stories too, such as Josh Kerr’s raw power in the mile and Emily Campbell throwing the weight of a couple of beer kegs above her head like they were beer cans.

It was so busy I never got the chance to write up one of my favourite interviews, with the South Africa swimmer – and Commonwealth medal record holder – Chad le Clos. At one point we asked after his father, Bert, who became famous at London 2012 for his celebrations, his beard and his larger‑than‑life chats with Clare Balding, but has had cancer since.

“He’s lost about 40kg,” Le Clos said. “He was 138kg. He weighs 99kg now. You won’t recognise him because he walks every day. But he still says: ‘This is my boy. He’s won 18, 19, 20, 21 medals. And he’s going to break the world record now.’ But people are like, ‘No, you’re not him. He’s the big old man, the Cookie Monster from the telly.’”

Even at the end, Glasgow was flying by the seat of its pants. Usually, the closing ceremony is practised on stage until everything is honed to perfection. This one had to be rehearsed at a compound at the back of the Hydro, because the netball was on, before Simple Minds closed the show with Alive and Kicking.

The Games is still that, all right. But for how much longer? We can all agree India will be spectacular. The opening ceremony is expected to be staged at the Narendra Modi Stadium, which seats 132,000. Many facilities are also already in place. India wants to stage the 2036 Olympic Games. It will not skimp on the trimmings.

Katie Sadleir, the chief executive of Commonwealth Sport, says Amdavad will stage between 15 and 17 sports – up from Glasgow’s 10 – from three buckets: core, optional and traditional.

The 10 core sports include athletics, swimming, gymnastics, boxing, netball and bowls. The five optional sports will be drawn from a list that contains cricket, triathlon and hockey. India can pick two traditional sports, which is where kabaddi and yoga may come in.

However, Sadleir cautions that the traditional sports have to be played around the Commonwealth, have a recognised international federation and be World Anti‑Doping Agency compliant.

That explains why she is more positive about kabaddi’s chances. Even if the possibility of yoga brings up the intriguing prospect of someone being asked for a sample while in a lotus position.

after newsletter promotion

But the trickier question for the Commonwealth Games is what happens after 2030. Durban pulled out in 2017 as the 2022 host because the finances did not stack up and while Birmingham stepped in it lost a fortune. Glasgow was cheaper, but it was funded by the AUS$380m fine paid by Victoria when it withdrew. So can the Games really survive?

Sadleir recalls a recent sports conference where she was sitting near the IOC president, Kirsty Coventry, and someone from the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. “I went right after Brisbane said they were going to raise $5.2bn. And I said, have I ever got a story to tell? We’ve gone from an £800m event to a £160m event because we’ve listened and we’ve learned.

“The only way we can continue is by resetting, reimagining, and making the Games affordable. Glasgow is a proof of concept with that in terms of cost and using existing facilities.”

But addressing the problem is one thing. Making enough to keep the Games going, quite another. While many remain sceptical, Sadleir is admirably indefatigable and optimistic.

She points out that Glasgow raised £30m in sponsorship and commercial revenue in a short space of time. She also promises to look at ways to attract more big names, including using the Commonwealths as a qualifier for world championships. Certainly something needs to be done. If Keely Hodgkinson, Summer McIntosh and Julien Alfred don’t want to show up, then why should the rest of us?

Sadleir says five countries are interested in 2034, including New Zealand and Nigeria, and to avoid another situation like Durban and Victoria, governments will have to be a bid underwriter in future. Abuja in eight years’ time anyone?

Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may work

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:00:21 GMT

Mikel Arteta’s team and the Brazilian star could be a perfect match. It also could be a risk that ends in disaster

Sometimes what is needed is something different.

There is a long history in football of counterintuitive thinking being successful, of the benefits of creative tension, of adding grit to the oyster to generate the pearl, but even so, the news that talks between Vinícius Júnior and Arsenal on personal terms are progressing comes as something of a shock. Mikel Arteta’s great followers of a blueprint adding a free spirit like the Brazilian? Really?

Vinícius returns to Real Madrid this week after the World Cup with movement on his future expected relatively soon. He has 12 months remaining on his contract and Madrid are keen either to tie him down to a new deal or to sell him while he will attract at least some kind of fee. As their squad rebuild goes on under José Mourinho, Madrid’s position is readily understandable. They have already signed Bernardo Silva, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella and Ibrahima Konaté this summer; removing Vinícius’s £420,000 a week (about $30m/year) basic wages significantly increases their financial headroom.

There’s been a sense since Kylian Mbappé joined Madrid two years ago that having him and Vinícius together left the squad unbalanced. Why would you need two rapid forwards who both prefer to cut in from the left, particularly when Rodrygo, who tended to be consigned to the right before tearing his ACL in March, would also prefer to play from the left? Yan Diomandé is likely to confirm his move to Real Madrid from RB Leipzig this week. Although the Ivorian has said he would rather play on the right, he too has spent much of his career on the left.

More broadly, Vinícius does not seem a natural Mourinho player. His pace and technical excellence are undoubted, but he has never been the most diligent at fulfilling his defensive responsibilities. Mourinho likes a forward who can improvise, and worked successfully with Cristiano Ronaldo at Madrid, but it’s difficult to see how he could indulge more than one such player at a time, and Mbappé will take precedence.

But those concerns about tracking, about the willingness to stick to a gameplan, about the capacity to retain possession are just as relevant to Arteta as they are to Mourinho – arguably more so, as Arteta believes far more in structured attacking planning than Mourinho. Is Vinícius, after years of freedom at Madrid, really going to accept those rigid structures?

It’s been fairly clear since the second half of last season that Arsenal would be looking to strengthen their left side. The sale of Leandro Trossard to Beşiktaş did not come as a huge surprise. The 31-year-old is reliable and played a valuable role last season, starting 21 of the 38 league games and coming off the bench on a further 10 occasions, but there is not much stardust about him. Gabriel Martinelli started 11 league games and came off the bench 19 times, and his pace can be a great asset, but it’s no longer clear that he is at his best on the left. The signing of Eberechi Eze last summer looked like an attempt to add creativity from that flank but his tendency to drift infield when Arteta needs his left-sided forward to stay wide meant that by the end of the season he tended to be used centrally behind a striker.

Vinícius would give Arsenal greater attacking thrust. At his best, under Carlo Ancelotti, he could transform a game in seconds. His pace, dribbling ability and finishing mean that no matter how stale a game seems to have gone, no matter how under pressure his team may be, they are never more than seven or eight seconds from a potential goal. It’s easy to see why Arsenal are tempted by him. He would immediately be their highest-profile player, adding a sense of direction to a summer that, at least from a recruitment point of view, has seemed to be drifting. Arsenal missed out on Morgan Rogers, who joined Chelsea, while Julián Álvarez, who would seem a much more natural fit on the Arsenal left, appears more likely to go to Barcelona, if sufficient financial levers can be pulled.

But the fact Vinícius is not a natural fit may be part of the attraction. It was, after all, the season after signing Erling Haaland, far from a typical Pep Guardiola player, that Manchester City won the treble. A player who does not quite fit, who kicks against the general philosophy, can make a process team less predictable. The friction can produce valuable sparks.

after newsletter promotion

Haaland, it’s fair to say, is a different personality from Vinícius and, as a center-forward, there was never a worry he was going to leave his full-back exposed. Vinícius is a bigger risk. He would certainly be an expensive one, not just in terms of his own salary but the inflationary pressure that could have on wages at the club more generally.

But he would also add a dash Arsenal have lacked that would make the accusation of being dead-ball plodders hard to sustain. And with Trossard gone, there is a left-sided hole that needs filling.
