Sunday Times and Sun columnist Rod Liddle dies aged 66

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 14:53:14 GMT

Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illness

The writer and broadcaster Rod Liddle, a prominent columnist for the Sunday Times and the Sun, has died after a short illness. He was 66.

Liddle, whose provocative style attracted praise and criticism, also wrote for the Spectator magazine and earlier in his career edited BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

Liddle worked as a speechwriter for the Labour party in the 1980s, but his later writing often critiqued and criticised the left.

Tributes to Liddle were paid by Piers Morgan, the former Sunday Times editor Andrew Neil and the Today programme presenter Justin Webb, who described Liddle as brilliant, kind and funny.

The former Sun editor David Yelland said Liddle “morphed into a brilliant and gifted writer who I could rarely agree with but always turned to first”.

He said: “It was because he was so talented he was able to behave so badly and write so (it has to be said) abhorrently on many occasions. And he knew this. It was his essence. RIP Rod.”

Liddle died at the James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening. His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said in a statement: “We’re all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

“He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous. Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

“He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life.”

Liddle was no stranger to controversy. In 2010 he became the first blogger to be censured by the Press Complaints Commission, for incorrectly stating in a Spectator piece that the “overwhelming majority” of violent crime in London was carried out by young African-Caribbean men.

Liddle left as editor of Today in 2002. At the time, it was reported that his departure followed a disagreement with the BBC’s then director general, Greg Dyke, about a regular column he wrote for the Guardian.

In one column Liddle had criticised Countryside Alliance marchers as “Mill on the Floss extras” and “those who own the countryside, or run it, together with a forelock-tugging menagerie of their better-paid servants”.

It was during his tenure at Today that Liddle hired Andrew Gilligan, the journalist whose 2003 report claimed the UK government had “sexed up” its dossier on Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction. Liddle left the BBC before Gilligan’s report was broadcast.

Liddle also presented a programme about infidelity, arguing that men were genetically pre-programmed to be unfaithful. His former wife had written about his adultery in a series of newspaper features.

Rebekah Brooks, the chief executive of News UK, which publishes the Sunday Times and the Sun, said everyone at the company had been “deeply shocked and saddened” to learn of his sudden death.

“Rod was an inimitable journalistic force, brilliant, provocative and immensely talented, whose sharp wit and uncompromising voice graced our pages and airwaves for decades,” she said. “He challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism.”

Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, said: “Rod Liddle had a wonderful way with words and used his unique talent to speak for the readers, highlighting the cant and absurdity that bedevils modern life. He was also supremely entertaining and for years his column was the first that many turned to every Sunday. We will miss him desperately.”

Victoria Newton, the editor-in-chief of the Sun, said: “A champion of press freedom, no topic was off-limits, and his writing – as funny as it was excoriating – was simply exceptional. A terrific observer of the frailties of our political class, he will be remembered for his razor sharp wit and for his huge intellect.”

Does Andy Burnham really hate London? He wouldn’t be the only one

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 14:17:41 GMT

Both left and right have it in for Britain’s capital. But is London a stabby wasteland, a den of faceless bureaucrats, or just a mess of overprivileged wokerati?

‘I’ve seen no evidence of Andy being anti-London,” the capital’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, told the Evening Standard last week, which is quaint and adorable: evidence is so 2009. This is all about feels. Some feel that the prime minister disfavours the capital because he frequently mentions that neoliberalism hasn’t delivered a fair deal for the north of England; tacitly, then, someone’s deal has been unfair in the other direction, and that would be the south, which must be London. Where else would Burnham mean – Hastings? The institution of No 10 North gestures audibly towards there being some problem with the OG Downing Street, and the use of the words “Whitehall” and “Westminster” as anything but geographical denominations – connoting “faceless” or “out of touch” or “rigid” or “having contempt for the ordinary person” – gives strong anti-London vibes, since Whitehall and Westminster are, indisputably, in London.

You could group all that as leftwing shorthand. For those moments when you want to describe a shallow, mammon-worshipping society, lurching blindly from one shiny, meaningless prize to the next, empty of proper feeling for others or for nature, “London” pretty well covers it.

That vibe – which only ever described a sliver of the capital, basically the bit of Notting Hill where Boris Johnson might once have lived and Canary Wharf – was repurposed by the (British) right wing a decade ago to become the “metropolitan elite”. In 2016, this version of the typical Londoner had all the same characteristics as before – they’re in a bubble, they’re rolling in gold, they neither understand nor care about the conditions of the common man – but with the appended trait of liberalism, or wokeratiness (if you prefer).

By a process so transparently syllogistic and stupid that for a while it was hard to even discuss it without howling like a wolf, the expression of any attitude that might distinguish you from Enoch Powell placed you squarely in the “metropolitan liberal elite” and therefore rendered you dispensable, inauthentic. There were a ton of other markers of privilege – coffee shops, public transport infrastructure, tofu, the Guardian! – so you were checkmated everywhere you went. This wasn’t really about living in London, or even any big city: you could get your passport to the metropole from drinking matcha, believing in universal human rights or knowing how to board public transport, rather than dithering near the door like an idiot. But obviously all of this was so much more rife in the capital.

This is quite distinct from what the global right wing hates about Londoners, which is, briefly, that we’re savages who won’t stop killing each other. As I’ve written before, the former Guardian staffer Gary Younge came back from the US in 2016, where he had been reporting on the Maga right, with a fascinating account of a dinner with some Republicans who had asked him how he could possibly feel safe living in London, now that the Muslims had elected “their” mayor and the rest of us weren’t even allowed guns.

It seemed so extraordinary then, and now is an absolute commonplace, to hear the capital described as a “stabby wasteland” where grinding poverty interlaces with intractable race wars to create a brutal place, the global nidus of civilisational decay. There’s some overlap with the British right, insofar as London is where multiculturalism is supposed to have failed, and taken society down with it. But there are no liberal elitists in the global right’s concept of “Londonistan”; it would be way too rough and dangerous for our luxury-softened paws. No data or firsthand testimonials can dispel this myth of the capital. It works better if it isn’t true; it makes insisting on reality that little bit more exhausting.

None of this answers, definitively, the question of whether the prime minister hates London, since there are signals in the other direction. His plan to give regional mayors a slice of their tax take would work better for Khan than almost anyone, what with London’s feverish mammon-love.

I will meet some of these detractors halfway and accept that Londoners definitely lack something in the areas of gentleness and humility. To everyone else, I’d channel Millwall: no one likes us, we don’t care. Multiculturalism in action, in a single London heart.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

‘The obsession with endless growth can only end in tears’: your questions on extreme weather this summer answered

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 14:14:47 GMT

From Europe’s deadly heat to floods in Asia, it’s been a terrifying summer. Environment writers Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan answered Reddit users’ questions about their work – and their sources of hope

Extreme weather supercharged by the climate crisis is fuelling an explosive wildfire season in Europe and extreme rainfall across Asia this summer.

Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather stoking wildfires at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France. EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.

Meanwhile, unprecedented rains continue across Asia. As South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides. Extreme rainfall across the world is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown.

The Guardian’s Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan has been covering the extreme heat and wildfires across Europe this summer, while global environment writer Jonathan Watts reported on the floods in Asia.

Ajit and Jonathan answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.

Desenrasco asked: How scared should I be about wildfires?

To consider it in the bluntest of terms, wildfires kill surprisingly few people: perhaps hundreds around the world each year, compared to thousands from floods and hundreds of thousands from heatwaves. That is, of course, of little comfort to the people across Spain and France returning to burned-out homes, or to the families of firefighters, locals and tourists who have died in the past few weeks. But what scares me far more is the smoke. Recent studies peg the global death toll from wildfire smoke at 1.5 million people per year. The wildfire season in Canada three years ago was so bad, one study found, that more than 80,000 people died from smoke inhalation – and 20,000 of them were in Europe, as winds carried the pollution over the Atlantic.

Sg_plumber asked: How come pretty much everybody (at least on TV) always forgets to mention that yes, the climate crisis is fuelling these extreme weather events?

Jonathan Watts: I agree. This is not just exasperating, it is frightening. The climate and nature crises are the greatest threats humanity has faced, yet many media organisations downplay or ignore it. Social media is even worse, propagating misinformation and distracting people from the root cause of the problem (petrochemical companies, big agriculture and every rising emissions of greenhouse gases). The Guardian is able to devote much of its resources to covering these topics because it does not have an owner and because our readers make very clear that they want a big share of their contributions to go to this topic. Economy-Fee5830 asked: You’ve written about oil majors profiting as the world heats. But European wildfire deaths and flood deaths are overwhelmingly determined by local building codes, evacuation planning and firefighting budgets. Does the Big Oil accountability framing crowd out the more boring domestic policy failures that actually determine the body count?

Ajit: I broadly agree with your question but slightly disagree with the premise. Rapid analysis studies in recent years have attributed 40-70% of the death toll from big European heatwaves to the increase in temperatures from carbon pollution.

With wildfires and floods it’s much harder for scientists to say how much climate breakdown contributed to the death toll. I’ve covered European floods where they’ve shown the rainfall that triggered the floods to have been made stronger or more likely by up to 20% but, as one scientist put it to me after floods in central Europe last year, it’s a binary problem: the dam will either fail or not. In cases like the floods in Germany’s Ahrtal in 2021, or in Valencia, Spain, in 2024, we saw both jaw-dropping evacuation failures and climate-exacerbated rain.

Cutting fossil fuel pollution is indeed a fundamental solution, and it must be accompanied by a never-ending list of other adaptation measures. I would argue our coverage is pretty good at including both bits. Every article I’ve written on wildfires this summer has included rising temperatures and land abandonment. Our flood coverage had the failures of authorities at the forefront.

Owl1917 asked: With climate anxiety on the rise, particularly amongst younger generations, what advice would you give to those who see the future as hopeless?

Ajit: More than anything else, I would challenge anyone who feels hopeless to be specific about what’s troubling them. This is obviously easier said than done, but if you take a couple of hours to write down what it is that scares you about climate breakdown, what makes you angry, and what leaves you feeling hopeless, the fears become (hopefully) easier to confront.

In my case, reporting on the climate has made me way less worried about some problems and way more worried about others. In terms of hope, I am, perhaps unpopularly, a firm believer in the idea that we have far more agency than anyone around me seems to realise (with the exception of a handful of scientists). Too many people my age claim a powerlessness that is not backed up by data. Sure, your ability to replace a coal plant with a wind turbine may be limited (it’s still not nothing, if you live in a democracy) but you have power over what you eat, how you get around, how much you buy. Consider diets: our collective choice to eat meat and dairy is responsible for 12-20% of planet-heating emissions, and doctors recommend people in rich countries eat far less of it for their own health, let alone the climate. Does this sound like our actions are pointless?

Gold-Loan3142 asked: How do we challenge the mainstream ‘“perpetual growth” economics that infuses almost all discussion of the economy?

Jonathan: You have touched on one of the core issues. The obsession with endless GDP growth on a finite planet can only end in tears. The only question is when. There have been numerous academic challenges to this and alternatives, such as Kate Raworth’s Doughnut Economics and Bill McKibben’s Economics as if the World Mattered. There are also some very interesting studies and books on degrowth by the likes of Jason Hickell and many others.

If I can stray outside my journalist role, I have long believed that what the world needs is not just economic degrowth but ecological regrowth. We need a system of trade, currency, taxation, incentives that rewards countries and companies for restoring the world’s battered ecosystems.

SurinamPam asked: A lot of carbon is emitted for road transportation, building heating/cooling, and electricity generation. And, the world is quickly switching to EVs, heat pumps, and building out solar, wind, and batteries. If all those carbon sources go to zero, how much of an effect will it have on future climate change?

Jonathan: That is a fascinating point. I haven’t done or seen the calculations on this. But, speaking far more broadly, the energy transition is one of four great causes for hope that I have right now. Wind, solar and electric vehicles have taken off far more quickly than almost anyone expected even a decade go. This has the potential to change the global balance of power and, I believe, may also be behind rising US aggression in terms of military conflict, tariffs and attacks on democracy.

Distracted-Nomad asked: In terms of advocacy, what are the most powerful things you can say to convince individuals that their efforts (ie lifestyle change) are important? Most people I know say whatever they do won’t make a difference and governments and corporations need to change before we do.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Jonathan: This is one of the most common and important questions that climate journalists get. I agree the priority must be political action because the required changes – higher taxes on fossil fuels, a wealth tax on billionaires, more investment in renewables, more incentives for plant-based diets, etc – need to come at a national and international level. That said, I disagree that individual action is meaningless. It can set an example to others. And it can show that change can be beneficial to health and wallet. Imagine, for example, how much money electric car owners have saved during the recent oil price spikes. The key is to do this while never letting the petro-companies off the hook. They have tried in the past to convince people that the responsibility for the climate crisis lies with individual consumers. That was why they pushed the idea of carbon calculators. But the real blame lies with them. Most of the big oil companies are expanding production and making record profits.

Karenadona asked: How much longer do we have until we run out of time to save the planet?

Ajit: In one sense, it is never too late, and in another sense, it already is too late. The planet will survive, and even apocalyptic scenarios do not really consider an end to life on Earth as a result of climate breakdown. But while there is technically no time limit to action – climate scientists stress that each extra ton of carbon dioxide heats the planet a bit more – the likelihood of triggering catastrophic tipping points rises the hotter it gets. The 1.5C global heating target, which world leaders agreed to in Paris in 2015, looks extremely likely to be missed. (I am not saying definitely, as it is physically still possible, even if emissions have risen to a level where it is perhaps societally implausible.) Keeping below 2C of warming is, however, very much still possible. Current projections put us on track for somewhere between 2C and 3C by the end of the century.

Szabolcs85 asked: Is there anything to be hopeful about? The future looks very bleak.

Jonathan: I am also pessimistic, but there are still many things to fight for. Every fraction of a degree of warming that we can prevent will help millions of people and billions of other forms of life. UN-led action have already helped in this way, but not enough. But international cooperation is worthwhile.

My four other causes for hope:

The energy transition, particularly in China.

The rise of the rights for nature movement, which - although imperfect – is confronting the core of our problems, which is a broken relationship with the non-human part of the planet.

Alternative ways of thinking and being found in the global south, particularly among indigenous communities.

The prospect of the global population peaking before 2050, which should reduce pressure on the environment.

Set against this, unfortunately, are the huge military and financial forces of petrostates, such as the US, Russia and Saudi Arabia, often aligned with big corporations.

Fraggin601 asked: How do you think our economic systems must change to cope with climate change?

Jonathan: Great subject. The first step should be a realistic appraisal of the economic risks posed by the climate and nature crises. Currently, most economists are absurdly complacent. The Nobel prize winner William Nordhaus assumes a very low hit to GDP but he omits – as the commentator Genevieve Guenther notes – the full costs of labour productivity, buildings, infrastructure, transportation, non-coastal real estate, insurance, communication, government services and other sectors. Most worrying to me is that most economic model assume smooth linear warming, even though many climate scientists warn of tipping points that are likely to bring jolts, acceleration and catastrophe. It is as though a doctor treats everything as a chronic, manageable ailment while ignoring the very real risks of acute, life-threatening diseases.

Nature also needs to be much more highly valued – and not just in economic terms. Then there is the question of inequality – between nations, communities and species. There is no GDP without a healthy environment. And there is no greater theft from the poor than the loss of clean air, fresh water, fertile soil and a stable climate. On a positive note, I have been very impressed by the recent work done by the World Inequality Lab to try to incorporate more planetary boundaries into their projections of what a cleaner and fairer world could look like.

Lightning7Bolt asked: What can a 17-year-old like me do to fight for change?

Jonathan Watts: Find out all you can from news articles, books and films. Then spread the word. The great climate science communicator Katherine Hayhoe says the most important thing you can do to fight climate change is to talk about it. Age can be to your advantage. Your generation is the future. Older people are threatening that. Greta Thunberg was 15 when she started fighting for change, sitting outside the Swedish parliament with a sign saying “School Strike for Climate”. By the time she was 17, the movement had gone global. Millions took to the streets and the head of Opec, the world’s biggest oil cartel, declared the youth protest “perhaps the greatest threat to our industry.”

Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 14:13:01 GMT

Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity

Explainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?

A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.

Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.

The extraordinary influx had overwhelmed the city of 84,000 people and set off a political crisis across the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain.

In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.”

He said local people watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.”

He drew a parallel with May 2021, when Rabat loosened border controls, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

This time around, analysts have suggested that Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s arch-enemy Algeria could have triggered a response from Morocco.

Speaking on Monday, Spain’s defence minister, Margarita Robles, also seemingly signalled Rabat’s involvement. “Neither Spain nor Morocco can look the other way when it comes to this tragedy,” she told reporters. “I ask the Moroccan government to fully investigate what happened.”

The insinuation appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage.

Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through.

In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. One local official told reporters that those who remained in the city included 862 unaccompanied minors.

Ashraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through.

“You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.”

Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children, aged 13 and 16.

She had left Morocco alone, finding out later that her two children had followed her by plunging into the sea to make their way around the border.

“I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.”

Across the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy said it had suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for one month, despite the fact that Ceuta is not part of Schengen.

Before an emergency video meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected.

“There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.”

What had transpired in Ceuta was “very unusual”, he said. “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” he added, while Italy “was the country with the highest number of irregular entries in Europe”.

He said he had been in contact with Moroccan authorities throughout the crisis. “They showed a willingness from the very beginning to mobilise police forces to help stem the flow of migrants.”

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, and she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said.

At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, had criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated.

There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said.

EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, the source added.

The concerns came into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks.

“We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.”

‘Clacton voters need a serious person’: the independent candidates taking on Nigel Farage – and Count Binface

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 14:05:56 GMT

Attieh Fard and Andy Erlam make their byelection pitch to voters, but Reform UK’s leader is conspicuously absent

In the town square in Clacton, in the blazing midday sunshine, some of the candidates for the upcoming byelection made their pitch to a scattering of potential voters, passing Deliveroo drivers and a giant gull.

But as the independent candidate Attieh Fard shouted into a megaphone that she would be a voice for Clacton, a passing youth shouted: “Where’s Binface?”

At one of the hustings being held before polling day on 13 August, the two main contenders in the election, Nigel Farage and Count Binface, were conspicuous by their absence.

Fard, a former Tory; and a fellow independent candidate, Andy Erlam, will be holding hustings at midday in the town centre of the Essex town every day until voting day. But Farage and the Count have failed to respond to the invitation.

The byelection has been regarded as somewhat of a joke by the main political parties, the media, and the novelty bin candidate, after Farage triggered it amid mounting pressure over his finances. Rather than wanting the parliamentary authorities to adjudicate whether he should have declared a £5m gift from a crypto billionaire prior to being elected, Farage resigned his seat in parliament and asked the people of Clacton to decide.

All the large political parties thus decided not to stand, hoping the public would see the ridiculousness of Farage spending the summer, as Rachel Reeves put it, having an argument with a bin.

New polling by Survation for Mandate Research suggests Farage would win 73% of the vote on a low turnout, but that 20% would vote for Jonathan Harvey, the comedian who pretends to be a space lord named Count Binface and who wears a bin as a helmet.

But Fard, a smartly dressed lawyer, said: “Clacton voters need a serious person to vote for.”

“Our democratic system should not be made into a joke or used in this way, this election should be about the people of Clacton,” she added.

She said she was disappointed there had been no hustings arranged by the council or other local groups.

“There has been nothing arranged; it’s been up to the candidates to organise hustings,” she said, “Farage should have shown up. I’m less surprised by Count Binface, whose campaign has been very much virtual and he said he wouldn’t show up in Clacton in person. But if either of them showed up we would probably have had a bigger audience for our hustings, so it is a shame.”

One 62-year-old spectator, Roy Andrews, seemed convinced by Fard’s campaign. “I didn’t vote last time but she’s got my vote. She seems like a very nice lady. I’m not about to vote for a bin,” he told the Guardian.

Farage had a clash in his schedule: he was busy in London announcing a policy to use warships to send people attempting to cross the Channel back to France.

Fard said: “Our hustings tomorrow is the immigration themed one. So if he wants to tell the people of Clacton his views on this, he should attend.”

Erlam, who was formerly an adviser to a Labour cabinet minister, told the small crowd that the anti-Farage vote should not be given to a bin. “Westminster is a jungle, and you don’t want a comedian to represent you.”

On the Reform UK leader’s failure to attend, he said: “Nigel Farage and his team have not responded, it remains to be seen whether he will appear alongside the rest of the candidates as an equal.”

Farage has kept somewhat of a low profile since he fired the starting gun on the campaign. Monday was his first national press conference since May, and he has not appeared keen to debate with Binface or the other 32 candidates.

Erlam was less impressed to be asked about Binface. “He is completely irrelevant,” he said. “The joke has run out. Only six candidates have bothered to put a leaflet in the post, they are who need to come to the hustings.”

Despite the lack of presence from the two frontrunners, and the seeming apathy gripping most of the residents of Clacton, the hustings will continue to be held every day. “We will be here to answer questions from the people of Clacton every day. It is up to Nigel Farage if he decides to find the courtesy to respond to our invitation,” said Erlam.

But on a sunny August day, the people of Clacton seemed more interested in the sandy beach, the amusement arcade and the rides on the pier than listening to what their would-be MPs had to say.

Count Binface told the Guardian that the invitation had been lost in his inbox.

He said: “I’m very sorry to have disappointed the candidates who took part, and I’m even sorrier to have disappointed any constituents who came to listen. If I’d known about the event, and if I couldn’t have made it, I would have at least sent through a written statement as I have done at previous elections.

“I did visit the constituency last week and really enjoyed meeting local residents in Clacton and Frinton, and I’m hoping to be able to do more in the days ahead. I can certainly say already that the people and the area are fantastic, and whoever wins the byelection, they deserve a devoted MP.”

Reform UK was contacted for comment.

The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 13:33:29 GMT

The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable

For the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making.

The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizens streamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s regularisation and leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finland backed Italy’s move and, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned a letter pointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”.

But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here.

Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame.

The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on the mass entry of Moroccans in 2021, after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis.

While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “gendarme” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement of Rabat’s plan for occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “new phase” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario.

Sánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according to Spanish intelligence – Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross.

It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call out Morocco as it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and often undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes.

This has been a favoured tactic for years across the external EU borders, from Muammar Gaddafi’s threats to Ankara’s antics. And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards.

The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since the Abraham accords were signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its military cooperation with Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committee stated that Ceuta and the other Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequent noises of this kind. Recently, Morocco named a highway through Western Sahara after Trump.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

What all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefit opportunistically and then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leaving more than 70 dead.

European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure, evidence shows, works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis.

Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining European solidarity – they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield.

We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity.

Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author of Age of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession (William Collins) out 13th August

‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 13:30:52 GMT

‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’

We were hanging out with the lovely producer George Drakoulias at Abbey Road. He said, “We’re going to bring in some instruments for you guys” – and replaced the fairly low-budget ones we’d been playing. I was given this beautiful 1960s Fender Jazz bass.

Sometimes you pick up an instrument you’ve never touched before and immediately start playing stuff you wouldn’t normally play. It made me want to come up with something cool, James Jamerson-style, with that Motown feel. I found the riff that became the bassline to Place Your Hands, showed it to Gaz, and he came up with this chilled melody about going down by the water. When Kenwyn House, our guitarist, added that classic opening guitar riff, it changed from something mellow into something much more action-packed.

It was just a lovely time to be alive. We were young and everyone in the band was talented, even though we didn’t really know what we were doing. We were rockers at heart, but we were very open-minded. We listened to everything from Motown and Bob Marley to Van Morrison’s Common One – Summertime in England can still make me cry. I eventually bought an old Telecaster bass – you can definitely hear the reggae influence in the bass during the bridge to Place Your Hands.

I’ve always thought the emotion Gaz brought to it was incredible, but I didn’t fully understand what he was singing about until quite recently. He explained that “put your hands on” was a metaphor for wanting a hug, to help him through the grief of losing his grandfather. I hadn’t realised at the time because we were young rockers, swept up in the moment and full of testosterone, with no time to think about anything. The 90s wasn’t really a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive – there were all the lads’ mags, and we were playing that game to an extent. We certainly didn’t discuss our feelings in the way we would now. Looking back, I think the lyrics are beautiful.

I don’t think we’ll ever get bored of playing it because it’s so funky and full of rhythm and spirit. We’ve had quite a few lineup changes, and Place Your Hands is the song that has always pulled us together. It gets people dancing and putting their hands up – even though the lyric is actually “Put your hands on”.

We were signed to S2 in 1993, under the legendary figures Lincoln Elias and Muff Winwood. Our first album reached the Top 10, we had three Top 40 singles and played Glastonbury, so we were really happy. We were touring the west coast of the US with stoner-rock band Kyuss when Lincoln suggested we meet George Drakoulias, who had worked with Rick Rubin at Def Jam and helped discover the Beastie Boys. George turned up wearing flowing white robes, which made quite an impression, and we decided to go with him for the second album.

We recorded three or four songs at Abbey Road. George hired a 1960s Fender bass. Jack was fiddling around with it and started playing what would become the bassline to Place Your Hands. Kenwyn dropped his guitar’s E string down to D and came up with the riff that sits over Jack’s bassline. At first, I sang it quite gently, but then thought: “That’s too airy-fairy.” We went to Los Angeles to finish the album with George, taking the bassline and guitar riff with us.

The lyrics are about the death of my grandfather, Kenneth. I was on the tour bus when I got a call saying he had died. I went to the morgue and my auntie said: “Do you want to see Ken?” I’d seen a dead body beside the road while on a surfing trip in Morocco when I was 18, but this had a different impact. The lyrics are essentially asking for comfort – for a cuddle. That’s why it’s “Put your hands on”. I’m sure if it was “Put your hands up” the song would have been even bigger.

Chris Evans was a huge supporter of the band and played the single to death on Radio 1. When you went on TFI Friday, it didn’t matter if you were Dave Grohl or Oasis – you had to do the It’s Your Letters segment and sing those words to the melody of the song you were on the show promoting. For some reason, our version of It’s Your Letters stuck. “Put your hands on” and “It’s your letters” have the same number of syllables, so they used it every week ever after.

The video cost about £250,000. We were turning head over heels on wires that had to be threaded through holes cut into our trousers. Place Your Hands accounts for a lot of my income. If we had 10 songs like that, I’d be a multimillionaire.

Reef perform at Lakefest festival in Eastnor, Herefordshire, on 8 August

‘They are such neat, busy little folk’: the unexpected superpowers of the common woodlouse

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 11:00:16 GMT

This detritivore – known by a range of colourful names – tidies up our world and can withstand toxic pollution

Revealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the year

Chucky pig. Slater. Monkey pea. Roly-poly. Boat-builder. Butchy boy. Cheeselog. Hobbling Andrew. Wood pig. If there were a prize for the range and joyfulness of a creature’s English-language names, the humble woodlouse would undoubtedly triumph over its million-plus invertebrate rivals.

Over centuries of easy cohabitation with humans, it has acquired more than 300 regional names in Britain alone, and many more in other languages (such as Gwrach y Coed, “witch of the wood”, in Welsh).

There are lovely words for woodlouse actions too: an animal rolling its body into a neat ball is known as conglobation, or volvation in zoology.

Their nicknames reflect our fondness for this most accessible of isopoda, an order of crustaceans, which is found in houses and gardens across Europe and the US.

The common rough woodlouse, Porcellio scaber, is more widespread and found in South America and Australia too but it does not curl up in a ball. Hopefully, woodlouse voters in all continents can set aside their love for their local representative and consider the common woodlouse to stand for the entire 5,000-species-strong suborder.

The woodlouse was a trendsetter, its ancient ancestors moving on to land about 500m years ago, long before most animals. The woodlouse hasn’t needed to make many design refinements over the years because it found such a useful niche from the start. As a detritivore, it feeds on rotting plant matter and breaks down wood.

Sally Roe, one of many Guardian readers to nominate the woodlouse, has a good story. When she installed biodegradable bamboo kitchen countertops, she used an offcut in the garden to weigh down the cardboard suppressing weeds in her pumpkin patch. After a (successful) harvest, she moved the solid slab of bamboo and found a large colony of woodlice underneath. “The formerly very solid, very heavy slab of bamboo worktop was now a paper-light wood honeycomb,” she says. “Woodlice demonstrated to me extremely clearly that something being ‘biodegradable’ relies heavily on invertebrates.”

As well as tidying up our world, another of the woodlouse’s superpowers is its ability to withstand toxic pollution and even store heavy metals within special compartments in its body. Studies have shown it can help stabilise heavy metals in compost.

Many readers have expressed their love for what one calls “detrivore royalty”. Another wants to get a woodlouse tattoo (great idea!). Chris Pickard is consoled by their longevity. “They will undoubtedly be here long after humans have followed dinosaurs and dodos into the extinct category,” he says.

And if you aren’t smiling at all their great names, you can invent your own. Peter Gregory calls them the “bumbling mumbling ombudsmen”.

So if you’re looking to celebrate an invertebrate that’s just brilliant company, vote woodlouse!

My olive oil is uncool, apparently. Welcome to the world of microsnobbery

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 10:00:15 GMT

Social media has supposedly ramped up our impulse to judge each other on the most trivial grounds – but is this really a new thing?

‘Are we living in an “era of microsnobberies”? Writing in the Washington Post last week, the lifestyle influencer Victoria Wolff asserted that we are, claiming that the fragmentation of American taste facilitated by, and expressed through, social media had created a new phenomenon of “hundreds of tribes” judging each other on highly specific sets of status signifiers.

Wolff cited a few – “your children’s lunch boxes, whether your roses are native and if your olive oil has a story” – that left me feeling like a grubby little peasant with my narratively inadequate oil, but also relieved not to live in Amagansett in the Hamptons, as she does. It sounds like a Nancy Meyers meets Edith Wharton hellscape. Indeed, I was reminded of reading earlier this year about the tiny-batch $80 (£60) fruit pies you’re supposed to bring as a “hostess gift” in those parts (etiquette specialists advise Hobnobs remain an acceptable hostess gift in the eastern suburbs of York).

I’m not convinced microsnobberies are new. If anything, when communities were more insular and less connected, surely the sets of rules they established were even more exacting and specific, the markers of difference in social status even more microscopic?

I’ve just read Julian Barnes’ The Man in the Red Coat, which paints “narcissistic and neurotic” belle époque Paris as a bitchy hotbed of microsnobberies, with incestuous social circles writing about trivial transgressions in place of today’s Substacks and Instagram posts. I bet even in the most austere 12th-century contemplative order, some unhappy monk was silently judging a novice’s “not quite us” stockings. It’s human nature, not a product of internet social atomisation – the impulse to judge each other, and feel judged, on minutiae is eternal.

The only real escape I ever found was in living abroad. During 12 years in Brussels, I internalised the broad-brush macrosnobberies – the “right” areas; the (vital) hierarchy of chocolatiers; the holiday destinations of the most chic neighbours – but remained happily oblivious if I was introducing myself gauchely or buying beyond-the-pale condiments. Man, it was mentally restful and I miss it – I could be tempted to move somewhere new just to be blissfully socially clueless again.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

‘I spent a week crying. I’ve never had an injury in my life!’ Why do so many fitness fans end up needing surgery?

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 09:00:46 GMT

From the 47-year-old runner who needs a double hip replacement to the 27-year-old CrossFitter with a ruptured ACL, those who push their bodies too hard often regret it. What are the lessons for the rest of us?

Jonathan Price has always been active and exercise-focused. Growing up in south Wales, rugby was his first love. Through school, university and beyond, he also surfed, rowed, played squash and ran competitively – on track, in 10k races and cross-country. Career and family demands meant that much of this fell away in later years, but the running stuck. He found time for marathons, half marathons – “I’d run a half marathon every weekend just for fun,” he says – and, through the working week, regular 30- or 40-minute runs to manage stress and clear his head. “I travel a lot for work,” says Price, now 50, a company CEO. “With running, all you need is a pair of running shoes and you can do it anywhere.”

By his mid-40s, though, Price’s body was beginning to object. He wasn’t recovering so well. “I could run just fine but I’d be in pain for two or three days afterwards,” he says. On top of this, every six months or so, his lower back seemed to seize up completely. A physiotherapist thought it was “tight hip flexors” and pointed Price towards “hip opening” exercises, designed to reduce stiffness and increase range of motion. Someone else prescribed him muscle relaxants, but the pain only deepened, and his range of movement continued to dip. Finally, in the summer of 2023, a chance encounter with a hip surgeon led to the diagnosis of osteoarthritis and, at the end of that year, Price, then 47, had a double hip replacement.

Was Price unlucky, or did decades of exercise accelerate his joint damage? After so many years, so many miles, and so many cycles of use, had he simply, as his surgeon, Giles Stafford, puts it, “hit his number”?

As a consultant orthopaedic hip surgeon specialising in sports-related hip disorders, Stafford often sees patients who are experiencing joint problems earlier than most. “They are usually active people who have done a lot of sport and knackered their joints through that,” he says. Stafford likens our joints to bearings in a car. “There’s clearly a genetic aspect, but also a big mechanical aspect too,” he says. “We all have a certain number of cycles in us before the damage sets in, and someone who is going to the gym, running marathons, taking on high-impact, high-intensity, repetitive exercise programmes might hit their number younger and faster.”

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the painful result of the breakdown of cartilage, the smooth, slippery tissue that cushions the ends of our bones so that we can move our joints freely without friction. OA is on the rise. Each year, more than a quarter of a million people in the UK have joint replacement surgery, and by 2060 demand is expected to have risen by 40%. While there is evidence of rising cases in younger people, by the age of 70 one in two UK adults will have OA. For some, that might just mean some stiffness while walking up the stairs. For others, it could mean needing help to wash and dress. In old age, OA will often determine whether someone can live independently and if their final years are spent navigating pain.

When it comes to causes, though, the picture is confusing. The way we are made is key. Our genes help determine our build, our gait, how we load our joints and where the pressure falls when we move. Genetics are also believed to play a role in the quality of our cartilage and the inflammatory responses that can damage it and drive OA forward. Price now knows that he was born with a subtle shape abnormality that is not uncommon. The ball of his hip joint’s ball-and-socket wasn’t quite spherical, so it didn’t rotate smoothly without friction, which quietly, over time, accelerated damage with each cycle of use. Beyond genetics, though, is asking too much of our bodies, or asking too little raising our OA risk? Should we worry about over-exercise, not enough exercise or the wrong kind of exercise? The answer, unfortunately, seems to be all three.

A sedentary lifestyle is a major driver. This is partly due to OA’s link with obesity, which increases the weight on our joints, and raises inflammation, but exercise matters beyond this. Cartilage relies on synovial fluid – joint fluid – for its nourishment, and we need to move around in order for that fluid to circulate. “Sitting for long periods of the day also seems to cause metabolic changes that are pro-inflammatory,” says Dr Benjamin Ellis, consultant rheumatologist at Imperial College Healthcare in London. Building strength and muscle also acts to absorb impact and stabilise our joints. “Our joints, our bones, our bodies strengthen under challenge and that is done by tiny micro-injuries,” says Ellis. “The body goes in to heal them and that healing builds bone and muscle.”

On the other hand, if we overload the body’s capacity to heal, or sustain too great an injury, we’re back in the OA danger zone, though it may take decades for the effects to be felt. An anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury – a tear or sprain in the centre of the knee – is one example. Professional footballers, who are prone to ACL injuries, have two or three times the average risk of OA in later life. Research also points to a raised OA risk among competitive runners – while recreational running seems to be protective. (Unhelpfully, the definition of “recreational” and “competitive” varies between studies.) Many orthopaedic surgeons – Stafford included – recommend cycling, swimming or an elliptical trainer over running, or running on grass or a treadmill rather than tarmac to soften the impact on our joints.

According to David Vaux, an osteopath, consultant for Arthritis Action and author of Stronger, exercise in midlife should be viewed a bit like a dosage of medicine. “If you do too much or too little, you’re going to be in trouble,” he says. “The main thing I see in clinic are people who are injured, and people who are burnt out – and those two things are kryptonite in midlife.” Both can lead someone to stop exercising altogether, or to keep going too hard before they have recovered. Either can result in OA.

For most midlifers, says Vaux, a healthy exercise programme is steady and consistent, with plenty of built-in recovery time. He says: “It can look quite boring, but boring is good.”

Saket Tibrewal, a consultant orthopaedic surgeon at Cromwell hospital in London who specialises in the knee, makes a similar point. “As we get older, our capacity to heal takes longer,” he says. “I do see a lot of runners who have taken it up in the last few years, and are starting to get knee pain and knock-on effects. They might be going for a run, then doing it again the next day, or maybe just having one day off. A lot of people don’t understand how important recovery is.”

Several orthopaedic surgeons have expressed reservations about high-intensity, high-impact exercise programmes. “Anything that involves a lot of deep-weighted squats, and repeatedly taking your body to end range under load, can damage your joints,” says Stafford. Gareth Jones, a specialist knee surgeon at Imperial College, has seen patients in their mid-20s and early 30s who have already lost a lot of cartilage from under their kneecaps through following such programmes. One of Tibrewal’s patients is Naomi Pannell, 27, who recently tore her ACL competing in a CrossFit event.

“I was in the semi-finals in Madrid, my biggest competition yet,” says Pannell. “It happened on day three, the last day, in 36C heat.” Pannell and her partner had completed the chest-to-bar pull-ups and the double-unders (like skipping except the rope passes under your feet twice in one jump) and next came four rounds of “sandbags” (lifting a heavy sandbag from the floor and resting it on the shoulder). “When I went to lift the sandbag for my second round, my knee popped out and popped in again,” says Pannell. “I didn’t fall to the floor. I went to lift it again and it did the same thing.” She completed some of the remaining circuit – including a handstand walk – and by the end her knee was badly swollen. “When I found out it was a full ACL rupture, I spent a week crying,” says Pannell. “I’ve never had an injury in my life.” Tibrewal, who will be operating on Pannell, blames fatigue. “These programmes are very good for cardiovascular fitness and strength, but they involve high repetition and high loading, and fatigue is a badge of honour,” he says. “After multiple rounds, if you’re pushed to the point where your muscles are really tired, then you can lose neuromuscular control of the joint. You lose proprioception – your body’s internal awareness of where it is in time and space – and that’s when something simple that you’ve done many times before can go wrong.”

According to Vaux, a healthy midlife exercise regime that’s protective against OA involves “steps and reps”. “A walk, a jog, a bike ride a couple of times a week and you need strength training, too. I usually prescribe following an isometric-only strength programme – such as wall sits and planks, which you can do anywhere – for at least two months before you do anything more dynamic [in terms of strength training]. If someone is doing that, I’ll take that person’s chances on healthy joints in 20 years’ time over anyone doing anything extreme and get-fit-quick.”

The most important thing is listening to your body. “Pain alone isn’t always a reliable guide because some discomfort can be a normal part of adaptation,” says Vaux, “but persistent joint pain, night pain or pain on certain movements, swelling and stiffness should not be ignored. It’s your body telling you there is an issue.” It’s also important to understand your level of fatigue. “Is your performance stable, improving or decreasing? Decreasing performance indicates you are not recovering properly. How are you sleeping? Is your heart rate significantly elevated first thing the day after exercise? The solution to any of these might be to get something checked out, or to modify your exercise and rest.”

Chris Dunn, 49, a dedicated runner, waited until he had grade-four bone-on-bone OA in his knee before he stopped running and had it looked at. “I can probably track it back to 2015, when a bad tackle in football twisted my ACL,” he says. Despite the injury, that same year he completed an Ironman triathlon and a marathon. In the years since, he had continued to compete in many more marathons, as well as regular triathlons. “My leg was probably weakened and I weakened it more, my alignment shifted to compensate, and that overloaded different parts of the knee joint,” he says. “Silly really – I left it too long – but once you’re in the runner’s mindset, you think: ‘It’ll be all right. It’ll repair itself.’ When you push yourself to the limits, it’s uncomfortable anyway! You tell yourself it’s just a twinge. By 2023, it had got to the point where I was only able to do 5 or 6km of running and afterwards it was so painful I could only hobble.”

In May 2024, Dunn underwent five hours of surgery to straighten his leg and try to offload the damaged area. It was very successful. “I was home the next day with a knee brace,” he says. “I stayed on crutches until August. The following April, I did the London Marathon and in July I did an Ironman. At the moment, running feels comfortable. There’s a chance that years down the line I might need a knee replacement, but we’ll play it by ear. I want to enjoy it while I can.”

Price also got back to running after his double hip replacement. Last year, he completed the world’s deepest marathon, which took place in a zinc mine in Sweden. “It took a while to get past that strange sensation where everything feels different, but once I started running, it got easier and easier,” he says. Pannell, meanwhile, is hoping to compete in the CrossFit Open in February.

“There’s no universal threshold beyond which exercise becomes harmful,” says Vaux. “It’s shaped by so many factors – such as age, genetics, previous injuries – and it isn’t fixed: it can expand as tissues adapt. That’s one of the remarkable things about the human body. But we need to give it time to get there, and to listen to what it’s telling us on the way.”

The most dynamic countries are surging ahead with high-speed rail. Others, like Britain, are stuck in the station

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 09:00:45 GMT

Around the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are high

Christian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed Rail

With all our grumbling about trains – and it is close to a national pastime – it is easy to forget the successes. There is a tale to tell, for example, about high-speed trains, that goes beyond the endless wrangling over HS2.

If you look at the history around the globe, as I have, you find that high-speed trains saved the railways. An industry that was gradually sinking into oblivion, thanks to motorways and aeroplanes, has been revitalised by a technological revolution that means trains travel faster, more safely and more comfortably.

Over time, beautiful but inefficient steam engines and their dirty diesel successors have been replaced by sleek modern trains that shrink distances and provide a service that their rivals on either land or in the air cannot compete with. Train travel that had been in decline has become the preferred mode of transport for many journeys previously dominated by aviation.

But this is a revolution that almost didn’t reach Europe. In 1964, Japan became the pioneer, creating the Shinkansen, known worldwide as the bullet train, in effect the first motorway on rail, with dedicated tracks, a small number of stops and an at the time unprecedented top speed of 210 km/h (130mph). Nowadays trains often run at 190mph and they may routinely reach 250mph before the decade is out.

But as Japan surged ahead, 1960s Europe had fallen out of love with trains. Beeching-type cuts were the order of the day across the continent and a new invention seemed in the 1980s to be about to supersede the iron road. This was levitation technology, with trains being elevated by air or magnetism and pushed forward at great speed by rocket propulsion or magnets. Tests in France of the Aérotrain saw it reach speeds of almost 270mph, while the German government was promoting maglev technology, funding a line running between Hamburg and Berlin.

Trains were 19th century, it was said, while maglev was a technology for the 21st. But then, just as with the hyperloop, Elon Musk’s recent failed reinvention of the maglev technology, the plans for maglev fell apart, as costs soared and the practicalities of developing a whole new system running into crowded city centres proved insuperable. A 2006 disaster on the German test track killing 23 people put paid to any hopes of reviving the idea.

This victory of the railways over its rivals guarantees that trains will be operating across the world in the 22nd century. The victory by rail meant high-speed rail systems emerging first in France and then across Europe in Germany, Italy and Spain. In addition, 25 countries in the rest of the world, ranging from Morocco and Turkey to Taiwan and Uzbekistan, have high-speed rail systems or are developing them.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The rewards are great, but the subject is always controversial because the route to high-speed rail is never easy. These are megaprojects costing sums with more zeros than any other government projects except possibly defence and space travel, and to see them through needs consistent government support, a clear understanding of their purpose and a long-term budget.

In all the high-speed rail schemes across the world that I examined for my book, it was a struggle to find any that were completed on time and on budget. Most achieved one of these – the UK’s HS2 and the California high-speed project being the exceptions, failing miserably on both counts – and by and large they have been successful in attracting passengers and in many cases seeing off domestic flights on their routes. Who now flies between London and Paris, or indeed Barcelona and Madrid, or Rome and Milan? Mostly only people who are interlining, that is, transferring to another flight. The sensible choice for most people will usually be a pleasant train ride with fewer security hurdles to overcome and city-centre to city-centre travel.

New high-speed lines have generally been designed to relieve congestion on the busiest existing railway routes, such as Paris-Lyon or Tokyo-Osaka. But high-speed rail has also been used as a catalyst for a wider modernisation scheme, notably in Spain, which surprisingly has Europe’s most extensive high-speed rail network, with about 2,500 miles of line, as a result of a clear government strategy to use trains to create better connections between regions and the capital, Madrid. The Spanish government, noting the success of its initial line built for the Seville Expo between Madrid and Seville, then embarked on a national programme that revived a dying rail system and changed the image of the country from a poor relative of its European counterparts to that of a self-confident, dynamic nation. High-speed rail can help do that.

But for the world leader, look to China which has built 70% of the world’s mileage of high-speed lines in under 20 years. The figures are so extraordinary that they seem almost unbelievable. There are now about 31,000 miles of high-speed line with about 10,000 services carrying an average of 10 million people daily.

Here, too, though, it is more than just a railway. The officials I talked to while travelling around China on its stunning network were clear about this. Many of the early lines were built between the largest cities but now the system, which they hope to increase by at least 10,000 miles by 2040, is being expanded to smaller towns and cities to create a genuinely national network. This remarkable project is seen as a way of uniting the country in the same way the railways in Germany and Italy created nations out of these fragmented countries in the 19th century.

That was the original concept in the UK when HS2 was first conceived and its progenitor, Andrew Adonis, registered HS3, HS4 and HS5 as companies. We can but dream that this will ever be realised. For the story of high-speed rail I found was of go-ahead nations embracing the future, while others, including alas Britain, are being left behind.

Christian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed Rail

The right hates The Odyssey because of its ‘wokeness’ – but it missed an even bigger threat to its worldview

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 07:00:43 GMT

The new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decision

Peter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. Before his election, he was a classics teacher and academic

For years, a small but vocal corner of the extremely online right has looked to the ancient world to justify its polluted brand of politics. The classicist Donna Zuckerberg (sister of Facebook founder Mark) wrote a book about it way back in 2018 called Not All Dead White Men – a deep dive into the corners of the internet where misogynists pretend ancient philosophy can justify their hatred of minorities.

You would think that these self-appointed guardians of the ancient world would be excited about a blockbuster retelling one of its greatest pieces of literature, the Odyssey. Especially when Christopher Nolan’s film has been getting rave reviews, “the vast majority … written by men”, as the Guardian’s Catherine Shoard has pointed out. The Odyssey is an action-packed thriller with a fight scene every five seconds. In many ways (and I don’t mean this as a criticism of Nolan; I loved the film for all its flaws), it’s a movie designed to appeal to their tastes. And yet.

Many rightwing commentators have been railing at the film’s perceived “wokeness” for months – since well before it hit cinemas. Nolan’s biggest crime seems to have been casting Lupita Nyong’o, a black woman, as Helen of Troy, the entirely mythical daughter of Zeus. In other versions of her myth, she was born out of a swan’s egg alongside her mortal sister Clytemnestra and her two brothers, who were either gods or mortals depending on which one you read. I can see why they’re worried about inaccuracy …

There have been plenty of other criticisms from keyboard warriors concerned about a lack of historical accuracy in a film adaptation of an entirely fictional myth. Having a PhD in classics means I agree with them that Corinthian helmets aren’t historically accurate to the film’s bronze age setting; having a sense of proportion and an understanding of artistic licence means I don’t really care.

Elon Musk has, perhaps predictably, emerged as the loudest critic, even calling Nolan an “anti-White racist” and suggesting he might use Grok to create an AI-powered Odyssey movie “that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer”. But as ridiculous as that all is, the right shouldn’t hate Nolan’s Odyssey for its inaccuracies. They should hate it because of what it has to say about the very real, very Homeric concept of xenia.

Xenia, which Nolan translates as “Zeus’s law”, was an ancient custom that governed how people were supposed to treat strangers. Zeus’s law is absolutely original to Homer. In fact, it’s a pretty fundamental part of the poem. When I taught GCSE students about the Odyssey, xenia was one of the first concepts I’d teach them. In Homer’s Odyssey, as in Nolan’s film, it drives how different civilisations and cultures are supposed to interact with one another in society. People (and monsters such as the Cyclops) who break Zeus’s law are punished; those who uphold it (such as Odysseus’s son, Telemachus) are rewarded.

But Nolan’s take on xenia is unmistakably modern. To me, it feels like an allegory for the fraying, rules-based international system. Whether it’s state sovereignty being undermined by Russia, international maritime law under threat from China or Donald Trump’s disdain for global multilateral cooperation on everything from trade to defence to the climate crisis, the rules-based order established after the second world war is under threat.

At the end of the movie – spoilers – Odysseus and Penelope see their entire bronze age Greek civilisation collapsing. This is based on an actual historical event, the Mycenaean collapse. In Nolan’s retelling, it happens because the people of the sea are raiding and warring, breaking Zeus’s law.

The message for a modern audience is, again, not subtle: society will collapse if we abandon our rules-based international order. If Nolan’s film really is “woke”, this is why – because it’s fundamentally a film about the value of multilateralism produced for an increasingly nationalistic world. Musk and co seem to have missed this message. But it’s the real reason why they should hate the film. It pushes back against everything the hard right are trying to achieve and instead makes clear that a commitment to international diplomacy isn’t a nice-to-have – it’s a prerequisite to civilisation.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And, yes, for all those complaining, that’s not in the original poem. Nolan’s film is a reimagining. But here’s the truth about classics. Nobody gets to decide how all those wonderful ancient stories get retold, rewritten for new times or redeployed to make new arguments or share new perspectives. No one person gets to own the ancient world. Especially not Elon Musk.

Peter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. Before his election, he was a classics teacher and academic
