On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 06:00:43 GMT

The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip

It is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Totti dusted it off for the internet generation at Euro 2000.

It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means. The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.

A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder. Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards, asked the man himself what constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible. Rob Smyth

Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)

This one needs no introduction. RS

Czechoslovakia 2-0 France

The next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsy with a sensual chip in a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80. RS

Napoli training

Most of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner to ensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d already seen him do it in open play. RS

Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)

In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackle of comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowd and tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot, he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset. Daniel Harris

Monaco 2-2 Sampdoria

In the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure: against Genoa in the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90. The first was against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16, the second in the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0 in the final. RS

Czechoslovakia 5-1 USA

It’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976. He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!” RS

Nottingham Forest 1-1 Tottenham

Nobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led to a brief post-match discussion in which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. This one was particularly sweet – the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final. RS

England 1-1 Brazil

A kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearer chuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak, as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record. Jonathan Liew

Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)

In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final, he’d gently rolled two penalties into the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the way only for the kick to sail over the bar as United lost 6-5. DH

Guarani 2-1 Internacional

Brazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for his signature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot. The first of many was scored against Sergio Goycoechea, whose elastic penalty saves had taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted. RS

Sheffield United 0-1 Aston Villa

Dwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule, but Yorke was true to his word and settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.” RS

Chelsea 2-4 Wimbledon

There’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. But Vialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line by a very different kind of chip earlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it. RS

Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal

“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman, who was Panenka-ed on the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called, Yorke sidefooted wide. RS

Torquay 0-1 Hull City

If only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue as this piece of effrontery floated gently past him. RS

Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)

In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti, whose falling leaf penalty foxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation. John Brewin

Hibernian 0-0 Hearts

A last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares. Mixu Paatelainen only took it because Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion. RS

Arsenal 3-2 Newcastle

Five days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner was teased softly down the middle by Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was just trolling Ruud van Nistelrooy. RS

Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)

For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka. Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup. Jeff Rueter

Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)

Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). On the Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.

double quotation markLL I’m gonna dink it.

BH No you’re not.

LL I am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final.

BH Liam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.

He dinked that ball against the bar – “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.” RS

Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)

Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty, a kick so under-amped it barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp. JB

England 6-0 Jamaica

The then-Liverpool striker scored an England hat-trick as part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ball well over the bar from 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.” Will Unwin

Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)

You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it came after 120 minutes of the most soporific football ever played. RS

Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)

The nerve to do it in a World Cup final. The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar, past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – until Marco Materazzi and the anger took over. Taha Hashim

Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)

To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier, dollied his kick into the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even has his own Bonnie Tyler adaptation. JB

Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)

If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one of the first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup. A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions. RS

England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)

When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ball wafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successes finishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards. DH

Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)

For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-final against Portugal. Bruno Alves missed Portugal’s next kick and Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final. RS

Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)

The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenka was saved in a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.” RS

SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)

Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpah to try a Pellènka? RS

São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)

No surprise that one of the great goalscoring keepers should beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he was fractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically. RS

Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)

Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to take one of the worst Panenkas ever seen. RS

Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)

It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone. His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – and unlike Czechoslovakia in 1976, they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria. RS

Serbia 1-1 Wales

The Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramsey unwittingly did so by scoring a Panenka at the same end of the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one. RS

Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua Bucuresti

A Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger. RS

Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)

Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend that Fedor Smolov’s opening attempt lacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour. JR

Barcelona 2-2 Atlético Madrid

If you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium, you might as well do it in style. RS

Reading 3-1 Aston Villa

This unusual penalty from Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority. RS

West Ham 1-0 Fulham

During his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the game but his feeble chip landed straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare moment of post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.” Yara El-Shaboury

Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al Sadd

Not many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right foot against Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021. RS

Man City 1-2 Chelsea

City were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided to chip down the middle; Édouard Mendy almost fell for it but had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüero issued a public apology. WU

France 2-1 Brazil

Birthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against France in sublime fashion. JR

Manchester City 4-3 Real Madrid

A moment of mischief at the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final. RS

Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)

If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final, you might as well do it in style. RS

Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FC

We can’t say for sure that this is the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition. RS

Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)

In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after saving one of the more pitiful Panenkas ever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille. RS

Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego Wave

If you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025, chipping in off the underside of the crossbar to secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill. Tom Garry

Roma 0-4 Barcelona

Even the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenka harmlessly over the crossbar during a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner. TG

Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)

A Panenka is a dish best served cold. RS

Morocco 3-0* Senegal

Brahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenka was easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding. Then again … YE-S

Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)

Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is that Mo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australia was the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream. RS

Finally, we have a PM for the digital age. But real change requires more than just being good on camera

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 05:00:41 GMT

Connection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New York

Andy Burnham is having a good time. I can’t remember the last time a prime minister (or indeed any high-profile British politician) actually looked as though they were enjoying what they were doing. I saw a clip the other day in which Burnham remembered arguing with his dad about the point of an English degree, quoted poetry and discussed the importance of mastering words. It was almost enough to make you feel sorry for Keir Starmer. In his entire time as leader of the Labour party and then the head of the government, Starmer delivered not a single unprocessed moment. No natural sentiment escaped the carapace. And here is his successor, practically oozing it.

It matters. It’s good and healthy to have a leader who looks as though they want to be where they are. Whose approach isn’t that of a scold or a receiver who has taken control of the premises, or someone whose sole aim is to tenaciously clamber up to the top job and hold on for dear life.

I hadn’t fully realised, until Starmer cleared off, how much his premiership gave off the sense that the public were doing a bad job. That it was somehow their fault Starmer wasn’t as popular as he thought he should have been. As though it were the public’s job to deliver stable government and stop being so restive and fickle; stop having feelings and opinions on your prime minister that show up in the polling. Poor Starmer, some said, smashed fatally against the rocks by the waves of the roiling, insentient electorate of an ungovernable country.

Burnham’s approach restores the basic principle, lost for so long, that you have to woo people and establish a connection. Over the past two weeks, it looks as though it has been easier to get a reply from his X account than for business executives to establish contact with his team. The videos he is posting on social media are, by any measure, a remarkable departure from the old way of doing things. They collectively have a voice, an almost salesman-like pitch. They say “just hear me out”. If anything, Burnham’s posts on everything from the importance of learning practical skills to ranking pub snacks show how late British politics is to the game. My first sense of it all wasn’t of how revolutionary it was, but why on earth it took so long.

The answer, of course, is that no one had the taste for it. The personalities of our last few prime ministers were not, to put it mildly, those of digital natives. Their styles were “cop”, “sidekick bully” and “Liz Truss”, rather than public-facing politicians keen to communicate via the platforms they actually use. Burnham’s performances may sometimes be perilously close to shtick, but he has an undeniable flair and energy for the sort of modern direct-to-camera address that could give him an edge in a media environment where the parameters have for too long been set by an overwhelmingly rightwing traditional media.

Burnham knows all of this. A little too much, perhaps. The bar is in hell and so is the discourse. It takes very little to break through the grim record of the past few years and outdo stale TV and radio formats. It would be easy enough to post some good, sharp stuff on your own social media and call it a day. And if it continues that way – that is, an approach to communication which does not tackle the positions that made the atmosphere so fetid in the first place – then it will all soon become background noise, and then an irritant.

Because digital political success is not just about being good on camera. Burnham’s style has been compared with that of the obvious originator of the model, Zohran Mamdani. But Mamdani shows that having a flair for direct communication is only the first stage, the part where you get people on board. (His videos speaking in different languages during the election campaign were gold.) You then have to keep at it and show you are new in both style and practice. That you are a strong advocate for people. And, most importantly, that you are a cheerful, unflappable threat to their enemies. “When I ran for mayor, I said I was gonna tax the rich,” Mamdani says in a recent video. Then he comes up close, knocks the camera. “Well, today we’re taxing the rich.” His pied-à-terre tax, he told New Yorkers, will be levied on properties like the one he’s standing under, a penthouse belonging to the hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Burnham has already done some tangible good by starting out with policies focused on people’s pockets – on bills and bus fares and VAT relief – and with an evocative drive to devolve power from London. He promises “a new political model and a new economic model”. Them’s fighting words. Or should be. But his narrative lacks a clear articulation of what actually separates the needy from the predatory. Yes, at this point it is revolutionary just to name the problems, let alone do anything about them. But it will not be enough.

Burnham seems satisfied with figuring out what he can get away with without that epic fight; with broadly gesturing to how bad Thatcherism and neoliberalism are, but not actually slaying them. He won’t target the under-taxed wealthy because he doesn’t want to “create new divisions and pitch people one against another”. He is willing to keep in place the punitive immigration regime of the previous administration (while valorising the foreign workers who care for his father). And while it’s early days on foreign policy, things look to be business as usual, suggesting Burnham has little appetite for resetting international relations in a period of historic flux. Even though he apologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza, he continues the previous government’s permission for the US to use some UK bases for air strikes on Iran, and is entertaining, at least according to Trump, friendly discussions on “North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait”. There looks to be no necessary reckoning afoot with the US’s calamitous actions in the Middle East.

First you change the political culture, then you can change the political model. That culture is style and presentation and some policy, yes, but to really capture lightning in a bottle, you must show that intellectual and moral barriers are being redrawn. If there is any lesson to be gleaned from our age of short-lived prime ministers, it is that all ostensible advantages – landslides, huge polling leads, mandates to deliver Brexit – dissolve under the harsh light of insincerity born from timidity. Authenticity comes from congruence. Burnham might be able to get away with a lot of the effect and some of the substance for a while, but he will only be the revolutionary prime minister he promises he is – people will only believe that he is – if he breaks something other than the fourth wall.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Liechtenstein’s archaic abortion laws need to be modernised. But a prince is standing in the way

The Guardian Mon, 03 Aug 2026 04:00:41 GMT

The hurdles for women who have to travel abroad to access abortion are considerable, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changes

The first person Maria* called when she found out she was pregnant was her doctor. The second person was a lawyer. The single mother of one was in shock, and considering terminating the pregnancy. But she first had to make sure that she wasn’t about to do something illegal, because all she knew was that abortions were forbidden where she lived. “On top of the emotional mountain that was already there, I also had to deal with this,” Maria told me.

She also knew she wouldn’t get any information about abortions in her own country – that’s illegal too. After making her decision, she drove to a clinic across the border. It was a stressful, if short, 45-minute drive, at the end of which another hurdle was waiting: “Oh, you’re from Liechtenstein?” the receptionist said, according to Maria. “Then you have to pay immediately – 680 Swiss francs (£620) please.” She was taken aback and asked: “What if I can’t pay that right now?” The receptionist replied: “Then you’ll have to come back tomorrow.”

Liechtenstein has one of the strictest abortion laws in Europe. This is probably not something you know about my “micro-state” – you might think of its banks, of Alpine scenery and castles fit for a Netflix romance. But in between them live real people with real lives, and every year, an estimated 40 women who wish to terminate their pregnancy on their own terms cannot do so in their country.

But if you ask Liechtenstein’s regent, Hereditary Prince Alois, our prime minister, or random people on the street, many will tell you the same thing: there is no problem at all. Since 2015, women are legally permitted to have an abortion outside the country, and the external border is never more than a 15-minute drive away. And anyway, it is allowed if the woman was raped or if her health is at risk, so what more could you ask for?

What I, and others who are part of a new people’s initiative are simply asking for is what is already standard in most European countries: decriminalisation of abortion up to 12 weeks, repeal of the national ban on information about abortions, and for the procedure to be covered by health insurance. A recent poll shows that 62% of voters would be in favour of it if a vote were held. It should be a done deal. But no matter what the people say: the hereditary prince has already announced that he would veto any change in the law, long before a single vote has been cast.

Liechtenstein is not your typical European monarchy, and the prince’s power is anything but ceremonial. Alois can veto any bill, dismiss the government or individual ministers, appoint judges, and propose changes to the law. He usually exercises this power with restraint, and has never actually used his veto. He has only threatened to use it once, in 2011, which was the last time a popular initiative tried to legalise abortion. With the prince’s veto looming over the vote, it was rendered effectively pointless, leading to a historically low turnout, and a 52% vote against.

A national debate over the monarchy’s role ensued, culminating in a vote in which more than 76% chose to preserve the prince’s veto power. This happened though after Alois and his father, Prince Hans-Adam II, had threatened to leave the country if the vote didn’t go in their favour – a move that would have plunged our nation into a severe crisis.

This is why it continues to be the case that speaking out in favour of legalising abortion is regarded as speaking out against the monarchy.

Alois says that the present laws are there to protect unborn life, even though he acknowledges that the abortion ban doesn’t actually prevent any abortions. And our prime minister, Brigitte Haas, says she’s pragmatic and doesn’t see a problem with sending women across the border. I have one question: have they ever spoken to a single woman who had to cross the border for an abortion? Because if they had, they would know that the abortion ban is indeed harming those affected in several ways.

Since 2022, I’ve conducted more than a dozen interviews with women from Liechtenstein who had to seek abortion care outside the country. Their stories have several things in common.

Just like Maria, Liechtensteiners who seek abortion care are completely on their own. A ban on information – the last one of its kind in Europe – prevents local groups and professionals from giving advice about procedures and where to go. Pressured for time by the 12-week limit for abortions in Switzerland and Austria, they have to make phone call after phone call to find the right clinic, for which they have to pay in advance, up to 2,500 Swiss francs (£2,360). They fear legal consequences, because many don’t realise that under Liechtenstein’s law only doctors are criminally liable. And they feel stigmatised by a law telling them to deal with their problems elsewhere. As Maria puts it: “You feel so awful when you want to do it, because it’s so taboo in this country. You feel like you’re a monster.”

Alois’s veto announcement may have been intended to discourage people from signing the initiative or to demotivate us campaigners. The opposite has happened: many people felt even more motivated to sign, and in a country of about 41,000 people (only around 21,000 with voting rights), we received 4,970 signatures, the second-largest tally of signatories for a popular initiative in the country’s history – equivalent to 10.5m signatures in the UK or 13.8m in Germany.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

A few weeks ago I went collecting some of those signatures in the streets of Vaduz. A dad with his two kids told me he had already signed, and his young daughter asked what we were doing. I said we were collecting signatures for a cause, and if we collected enough of them, all the people in the country could vote on it. Her father added: “Well, one person has already cast his vote.”

There is only one man we have to convince. We hope a very clear vote might do the trick.

Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel is a campaigner and journalist from Liechtenstein, focusing on reproductive rights

The German Auto Industry, a Pillar of the National Psyche, Is Trembling

The New York Times August 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The country’s iconic carmakers are struggling with tariffs, the growth of electric vehicles and intense competition from Chinese companies.

By Jack Ewing and Jim Tankersley

Jack Ewing reported from New York and Jim Tankersley from Berlin and Stuttgart, Germany.

The centerpiece of Mercedes-Benz’s 140th birthday party in January was a patent application filed in 1886 by an engineer named Carl Benz for a “vehicle with gas engine.”

The way Mercedes executives spoke of the handwritten document, which at one point was projected on a large wall on the company campus in Stuttgart, Germany, it might have been a sacred parchment. It not only certifies that Germany is the birthplace of the automobile but also helps explain why the woes of the country’s automakers — Volkswagen, Mercedes and BMW — are a threat to more than just the German economy and the livelihoods of thousands of workers.

The carmakers’ woes also threaten the national identity, rattling a fragile governing coalition and fueling support for far-right politicians.

Germany’s automakers are struggling under the weight of American tariffs, Chinese competition and a rocky transition to electric vehicles. The gravity of the situation became clear this summer as Volkswagen executives discussed closing factories, canceling models and culling tens of thousands of jobs.

The crisis raises questions about whether the German approach of balancing profits with job security by, among other things, giving workers a strong voice in management is capable of adapting to breathtaking technological change. Chinese carmakers churn out new models in 18 months or less, a fraction of the time most Western carmakers take.

Along with chemicals and machinery, autos are “one of three sources of German strength rooted in the 19th century in areas where German engineers made great strides,” said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Berenberg Bank.

When the industry is changing rapidly, “German labor relations are a hindrance,” Mr. Schmieding said. “A modest downsizing you can discuss with your workers. When it’s a dramatic shift, that’s more difficult.”

Ola Källenius, the chief executive of Mercedes, said Germany still possessed the skills that had allowed Mercedes, BMW and Volkswagen’s Audi and Porsche units to dominate the high end of the market.

Speaking in January when the company unveiled the latest version of its top-of-the-line S-Class sedan, he said the car “has German origins, spirit, DNA, engineering skills, precision, quality thinking.”

But he added that the design was the product of “a global team.” And he said the country was hurt by high energy costs and taxes as well as rules that made it difficult to lay off workers.

“There’s a lot that needs to be done in Germany to improve competitiveness — or, I should rather say, Europe,” Mr. Källenius said in an interview at the company’s headquarters in Stuttgart.

When German companies expand or build factories, it is often in places like Hungary, China or Mexico. The number of cars produced in Germany has fallen 28 percent since 2016, according to the VDA, the German automakers’ association, putting the country well behind China, the United States, Japan and India. Germany could soon also be overtaken by South Korea and Mexico.

U. S. automakers may soon face similar challenges. For now, General Motors and Ford Motor are protected from Chinese competition by tariffs. But “we can’t expect to keep them out forever,” William Clay Ford Jr., the executive chair of Ford, said at an Axios event this month in Washington.

The German carmakers face an assault on two fronts. In China — the world’s largest car market — sales of foreign car brands are plummeting. And Chinese automakers are making big strides in Europe. In June, Chinese carmakers outsold Japanese carmakers in Western Europe for the first time, according to figures compiled by Schmidt Automotive Research.

China was once a lucrative market for the Germans, accounting for 37 percent of Volkswagen sales in 2019. But after Chinese automakers learned how to manufacture cars through joint ventures with foreign carmakers, the tables turned.

BAIC Group, an automaker owned by the Chinese government, has become Mercedes’s largest shareholder, with a stake of almost 10 percent. Chinese companies like BYD and Geely Auto were quicker to develop electric vehicles that were heavily promoted by the Chinese government and are selling briskly in Europe.

The Germans took too long to offer appealing electric vehicles. Volkswagen sold 26 percent fewer cars in China in the first six months of the year compared with a year earlier, while Mercedes reported a 28 percent decline and BMW a 20 percent slump.

“Despite better products, we cannot match the cost and pricing of export models from China,” Oliver Blume, the Volkswagen chief executive, told employees this month.

Mr. Blume expressed doubt that Volkswagen factories in four German cities were competitive, though he said there might be ways to avoid closing them by, for example, converting them for use by the defense industry.

Volkswagen’s labor representatives agreed in 2024 to cull 50,000 people from the company’s work force by 2030, through retirement and buyouts. With 657,000 employees worldwide, the company still has 50,000 more people than it needs, Mr. Blume said.

Making such deep cuts is especially difficult at Volkswagen.

Workers at the company, as is the case for all three German carmakers, hold half the 20 seats on the supervisory board, in line with the country’s laws. The boards oversee top management and can fire the chief executive. Shareholders also have 10 seats and name the chair, who can exercise a tiebreaking vote.

But what’s unique at Volkswagen is that two of the shareholder seats are held by the State of Lower Saxony, which owns 20 percent of the company’s voting stock. The state, home to Volkswagen’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, almost always takes the side of workers.

Olaf Lies, the prime minister of Lower Saxony and one of the state’s representatives on the Volkswagen board, said in a statement that he would not agree to any plan “that depends on factory closures as a supposedly simple solution.”

Historically, Volkswagen and its workers have found compromises in times of crisis, but cooperation has been strained recently.

“There is already an enormous loss of trust amongst the work force in the man who, in his early days as C. E. O., presented himself everywhere as ‘Olli’ and a ‘local lad,’” the Volkswagen Works Council, which represents workers, said of Mr. Blume in a statement.

Candidates for the far-right Alternative for Germany have seized on the industry’s woes, promising to usher in a return to a heyday of German manufacturing. The appeal has helped the party attract voters in parts of Western Germany where the AfD is generally much weaker than in areas that were once part of Eastern Germany.

The far left has also tried to exploit the crisis. This month, members of the German Marxist-Leninist Party distributed pamphlets outside the gates of an Audi factory in Neckarsulm, in southwest Germany, calling on workers to strike.

The center-right chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has linked the industry’s problems directly to China. He promised to work with France and the rest of Europe to push back against the Chinese imports. The French carmakers Peugeot, owned by Stellantis, and Renault face similar problems.

“We are doing everything to stabilize the automotive industry again,” Mr. Merz said in an interview this month with the public broadcaster ZDF. “At the moment, that is the most difficult sector in Germany.”

Automakers often complain that Chinese companies have an unfair advantage because they receive subsidies from their government. But Chinese automakers are also adept at equipping cars with features like rotating screens, fast-charging batteries and advanced self-driving systems at lower costs than Western carmakers.

Much of the auto industry’s malaise “is due to wrong decisions and arrogance” in addition to increased competition from China, said Thorsten Benner, the director of the Global Public Policy Institute in Berlin.

Jörn Buss, a German who is head of Americas for the automotive and manufacturing group at the consulting firm Arthur D. Little, noted that Chinese companies also had problems. They lose money or earn modest profits because there are dozens of carmakers in China. Most of those companies have been making cars for only a few years, which means nobody knows if those vehicles will turn out to be reliable or durable.

“They haven’t made the errors yet that all the other guys have learned from over 50 years,” Mr. Buss said.

The Germans still excel in at least one area: lavish marketing events. The party in Stuttgart celebrating Mercedes’s 140th birthday culminated in the unveiling of the S-Class sedan, which is made in Germany.

The car debuted in a livestreamed show featuring laser lights, drone cameras, a digital John Lennon and the real-life Roger Federer. It comes with an A. I.-powered screen the size of a small windshield, a glowing hood ornament and heated seatbelts.

But the seatbelts became a sort of national joke in German media, mocked as an example of how Mercedes is falling behind on the whiz-bang innovations the Chinese have become so good at.

“These German companies will survive,” said Tom Narayan, lead autos analyst at RBC Capital Markets. “But they will likely be smaller companies than they are today.”

Theresa Rauffmann contributed reporting from Neckarsulm, Germany.

For decades, China was a gold mine for German automakers like Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, and BMW. They were pioneers in the 1980s, trading technology through local joint ventures to capture the world's largest market. But Beijing’s play was always long-term: learn German engineering, then take back the domestic market. That day of reckoning has arrived — and it's triggering a full-blown crisis for Germany’s economy.

Reporting this story is also a bit of a role reversal. Jack and I have worked together in the past, including when he covered the German auto industry in Frankfurt and I covered economics at the White House. Now he's in New York writing about the global auto industry and I'm covering Germany from Berlin. We are seeing long-running coverage themes in our work together, but from different viewpoints.

Jack Ewing covers the auto industry for The Times, with an emphasis on electric vehicles.

Jim Tankersley is the Berlin bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

After Colleges Reject ‘Compact,’ Trump Officials Try a Letter

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The open letter from Education Secretary Linda McMahon fell far short of the attempt at a compact last year that dangled research money in return for embracing the Trump administration’s agenda.

By Michael C. Bender and Alan Blinder

The Trump administration is making another push to persuade university leaders to address policies that it says have eroded trust with the American public, sending an open letter on Monday to college leaders asking them to respond to concerns over academic standards, admissions procedures and tuition costs.

The letter, signed by Education Secretary Linda McMahon, is a significant departure from an attempt last year to incentivize universities with a so-called compact that dangled easier access to research funding for schools that embraced the administration’s agenda. That proposal was widely rejected.

This time, the administration is not proposing any new legal or regulatory mandates and avoids any specific requests for eliminating protections for transgender students. Instead, Ms. McMahon asks every postsecondary institution in the nation to publicly state its commitments and planned changes “before the end of 2026.”

University presidents and governing boards are asked to address seven subjects — including free speech, foreign influence, artificial intelligence and academic rigor — and post the statements prominently on their websites.

Ms. McMahon’s letter, which does not include any funding threats, suggests that changes will improve academia’s reputation among American parents and students.

“The dilution of academic standards, opaque admissions policies and a domineering monoculture have badly eroded public trust,” she wrote, adding that “only full candor and transparency can begin to strengthen the bonds between higher education and the American people.”

It was not immediately clear how the nation’s thousands of colleges and universities would respond to Ms. McMahon’s letter. But Ted Mitchell, the president of the American Council on Education, which was not involved in talks with the government before the letter’s release, said he regarded the missive as “a tentative handshake” between the administration and academic institutions. He predicted a significant response.

“For many institutions, this is kind of a no-brainer — it’s a fill-in-the-blanks kind of thing if they want to do it,” said Dr. Mitchell, who noted that many of the topics Ms. McMahon asked schools to discuss had already been subjects of immense debate among education leaders.

Barbara R. Snyder, the president of the Association of American Universities, said she had engaged with administration officials before the missive’s release on Monday. She was joined in the discussions by the chairman of the group’s board, Chancellor Douglas A. Girod of the University of Kansas, and the board’s vice chairman, President Ronald J. Daniels of Johns Hopkins University.

In an interview, Ms. Snyder said that the three had “approached this opportunity in good faith” and that she believed the discussions could advance “a working relationship with the government.”

Ms. Snyder said she had communicated a four-word mantra to administration officials: “No carrots, no sticks.”

The new push comes about 10 months after administration officials, including Ms. McMahon, proposed a compact to try to pull schools into ideological alignment. The document called for, among other conditions, a cap on international enrollment; a tuition freeze; and consideration of “transforming or abolishing institutional units that purposefully punish, belittle and even spark violence against conservative ideas.”

It also called for institutions to pledge to adhere to the administration’s preferred definitions around biological sex. And it encouraged policies to “recognize that academic freedom is not absolute, and universities shall adopt policies that prevent discriminatory, threatening, harassing or other behaviors that abridge the rights of other members of the university community.”

But the effort collapsed after many of the schools the White House handpicked for feedback on the idea condemned the proposal in scathing terms.

A central grievance was the administration’s suggestion that it would give schools preferential treatment for federal funding in exchange for backing the compact’s ideas. That proposal collided with generations of history, practice and competition among universities to secure funding on the basis of merit. And since the idea emerged months after the administration sought to choke off billions in money to schools it disfavored, it deepened fears that the White House was eager to trade largess for loyalty.

The compact envisioned stiff financial penalties, such as the reimbursement of “all monies advanced by the U. S. government during the year of any violation,” for any participating university that the Justice Department alone deemed out of compliance.

Although a handful of small institutions volunteered to sign, only one of the name-brand schools that the government initially asked for feedback — the University of Texas — was sweepingly enthusiastic. Most others, in public and in private, sounded notes like Sally Kornbluth, M. I. T.’s president, who warned that the proposal included ideas “that would restrict freedom of expression and our independence as an institution.”

Confronted with rare, largely united resistance from higher education leaders, the administration backed down, and its ambitions for a celebratory event in the autumn faded. Administration officials insisted at the time that they were not surrendering on the idea of a reworked compact.

They also began inserting some ideas into policy. The State Department, for example, started prioritizing visa requests for students at schools that were under a 15 percent cap on international students enrolled in undergraduate classes that the compact had envisioned.

But Dr. Mitchell said he was pleased by “the change in tone” that Monday’s letter seemed to suggest.

“It’s much less pugilistic than many things that have come out of this administration,” he said. “I think that it identifies several important positive principles — and it calls out a couple of things that we know we need to do better.”

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

Nanit and other start-ups want to track your children through the night — and soon, for much longer than that.

Young parents are increasingly willing to embrace tracking and analytics for their children — part of a broader cultural obsession with health data and optimization. Credit... Photo illustration by Margeaux Walter for The New York Times

Supported by

By Sapna Maheshwari

For all but a few nights of my first child’s life, her sleep has been recorded and analyzed by the Nanit Smart Baby Monitor System. A sleek white camera, bolted to the wall, points straight down at her body. High-definition footage is beamed to a server, where machine-learning algorithms log her movements and the precise moments her eyes open and close. The data are distilled into charts and insights that my husband and I review in the Nanit app: a daily “sleep efficiency” score, from zero to 100; minutes until sleep onset; the number of times we were needed over the course of a night.

Initially, we’d purchased the monitor simply for the ability to check on our daughter from anywhere using our phones. But we were quickly awed by everything else it could do, even as I recognized how unnecessary it was to have this much data about our baby, who was in fact a pretty decent sleeper. “SO MUCH INFORMATION,” I texted a friend. “it’s honestly TMI but i love it so much.” The Nanit straddles the line between creepy and delightful. It is the Eye of Sauron, but it also knows when we enter our daughter’s room in the morning and joy hits her face — and it sends us intelligently edited montages of these moments.

When I became pregnant with a second child in 2025, my husband and I did not even have a conversation about buying another Nanit camera. We had it waiting the day she came home from the hospital.

As a tool that crams together the sweetest thing on earth — a newborn — with relentless data collection by a for-profit tech company, the Nanit has always been a little disconcerting. A branding consultancy that helped create the product’s “visual identity” notes in a case study on its website: “The central challenge in this project was how to introduce this novel technology to the parenting market while transcending the negative connotations of ‘surveillance.’”

Millennial and Gen Z parents seem to have been persuaded. Nanit says it has one million daily users and annual revenue of more than $100 million. The most expensive version of its kit costs $474 and roughly $100 a year in subscription fees. And the market for babytech is only getting more crowded.

Owlet, Nanit’s biggest rival, offers a $300 pulse oximetry tracker that attaches to a baby’s foot through a sock. Huckleberry, a free app for tracking feedings and diaper changes, markets a $120 upgrade membership with “optimized nap predictions” and access to an artificial intelligence chatbot that, after logging your baby’s habits, can deliver personalized guidance and pep talks. CuboAi’s $359 Smart Baby Monitor 3 touts “A. I.-scheduled lullabies” and sends alerts when a baby’s face is covered.

As the products and their promises proliferate, I’ve gotten a little unnerved by how easy it’s become to outsource daily parenting decisions to technology. The downsides of this rush are manifest: sneakily high costs; the erosion of parents’ autonomy and self-confidence; giving sensitive data to corporations. But there may be no stopping the growth of babytech as a category. Parents my age and younger are increasingly willing to embrace tracking and analytics for their children — part of a broader cultural obsession with health data and optimization. Nearly half of Americans own a wearable device, and the companies that make smart rings and smart wristbands have valuations north of $10 billion.

Nanit and its rivals want to own 24/7 health tracking for the sub-four-foot set. And their already astonishing levels of baby data collection are just the beginning. Nanit recently raised $50 million from investors to expand its use of A. I. and use its camera to track speech and language development, motor skills and more, while extending its presence in children’s bedrooms into early adolescence.

My older daughter is now 4 and has become aware of “the Nanit,” which she refers to by name. I decided I wanted to know more about the company whose products stare at my kids all night — and which has designs to start tracking them far more.

When I visited Nanit’s office in downtown Manhattan recently, I was greeted by the sight of a lifelike baby doll lying in a $600 crib under one of the company’s cameras. The doll was clad in a onesie and a $20 Nanit Breathing Band, which was printed with a sequence of squares and diamonds. By analyzing the movement of pixels, the company’s software can quantify every rise and fall of a baby’s chest and send alerts to parents’ phones if it detects danger.

Nanit was founded in 2014 by Assaf Glazer, an Israeli who had just completed a Ph. D. in machine learning and computer vision at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology. Dr. Glazer and his wife had welcomed their first child, and he was sleep-deprived. With a friend, Tor Ivry, who was expecting his third child, he began to dream up a device that could identify and analyze sleep beyond the rudimentary baby monitors then on the market.

“Nanit” was conjured with words like “nanny” and “nano” in mind, and was meant to evoke “cutting-edge technology for parents,” Dr. Glazer has said. (He is now the chief executive of Vinst, a food tech start-up in Israel.)

Since 2024, Nanit has been led by Anushka Salinas, 44, the former president of Rent the Runway. She oversees some 150 employees, most of whom are parents, who work under the tagline, “Turn second-guessing into: “I’ve got this.” When we met at Nanit’s office, Ms. Salinas was wearing an Oura ring and was also testing a Whoop band, and she spoke earnestly about how Nanit is “effectively the child answer” to such devices.

“What’s happening with adult tracking is beginning to trickle down now in a much more meaningful way to kids,” said Ms. Salinas, who has two of her own. “Kids aren’t really starting to wear Apple Watches and things like that until around age 10 for the most part, sometimes a little younger. So we really think of that zero-to-10 for Nanit as kind of the place that we live.”

Sleep tracking and optimization will remain the base of Nanit’s business, Ms. Salinas said. But already, the app offers some health features, such as automatically detecting and recording audio of coughs that can be shared with pediatricians. The company sees growth potential in giving its app the ability to weigh in on speech and motor development, which Nanit’s camera could track ambiently. Hypothetically, Ms. Salinas said, the app could flag a delay and offer parents tips for improvement, like reading more bedtime stories.

Children might one day grow up to resent this intrusion, with data on their formative years stored indefinitely on a corporation’s servers. (Nanit says that its data is secure and is never sold or used for marketing.) But Ms. Salinas argues that children, in the future, may want access to their earliest health analytics for a variety of reasons. “Maybe a kid wants to be a professional athlete later on and they want to be able to go back and understand how their sleep developed and what that means for their potential,” she said.

She also suggested that when our own Nanit-tracked children have children, they’ll value the ability to go back and look at their own bedtimes. Nanit does not store video footage forever, but her comment made me wonder if that function was inevitable. I shuddered to imagine a permanent record of every time I’ve testily denied a fourth book over vocal protest.

Nanit’s people are upfront about not being entirely sure about all the potential uses of their devices. “I’m not going to sit here and pretend that we know the answer to what all of this data is going to unlock in the future,” Ms. Salinas said. She pointed to recent breakthroughs from adult wearables, like detecting atrial fibrillation and the early signs of Parkinson’s disease, as proof that the possibilities could be significant.

Company executives seem to have absolute conviction in the benefits of their technology. Mr. Ivry, the chief technology officer, shared more ideas. What if a 4-year-old was diagnosed with a medical condition, and unique patterns from the Nanit could help explain it? “Maybe you have a super introverted kid and you want to understand if some of the motion patterns when they were babies kind of predicted that,” he said. “It doesn’t have to be a bad thing.”

For the Nanit-pilled, it’s almost silly to object to the idea of precisely tracking a baby. Victoria Vaynberg, the company’s marketing chief, pointed out how thoroughly surveillance-like behavior has infiltrated every part of our lives. “We care about where our food delivery is and we want to be able to track it to the exact block until it arrives,” she told me. “Yet there’s a hesitation about knowing exactly how long your baby slept?”

Baby monitors are a relatively small industry, with sales of just $316 million last year, according to Circana, a market research firm. Turning passive monitors into active health trackers is a way of accessing a far larger pot of money. Various estimates put the size of the wearables market as approaching $100 billion, and as more consumers use them to track their activity and get algorithmic advice, applying the promise of more data = better life to children can seem like an obvious next step.

To hear the companies tell it, the benefits of embracing babytech are life changing. Nanit has claimed that its users get 36 extra nights of sleep a year, because parents feel more confident shifting babies to their own rooms earlier, and that its monitoring can prevent a baby’s skull from getting flat. The company has paid for studies on new parents’ sex habits and suggested that buying a Nanit can lead to more intercourse. Owlet and Huckleberry claim that more than 90 percent of their customers enjoy better sleep.

Kurt Workman, the chief executive of Owlet, which he co-founded in 2012 in Utah, told me that he’s noticed parents are asking “way fewer questions on how the data can be useful, and what it could mean, and is it safe.” The company, which is public, had revenue of $106 million last year and says that more than 2.5 million people have used its products. “We have parents who are like, ‘I know I can put my baby to sleep when their heart rate goes below this level, and they’ll stay asleep,’” said Mr. Workman. “We’re already starting to hack that.”

In 2021, the Food and Drug Administration sent Mr. Workman a warning letter after finding that Owlet had violated a federal law with marketing that veered into the realm of medical devices: Ads for Owlet’s Smart Sock product had promised the device would alert parents about dangerous changes in their children’s pulse rates and blood oxygen levels. Now Owlet sells an F. D. A.-cleared Dream Sock, touting “medical-grade monitoring” that “gives you real-time visibility into your baby’s wellness, so you know, not guess.”

Some pediatricians have criticized Owlet for marketing that makes use of fear — its website includes testimonials from families who say their babies could have faced “heart failure” had they not been wearing its device — and for causing unnecessary anxiety. When the Dream Sock malfunctions, parents think their baby has stopped breathing. Mr. Workman argues that the stories about Owlet catching life-threatening conditions are “incredible” proof points. “That’s a real-world, tangible impact to having access to health technology,” he said. “It’s not to scare people but to show that this is real.”

A different read of the babytech industry is that it’s all nonsense: Infants survived just fine before cameras with infrared night vision, humidity sensors and 256-bit encryption. My mother, who raised three of us, has made no secret that she thinks my generation is crazy. Recently, she got together with some of the Indian aunties whose children I grew up with. They bonded, laughing, over the protocols they were subject to when asked to handle their grandchildren’s bedtimes — the Nanits and Owlets, the sound machines and temperature controls, the precise sequencing that would make a nuclear reactor shutdown seem casual. The aunties were entertained and baffled by how different these routines were from their own experiences of early motherhood, which they recalled as more relaxed.

When I put the Nanit app on my mom’s phone for an evening of babysitting, she was bewildered by the phone notifications and mystified by why I would even want the analytics. And she plainly doesn’t like it when I use the app to check, a little compulsively, if my sleeping kids are, in fact, sleeping. In her view, it’s all anxiety inducing. She was weirded out by the idea that my kids’ data would live on a server and that they would perhaps be able to retrieve it someday. “Too much,” she said.

Plus, for all of Nanit’s claims and ambitions, parents often take to social media to complain that its most basic data can be wrong. The camera will flag visits or cries that didn’t actually happen.

Rebekah Diamond, a pediatrician and assistant professor at Columbia University, worries that parents who rely on these devices are numbing their natural instincts and allowing technology to interfere with one of the most universal and meaningful of human experiences. “I’m very cautious and wary of the big picture of kid-tracking and health-tracking and health monitoring, when it comes to this hyper-detailed, hyper-obsessive way it seems to be unrolling,” she told me. “Parents are losing a little bit of the muscle of their own confidence and decision-making.”

In other words, baby-tracking devices can be infantilizing. “What would you do if you didn’t have this app that said your baby needs a nap?” Dr. Diamond said. “You’d look at your baby. And see that they look tired.”

Baby monitors have their roots in fear. In 1932, American parents were horrified to learn that Charles A. Lindbergh’s toddler son had been taken from his second-floor nursery, and eventually killed, while five adults were in the home. A few years later, Zenith Radio Corporation introduced the first commercial baby monitor. The “Radio Nurse” was designed to be “on guard” for babies and the sick and elderly. An instruction manual read: “If the baby cries — if the invalid wants a glass of water — if there is a fire — if an intruder enters — YOU KNOW IT INSTANTLY!”

Nanit, Owlet and their competitors still operate in this space. The comedian John Mulaney recently riffed on his toddler son’s sleep setup, saying his bedroom looked like a “C. I. A. black site,” with a blackout tent over his crib. “I don’t know why we have 24-hour CCTV footage of my son’s crib, he’s not going anywhere — he sleeps in a bag,” he said. “We then have three sound machines going at full blast. And because we read it once on Instagram, we keep his nursery at 68 degrees. Any warmer and your infant will die automatically.”

One person who remains oblivious to all this parental anxiety is my older daughter. The Nanit is just a feature in her room. She understands that she can speak to my husband and me through the device, whose four red lights blink to power its night vision, and that we can see her at night through our phones. I imagine that she would develop sharper feelings about the camera if it started to play an extended role in her life, for years to come.

Nanit believes that one solution for that, as it looks to extend its presence in children’s bedrooms beyond toddlerhood, are new covers, known as “Cammies,” that can make the monitor look like a bunny, a bear or an elephant. Ms. Salinas said that making the camera look like a little friend or toy can “generate a lot more love” for it. But she added, “Each family is going to have to decide on their own if their child is OK with having the camera in the room as they get to the age that they’re making their own decisions.”

In her view, this is the start of a new future, a library of health data from cradle to grave. “The adoption curve accelerated significantly over the last few years,” Ms. Salinas said, “and I expect that to continue — such that it’ll be almost every parent that will have some product like Nanit that will help them have much richer insights on their child and who they’re becoming.”

Even before I first met Ms. Salinas, I had been wondering when to remove the Nanit from its perch above my older daughter’s bed. She may simply outgrow it before my husband and I come to a formal opinion on privacy versus convenience. These days, she no longer naps, and in the mornings she is as likely to greet us in our own bed than the other way around. There’s still joy on her face, and I make sure to see it there, rather than on a screen.

After I had my second child last fall, I felt like there was no end to the apps and devices that were trying to sell us sleep advice. I’m fascinated by how technology and A. I. are influencing modern parenting and where it will go in the future.

Sapna Maheshwari reports on TikTok, technology and emerging media companies. She has been a business reporter for more than a decade. Contact her at sapna@nytimes. com.

Education Dept. to Wipe Out Student Loans of 170,000 More Defrauded Borrowers

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The sprawling case, centered on students defrauded by for-profit schools, has now become the largest class-action settlement in American history.

By Stacy Cowley

More than 170,000 federal student loan borrowers who said they were defrauded by their schools are set to have $11 billion in debt erased, after an appellate court sided with the borrowers and rejected a request from the Education Department for more time to review their claims.

The decision is the latest grant of mass relief in a class-action suit that was originally filed during President Trump’s first term. The suit centered on federal loans taken out by students who attended dozens of predatory for-profit schools. The government settled the case in 2022, under former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., and forgave the student loan debts of nearly 300,000 borrowers who had become plaintiffs in the class action.

But the settlement required the government to keep reviewing fraud claims from borrowers who filed after the 2022 deal was announced. The agreement set a deadline of early 2026: If the Education Department had not adjudicated the additional claims by then, they were to be automatically approved.

In late 2025, the Trump administration asked for an additional 18 months to review the cases. A federal district judge rejected the request, and last month, a panel of three judges from the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit unanimously upheld his decision.

The total size of the class-action settlement has now expanded to nearly 500,000 borrowers, who will have debts totaling $23 billion wiped out.

That makes it — by a substantial margin — the largest class-action settlement in American history, according to the Project on Predatory Student Lending, the nonprofit group that represented the borrowers. It is also, by their calculation, the largest financial settlement against the federal government.

Eileen Connor, the executive director of the nonprofit group, said she saw parallels between this case and the 1998 settlement that required tobacco companies to pay states more than $200 billion to settle dozens of lawsuits over the health care costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.

“Tobacco is a toxic product — and a lot of times, these schools are peddling these loans, and they turn out to be toxic,” she said.

An Education Department spokesperson, Ellen Keast, said the original settlement “imposed an unrealistic deadline” on the department. “The Department has complied in good faith with court orders,” she said, “and we believe the court erred in not granting our reasonable request.”

Here’s what to know about the student loan fraud case:

The case — filed in 2019 and named for Theresa Sweet, one of its original plaintiffs — centered on claims that certain for-profit schools fraudulently lured students into enrolling with false claims about their graduates’ earnings and other predatory tactics.

In most circumstances, federal student loan borrowers are required to repay their debts, even if they drop out of school, can’t find a job or are otherwise unhappy with their educational experience. But there’s a caveat: If schools misled borrowers and defrauded them, debtors can seek to have their loans discharged through a program known as “borrower defense.”

A decade ago, after the collapse of several large for-profit education chains, hundreds of thousands of borrowers applied for relief through the program. Their claims languished for years, unaddressed.

Borrowers filed a class-action lawsuit seeking to have their claims decided. The first Trump administration denied nearly all of the claims, but a federal judge rejected those decisions, describing the Education Department’s process for evaluating the claims as “disturbingly Kafkaesque.”

The Biden administration settled the suit in 2022, under which all of the original plaintiffs would have their loans eliminated.

That deal created a five-month window in which additional borrowers — those who had not joined the original class — could submit claims.

The “post-class” settlement created two additional groups of borrowers: Those who had attended one of more than 150 schools, mostly for-profit institutions, specifically named in the settlement; and those with claims against other schools.

The government was required to make decisions about the applications of those in the first group by Jan. 28, 2026, and to make decisions on the claims of the second group by April 15, 2026.

It missed both deadlines. That means borrowers with unresolved claims would automatically have their loans discharged. The government has one year to carry that out and eliminate those loans.

The government had more than 463,000 pending borrower defense claims awaiting a decision as of March 2026, according to the latest Education Department data. About a third of those will be resolved in this settlement, but the others may languish for years.

Borrowers who believe they were defrauded can still submit new claims, but rule changes made during the first Trump administration significantly limited the relief available to those who took out federal student loans, or consolidated their existing ones, since 2019.

Stacy Cowley is a Times business reporter who writes about a broad array of topics related to consumer finance, including student debt, the banking industry and small business.
