How a Centrist Split Boosted Progressive Hopes in a Democratic House Primary

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Unable to unite behind a single candidate in Michigan’s Seventh District, moderate Democrats worry that they’ve complicated their chances in a key November battleground.

By Evan Gorelick

Democrats in a battleground congressional district in Michigan are eager to oust a vulnerable Republican incumbent, as they look to win back control of the House in November.

But first, they must settle, in their own ranks, a messy and bitter competition that some worry could complicate their plans this fall.

The Democratic primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which will be decided on Tuesday, has been consumed by hostilities. Two moderate candidates — who have refused the other camp’s calls to drop out — could split the vote and help open the door for a left-wing hopeful who centrist Democrats believe would alienate swing voters in the general election.

Progressive supporters believe he can win, and they see the race as one of several opportunities on Tuesday to build momentum this year.

The more moderate candidates are Matt Maasdam, a retired Navy SEAL, and Bridget A. Brink, who resigned as ambassador to Ukraine over President Trump’s coziness with Russia. As they have competed bitterly, William Lawrence, a progressive organizer backed by Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont, has emerged as a strong contender in the primary. The winner will take on Representative Tom Barrett, seen as one of the most at-risk Republican incumbents in the midterms.

“People are absolutely worried about Lawrence being able to beat Barrett,” said State Senator Sarah Anthony, who represents constituents in Michigan’s Seventh District but has not endorsed in the House race. The recriminations “could be harming our party in ways we can’t see yet,” she added.

The primary is one of several Democratic contests on Tuesday in which an insurgent progressive movement that has secured some high-profile victories this primary season faces a fresh test of its appeal. From Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s push to defeat an establishment-backed rival in Michigan’s marquee Senate primary, to the comeback attempt by a former “Squad” member, Representative Cori Bush, in Missouri, to the effort by Donavan McKinney, a democratic socialist, to oust an incumbent Democrat in Detroit, there is much at stake for the left.

And the unusual scrum in Michigan’s Seventh District is raising progressives’ hopes.

The rivalry between the two moderate campaigns turned ugly last month when Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat who held the seat before Mr. Barrett, formally endorsed Mr. Maasdam, filmed a super PAC ad on his behalf and put her name on his fund-raising materials. Ms. Slotkin’s intervention for Mr. Maasdam stunned and upset some Democrats, especially those in Ms. Brink’s camp, who felt that the former ambassador had a clearer path to victory.

Recently, tensions in the race have risen, with negative ads and accusations flying.

“It’s been very difficult, particularly in the last two weeks with the endorsing and the terrible TV ads,” said State Representative Jennifer Conlin, who represents constituents in the Seventh District and has endorsed Ms. Brink.

The House Democratic campaign arm has not made an endorsement in the primary. Meanwhile, Mr. Lawrence, who supports Medicare for all and the end of arms sales to Israel, has appeared to build momentum through the final stretch of the race.

He also faced criticism after a comment he made in 2024 saying an older generation of Black Democratic leadership “defangs the white left” surfaced online. The Congressional Black Caucus’s political organization said his backers should withdraw their support for him. Mr. Lawrence said he regretted the comment.

Mr. Lawrence said in an interview that he was “someone who has always been learning and growing.” He added that he had been in contact with House leadership and that, if elected, he would support Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, for speaker.

Republicans are eager to run against left-wing candidates and portray them as outside the mainstream. So when a shadowy super PAC sprang up late last month and began running ads attacking Mr. Maasdam — and promoting Mr. Lawrence — some Democrats accused Republicans of meddling. Democrats pointed to a little-known South Dakota bank it uses that has been linked with G. O. P. operatives. The group, called Michigan Sunrise PAC, did not respond to requests for comment

Ms. Brink said in a statement that voters she talks to “see through the desperate lies, mudslinging, and smears that have been launched in this race and are fed up with this kind of politics.”

Emma Grundhauser, Mr. Maasdam’s campaign manager, said in a statement that the campaign was “not focused on finger-pointing in Washington DC” but on speaking to voters.

When Ms. Slotkin endorsed Mr. Maasdam and cut an ad for him, some allies of Ms. Brink were confused by the timing — and worried that Ms. Slotkin would undercut the momentum they felt Ms. Brink’s campaign had built earlier in the race.

Ms. Slotkin had distributed polling data touting Mr. Maasdam’s prospects in June 2025, a review of polling materials and related written correspondence show, and recruited him to run, according to multiple Democrats familiar with the situation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private talks.

“Senator Slotkin is singularly focused on one thing: flipping her old seat from red back to blue,” Josh Stewart, a spokesman for Ms. Slotkin, said.

Evan Gorelick is a New York-based writer for The Morning, the flagship daily newsletter of The Times.

California Democrats Want to Tax Billionaires. They Can’t Agree on How.

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Leaders of the state Democratic Party endorsed the ballot measure slated for November, but the party remains far from united on the issue as Democrats nationwide grapple with a growing wealth gap.

By Laurel Rosenhall and Soumya Karlamangla

Laurel Rosenhall reported from Sacramento. Soumya Karlamangla reported from the California Democratic Party’s meeting in San Diego.

A teachers union leader rose to her feet in a hotel ballroom packed with Democratic activists, many of them wearing T-shirts that said “Tax the Billionaires.”

She addressed the obvious tensions among them, with labor unions that are often allies finding themselves at odds.

“This is a weird place for us to be,” the leader, Teri Holoman, associate executive director of the California Teachers Association, said Saturday at a California Democratic Party meeting in San Diego. Even though her union supported taxing the rich, Ms. Holoman said the billionaire tax measure on the November ballot was not the right way to do it.

Schisms over the proposal — a one-time tax on state residents with assets worth at least $1 billion — were evident throughout the weekend meeting, where the party’s executive board ultimately voted to endorse the ballot measure after three days of contentious debate. The endorsement passed by the barest of margins, and only after an initial vote by delegates failed to garner sufficient support.

The debate comes as the country confronts a rapidly growing gap between the wealthiest individuals and the masses struggling with everyday expenses. Though Democrats broadly support raising taxes on wealthy people, they differ intensely on how to do so. It’s a divide that could shape the 2028 presidential contest.

California’s fight over the wealth tax measure, known as Proposition 40, is being watched nationally because the state often serves as a testing ground for progressive policymaking. If approved, it would be the first tax in the nation assessed on a person’s total net worth, including wealth held in stocks, trusts and possessions like art and jewelry.

The weekend endorsement puts the California Democratic Party at odds with the state’s top elected Democrats. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate to replace him, both oppose the billionaire tax, saying it will reduce long-term funding for schools and other services by driving entrepreneurs away from California.

“They are, frankly, just out of step with the great majority of the people they claim to represent,” said Dave Regan, president of the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsored the ballot measure.

The conflict in California echoes larger divides in the Democratic Party that have pit progressives against moderates and populists against the political establishment in primary races across the nation this year. Supporters of the billionaire tax are framing it as a critical opportunity to salvage Medicaid funding in California and steer the direction of the Democratic Party nationally.

“This is the defining fight of our party: Are you on the side of the corporate donor-wing billionaire class, or are you on the side of economic populism and the working class?” said Representative Ro Khanna, one of few Democratic elected officials in California publicly in favor of the billionaire tax so far. “California’s fight is really the biggest symbol for that divide.”

But the politics may not be that clear cut. The billionaire tax was sponsored by a single labor union, whose members stand to benefit from it. The tax would generate tens of billions of dollars that would go toward health care programs that were slashed last year by President Trump. Without the funding, the union argues, millions of people will lose insurance and hospitals will close.

Other labor unions and health care organizations, including progressive groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, object to the tax because it does not provide long-term funding for a range of services, not because they are ideologically opposed to taxing billionaires. They support a different tax on the November ballot: Proposition 3, which would make permanent a temporary income tax hike on high earners.

Willie Pelote, a political consultant working for the No on 40 campaign, called the measure inherently divisive, pitting the interests of health care workers against those of educators and others whose salaries depend on state spending. He said that labor groups should have collaborated to put a measure on the ballot that would have helped all sectors. And he warned delegates that supporting the billionaire tax measure would ultimately deepen rifts in the Democratic Party.

“Prop. 40 is making losers and winners, and that’s not the appropriate way that we should act as labor brothers and sisters,” Mr. Pelote said at the meeting in San Diego.

Opposition from progressive groups will signal to voters that California’s debate over the billionaire tax is different from other conflicts that divide Democrats nationwide, said Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster based in Washington, D. C. In many Democratic primaries, the schism between candidates amounts to a disagreement over values, Ms. Lake said. Not so with California’s billionaire tax.

“This is a pragmatic debate, like whether or not this is a good idea or a flawed proposal,” she said.

For Republicans, the measure provides another line of attack against Democrats, a way to cast California as hostile to business and eager to expand government spending.

Democratic politicians around the country are experimenting with ways to tax the rich. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have embraced a tax on second homes worth $5 million or more. In Washington State, lawmakers passed a “millionaires’ tax,” creating the state’s first income tax, which would apply to earnings over $1 million. Opponents are seeking to overturn it on the November ballot.

But California’s proposal may prove to be the most contentious of them all. The state is home to more billionaires than any other, including some of the richest people in the world, and a handful of them have already poured more than $118 million into a committee that is backing two ballot measures that could negate a billionaire tax.

Democratic presidential candidates will likely examine the results of California’s battle over the billionaire tax as they formulate their economic proposals for 2028, said Jim Kessler, a co-founder of Third Way, a center-left think tank in Washington, D. C.

“I don’t think there is a division within the Democratic Party about whether very wealthy people — multimillionaires and billionaires — need to pay more in taxes,” he said. “The question is how you do it.”

Mr. Kessler believes a wealth tax like the one proposed in California is an impractical, constitutionally questionable approach. His organization favors other ways of raising taxes that do not involve the challenging task of calculating the net worth of people’s assets. Instead, he said, Democrats should consider hiking income taxes for high earners and taxes on capital gains and estates, or closing loopholes that allow people to avoid taxes on certain assets. Mr. Newsom, who is considering a run for president, took a similar approach with his proposal to tax the rich through changes to federal tax law. Mr. Khanna, the California congressman who supports the billionaire tax, is also exploring a potential run in 2028.

The billionaire tax, Mr. Kessler said, amounts to “a slogan over a solution.” But he said it had caught the attention of progressive populists nationwide who see the vote in California as a way to build momentum for their movement.

“Activists on the far left across America want this referendum in California to be the next pole in the tent that they put up,” Mr. Kessler said. “The more centrist wing of the Democratic Party has focused on this almost not at all.”

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting from Washington.

Laurel Rosenhall is a Sacramento-based reporter covering California politics and government for The Times.

Soumya Karlamangla is a Times reporter who covers California. She is based in the Bay Area.

How Democratic Socialists Are Wrestling With Their Next Moves

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

After notching primary victories, D. S. A. members in Chicago debated whether socialist candidates should be free to distance themselves from goals like abolishing prisons as they chase more seats this fall.

By Kellen Browning

Reporting from the Democratic Socialists of America summit in Chicago

When a leader of the Democratic Socialists of America recently appeared on “Fox News Sunday” and enthusiastically affirmed the group’s platform — including goals such as eliminating the U. S. Senate and working toward abolishing prisons — Democratic strategists wrung their hands and Republicans licked their lips.

Acknowledging such aims, both parties predicted, could hinder progressive candidates and other Democrats painted with an extremist brush in the midterm elections.

At the D. S. A.’s national summit in Chicago over the weekend, many democratic socialists who had seen the Fox interview felt something different: pride.

“You’re going to have to constantly push and advocate for things that people don’t think, until they think it,” said Chanpreet Singh, a D. S. A. leader from Seattle.

Hundreds of members of the group, the country’s largest socialist organization, gathered here at a moment of surging political influence, some wearing bright red shirts, swapping labor-strike tips with their “comrades,” sharing voter turnout strategies and admiring far-left merchandise (guillotine earrings, “Land Lords Suck” pins and red roses, a symbol of the group). Many dismissed the notion that their positions could be a political problem and said they felt no need to moderate them. Electoral wins were proof, they reasoned, that Democratic voters were moving closer to them.

As an ardent socialist movement has encroached more deeply into the Democratic Party, with D. S. A.-backed candidates ousting incumbent Democrats from New York to Colorado and notching other victories this year, the challenges associated with that often-fraught cohabitation are coming into sharper focus. Those include questions on each side about the utility of working with the other.

“Toxic to a broad majority of the country” was how Neera Tanden, the president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic think tank, described aspirations such as prison abolition and doing away with the Senate. She predicted that Republicans would make socialist policies “one of their main attack lines.” Already, President Trump and other Republican leaders are going further, seeking to brand recent Democratic nominees, falsely, as “communists.”

The next big tests for democratic socialists will begin on Tuesday in Democratic primaries in Michigan and Missouri for the U. S. House. And Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive doctor who is not a democratic socialist but shares many of D. S. A.’s priorities, is running for the Senate in Michigan, a major battleground.

A week later is the Democratic governor’s primary in Wisconsin, where Francesca Hong, a state assemblywoman and D. S. A. member, is the front-runner. Unlike many of the left-leaning areas where democratic socialists have won primaries this year, Wisconsin is a perennial swing state.

Though she has embraced the D. S. A. label, Ms. Hong has backed away from her own past statements in favor of abolishing the police and the Senate. Last week, she said at a debate that she did “not support the full platform of the national D. S. A.” and was “not endorsed by D. S. A. national.”

In an interview, Ms. Hong said that it was “concerning to me when I’m pigeonholed as the D. S. A. candidate.”

“You can be a democratic socialist and be endorsed by your local chapter, and disagree on other decisions,” she added.

No one interviewed at the summit suggested the D. S. A. back away from its core ideas. But there were plenty of disagreements over whether the candidates supported by the organization should be required to be open about their socialist affiliation and strictly adhere to every priority in the group’s recently updated platform, or if the D. S. A. should allow them some distance as they try to appeal to skeptical voters.

“There’s no expectation that you have to fall in line and agree and parrot the party line on everything,” said Cliff Connolly, a D. S. A. member from Orlando who is on the organization’s governing council.

Some appeared to feel differently.

“I believe that if she had read the platform and actually knew what was in it, she wouldn’t disagree with any of it,” Michaela Brangan, a D. S. A. leader in New Jersey, said of Ms. Hong.

The differing viewpoints on how ideologically rigid D. S. A. candidates should be reflected the spirit of disagreement in the socialist movement, whose members often join caucuses with diverging priorities.

Attendees said messy debates were a feature, not a bug, of a democratic organization.

On one side are two caucuses, Groundwork and Socialist Majority, considered more pragmatic (even right-leaning, by D. S. A. standards). Their members have focused on working within the system to get socialists elected on the Democratic ticket and are more tolerant of politicians making concessions as part of advancing a progressive agenda. They have a particularly strong presence in New York City, home to the D. S. A.’s two most famous members: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Ashik Siddique, one of the group’s national chairs and a member of Groundwork, said he wished the organization more clearly detailed which of its priorities were urgent, like economic relief, and which were aspirational, like prison abolition. That could help the group’s candidates, Mr. Siddique reasoned, because he felt its opponents were often fixated on the most aspirational goals.

The other wing of the movement features caucuses such as Marxist Unity Group, Bread and Roses, and Red Star, that have more sway nationally and focus on enacting socialist policies by upending the system. They have stronger ideological purity tests, with some members arguing D. S. A. should break away from Democrats entirely and form its own party.

Cerena Ermitanio, a more left-wing member from Houston who belongs to Bread and Roses, argued that the moderate caucuses were too comfortable with candidates who “hide the rose,” she said, and “don’t mention that they’re a democratic socialist.”

“We believe that our candidates need to wear their rose proudly,” she said.

Equally concerning, in the eyes of some activists, are candidates perceived to have drifted away from the movement on important policies.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, for example, who has made inroads with mainstream Democrats and is seen as a potential presidential candidate, remains a contentious topic among left-wing members of D. S. A., who said they still resented some of her past positions over the war in Gaza.

Though the congresswoman is one of the most outspoken critics of Israel in Congress, some on the left argue that she has not been strong enough in voicing support for Palestinians. In 2024, the national D. S. A. withdrew its conditional endorsement of her.

In Chicago, strong support for Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was mostly confined to a party at a nearby bar hosted by Groundwork, where members chanted her nickname, A. O. C., and vowed to convert skeptics to support her for president. She has not said if she will run.

“I don’t subscribe to letting perfection becoming the enemy of the good,” said Dieter Lehmann Morales, a Groundwork member and supporter of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez.

In an apparent effort to project unity, summit organizers asked that the news media speak only to the roughly 40 members who appeared on a list, many of them holding leadership roles. But outside the summit and at parties such as the Ocasio-Cortez gathering, others spoke openly.

Sitting in a dimly lit bar across from a taxidermy deer head wearing a D. S. A. hat (“Deer Leader,” as some called it), Johanna Von Maack wondered how much longer the Democratic Party would put up with the socialists in its ranks.

“I kind of wonder if what will end up happening is the Democrats kick us out,” said Ms. Von Maack, a New York D. S. A. member. She didn’t sound too unhappy about that prospect, reasoning that Democrats needed the socialists more than D. S. A. needed them.

For now, the group has been content to run its candidates on the Democratic ballot line, but some in Chicago mulled over the idea of forming a new party or running as independents.

Many in D. S. A. are also considering which Democratic incumbents they could unseat in the future. As early as the night of the New York primary victories in June, Hasan Piker, the provocative socialist influencer, was already taunting Representative Ritchie Torres of New York, a pro-Israel Democrat.

“You better act right, Ritchie,” Mr. Piker said on his livestream, threatening to find a primary challenger in 2028. “You got two more years.”

That kind of swagger permeated the summit, where members speculated about toppling high-profile New York Democrats such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, and challenging Gov. Kathy Hochul and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand in 2030.

“We’re thinking about all of those things,” said Olivia Gonzalez Killingsworth, a New York D. S. A. leader. “We would be fools not to.”

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

Brown’s President Will Resign After a Tenure That Included Trump Deal

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The president, Christina H. Paxson, led the campus for over a decade, but in recent years faced protests, political pressure and a shooting that killed two students.

By Alan Blinder

Brown University’s president said Monday that she would step down at the end of the coming academic year, after steering Brown through fraught negotiations with the Trump administration and the agony of a campus shooting that left two students dead.

The president, Christina H. Paxson, has been in her post longer than any other current leader of an Ivy League university. She became president in 2012.

In an open letter on Monday, she described her resignation as “the right decision for me and my family” and noted that she had previously extended her tenure to manage the university’s clash with the federal government.

The university extinguished some of that fight last summer, when it agreed to a settlement that included Brown’s $50 million commitment to work force development programs in Rhode Island. Brown forged the agreement after the Trump administration moved to block $510 million in research funds, which was part of a broader campaign to punish elite universities for perceived antisemitism and inaction over protests against the war in Gaza.

Although the Brown agreement explicitly preserved the university’s authority over academic matters and restored the research money, its terms also aligned the school with the administration’s approaches to transgender athletes and “merit-based” admissions policies.

Dr. Paxson faced substantial campus criticism over the settlement, which some regarded as an act of capitulation to an administration abusing its power. But later in the year, she forcefully rejected a Trump administration proposal for a compact with colleges and universities that floated tying research funding to ideological alignment.

At the time, Dr. Paxson said she was worried that the compact “would restrict academic freedom and undermine the autonomy” of Brown.

(Hours before Dr. Paxson’s announcement on Monday, the administration effectively abandoned talk of a compact and encouraged universities to detail on their websites how they are responding to a litany of complaints about higher education.)

Brown’s year of turbulence turned to tragedy in December, after a former Brown student opened fire on campus, killing two and injuring nine others. As Dr. Paxson tried to lead the university through the aftermath, her leadership came under scrutiny, especially over the school’s approach to securing its campus in Providence, R. I., where visitors have long had easy access.

Brian T. Moynihan, the Bank of America chief executive who is the university’s chancellor, said Dr. Paxson had led Brown through its challenges with a “balance of commitment to academic excellence, operational excellence and a collaborative philosophy.”

Mr. Moynihan said that the cycle of strategic planning had played a role in the timing of Dr. Paxson’s exit. He added that there would be a national search for the next president.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

House Panel Finds Lawmaker Likely Violated Rules on Sexual Harassment

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Ethics Committee called for the censure of Representative Chuck Edwards, Republican of North Carolina, who showered two female staffers with lavish gifts and affection.

By Robert Draper

Reporting from Washington

The House Ethics Committee concluded in a damning report on Monday that there was “substantial reason to believe” that Representative Chuck Edwards, Republican of North Carolina, “violated House rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.” Specifically, the report found that Mr. Edwards “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

The committee recommended that Mr. Edwards be censured by the House. According to the report, Mr. Edwards was interviewed by the committee and said that he had not done anything inappropriate. A spokeswoman for Mr. Edwards, 65, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The report, which did not name the women, found that they both received numerous gifts from Mr. Edwards, including jewelry totaling more than $1,000 in value, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and a cellphone, a KitchenAid mixer, a robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances and one-on-one dinners.

Axios previously reported that the congressman gave the two women matching handguns, one pink and the other blue. The attorney for one of the women said that she legally disposed of her handgun and later rebuffed her boss’s offer of other gifts.

The report described how Mr. Edwards would make flattering comments about the appearance of the two female staffers, calling them “pretty” or “breathtaking.” Axios also reported that Mr. Edwards wrote a handwritten note to one of the women after she resigned, saying that she had “written a complex chapter in my heart.”

The report found that Mr. Edwards also wrote her poems, did yardwork at her house, paid for her massages at a spa and skipped votes in the House so that he could help decorate her Christmas tree. When she told Mr. Edwards that she had received another job offer, he replied in a text: “I don’t cry often, but I have today. It caught me off guard.” The woman did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Edwards, who has been married since 1980, took one of the women to the December 2024 White House Christmas party. A copy of the official photograph obtained by The New York Times showed Mr. Edwards and the woman standing in between President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Jill Biden on their right, and Vice President Kamala Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, on their left.

In an interview, an attorney for the woman who attended the White House event said she did so without knowing that spouses or dates more typically attended as guests. The attorney added that his client received emails from the congressman that made her feel uncomfortable and felt that she was being groomed by him to be a romantic partner. The attorney, Elliot S. Berke, said the situation compelled the aide to resign earlier this year.

Though Mr. Edwards turned over several of his text messages and emails to the committee, the report notes that he did not furnish several relevant communications “that were central to the committee’s investigation.” Mr. Edwards responded to investigators that he often deleted messages “at a whim.”

Until recently, Mr. Edwards has cut an inconspicuous figure in Congress. He is a former operator of several McDonald’s restaurants in western North Carolina, as well as a three-term state senator. He won his congressional seat in 2022 after first defeating the scandal-ridden Republican incumbent congressman, Madison Cawthorn.

Like most of his House Republican colleagues, Mr. Edwards has assiduously praised President Trump, singling out the administration’s policies on trade, education and Iran. In 2023, he introduced legislation that would withhold federal funds from so-called sanctuary cities that impeded activities by U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Mr. Edwards now faces political headwinds that are likely to be exacerbated by the ethics report. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has targeted his district, which the Cook Political Report recently moved from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

His opponent, Jamie Ager, a farmer and self-described “mountain Democrat,” has raised over $3 million to date. Mr. Edwards has $940,000 in his campaign coffers.

Robert Draper is based in Washington and writes about domestic politics. He is the author of several books and has been a journalist for three decades.

Trump’s Meddling in Justice Dept. Causes Problems of His Own Making

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

In the past week alone, President Trump’s interference has imperiled one criminal case, set the stage for sanctions in a second and hindered the confirmation chances of his pick for attorney general.

By Alan Feuer

From the moment President Trump was re-elected, he has muscled his way into the driver’s seat at the Justice Department, leaving tread marks on its time-honored independence from the White House by demanding, and sometimes directing, investigations into his enemies.

But his tight grip on the steering wheel has often threatened to lead the department off a cliff.

Last week offered a particularly vivid portrait of the consequences of Mr. Trump’s meddling, which, in the span of only a few days, imperiled one criminal case, set the stage for sanctions in a second and gummed up the chances that his pick for attorney general will be confirmed by the Senate.

Mr. Trump has long believed that he is his own best adviser and that, as the leader of the executive branch, he enjoys complete control over the agencies beneath him. But there is a reason the department in charge of federal law enforcement has traditionally stood outside of the president’s personal purview, said Norman L. Eisen, a lawyer involved in some of the recent cases who, earlier in his career, worked on the Obama administration’s “no contact” policy with the Justice Department.

“When presidents meddle in the department,” Mr. Eisen said, “it tends to disrupt its normal functioning.”

The problems last week began on Wednesday, when lawyers for James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director, filed court papers revealing that Secret Service agents who questioned their client about a photograph he posted showing seashells on a beach arranged to read “86 47” were ordered to quickly send a summary of the interview to Mr. Trump on Air Force One. The interview was “a hot topic on the plane,” and the president was “very interested,” the filing said. In fact, it added, Mr. Trump wanted to use the agents’ notes as fodder at a coming media appearance even though they presumably contained sensitive and unverified investigative information.

The request for the notes was a shocking breach of the distance that most presidents have kept from the day-to-day oversight of criminal investigations and indicated the intensity of Mr. Trump’s personal involvement in the pursuit of Mr. Comey, one of his most reviled political adversaries.

But his insistence on interfering with the case could come back to haunt him. After all, Mr. Comey’s lawyers pointed to the episode as evidence that the Justice Department had indicted him — on charges of making threats against the president — only as an act of retribution. If that claim is proven true, it would result in the case being dismissed.

Mr. Trump’s intrusive instincts also played a role last week in the demise of another criminal case, one that accused the former Olympic canoeist David Hearn with vandalizing one of the president’s pet projects, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

When Jeanine Pirro, the U. S. attorney in Washington, announced the indictment of Mr. Hearn last month, she made it clear that the charges had been brought, at least in part, because Mr. Trump wanted them.

“This is not only a priority for the president,” she told reporters, “but for myself.”

On Friday night, however, the case fell apart in a spectacular fashion. Ms. Pirro, in a court filing, suddenly acknowledged that new information from Mr. Trump’s Interior Department had made her realize that shoddy construction, not anything that Mr. Hearn had done, caused the problems with the pool’s lining.

But even that confession did not stop Mr. Trump from doubling down on the vandalism narrative. On Saturday morning, he posted a message on social media saying that he disagreed entirely with Ms. Pirro, a veteran prosecutor and a friend of his for more than 40 years.

“I don’t know what she was thinking?” Mr. Trump wrote.

While Mr. Hearn's lawyers have not disclosed what they might do next, the case’s collapse gives them an opening to argue that the president’s stubborn statements about the matter suggest the prosecution was vexatious, frivolous or brought in bad faith.

Should a move like that succeed, it would add to the roster of Ms. Pirro’s failures to go after Mr. Trump’s enemies — a list that already includes six Democratic lawmakers accused of sedition by the president after they posted a video reminding military personnel of their obligations to ignore illegal orders. It would also allow Mr. Hearn to recoup legal fees for the cast of lawyers he hired to defend himself.

The president also intervened on another important bit of business at the Justice Department: the effort to confirm Todd Blanche, Mr. Trump’s former personal lawyer, as attorney general.

As the week came to an end, Mr. Blanche seemed well on his way to removing the main hurdle to his appointment, calming the concerns expressed by two Republican senators — John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina. The lawmakers have repeatedly voiced unhappiness with the $1.8 billion compensation fund and the extraordinary personal tax protections that emerged this spring from Mr. Trump’s deal to drop his lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

But as the weekend neared, the president seemed to throw Mr. Blanche under the bus that he himself was driving, issuing a series of confusing and contradictory messages.

On Friday, he appeared to step back from his earlier threat to withdraw Mr. Blanche’s nomination and repeated his support for creating the fund, which Mr. Blanche had already said was dead. On Saturday, Mr. Trump again asserted that he would revive the fund, which could be used to compensate rioters who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, if the Senate did not confirm Mr. Blanche.

Mr. Tillis, for one, seemed baffled and dispirited by Mr. Trump’s chaotic interference in the confirmation process, holding out hope that the president’s back-and-forth approach would end before the Senate went on summer recess early this week.

“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal,” Mr. Tillis wrote on social media. “Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday.”

There appeared to be a breakthrough on the matter late Sunday night when Mr. Blanche posted two documents: a signed memo in which he said that the Justice Department was formally rescinding an order that created the fund and an unsigned statement in which the agency clarified the terms of the tax protections.

Mr. Blanche’s message said that the documents had emerged from “good faith discussions” with senators, and by Monday afternoon, Mr. Trump was insisting he had no part in the revised plan.

“I didn’t look at it,” Mr. Trump said in the Oval Office. “All I know is that Todd Blanche is great.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis expressed support after Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, issued a memo abandoning part of a deal the Justice Department had struck with President Trump.

By Michael Gold and Andrew Duehren

Reporting from Washington

The two Republican senators who had threatened to block Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general said on Monday that they would support his nomination after the Justice Department committed in writing to abandoning elements of a deal it struck with President Trump to resolve his lawsuit against the I. R. S.

Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina said in a joint statement that they were “pleased” that Mr. Blanche issued a memo and a statement on Sunday night appearing to concede to demands they had made about the settlement.

Both men had vowed that they would not confirm Mr. Blanche unless he provided written assurances that the Justice Department had formally killed a planned $1.8 billion fund to pay those who claim they were unfairly persecuted by the government.

They had also insisted that Mr. Blanche narrow the scope of the sweeping immunity from I. R. S. scrutiny that was granted to Mr. Trump, his family and their businesses under the same agreement.

Mr. Blanche posted two documents on social media on Sunday night: a signed memo in which he said the Justice Department was formally rescinding an order that created the so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and an unsigned statement in which the agency clarified the terms of the I. R. S. protections.

Mr. Blanche’s announcement came just days before the Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to vote to advance his nomination on Tuesday. With all Democrats expected to oppose his confirmation, any one Republican on the panel could have blocked Mr. Blanche’s nomination from advancing.

Critics questioned whether the new memo and statement from Mr. Blanche were truly legally binding. And even in its new form, Mr. Blanche’s order for the I. R. S. to abandon any audits of Mr. Trump’s previous tax returns is an unprecedented and potentially illegal benefit to a sitting president, worth potentially tens of millions of dollars in lower taxes and avoided penalties.

But on Monday morning, Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis, who are both on the Judiciary Committee, said in a joint statement that they would allow his nomination to move forward.

“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” the senators said. They also said they believed the department had “acknowledged in a binding written order” that the audit protections were limited, “addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.”

Mr. Blanche, who said in his social media post that his announcement came out of “good faith discussions” with the senators, posted the documents after days of negotiations. Although the senators had been working with Mr. Blanche in a bid to end the impasse, Mr. Trump had complicated their efforts in recent days by pushing publicly for the restoration of the fund.

Asked about the agreement on Monday, Mr. Trump said he had not reviewed it. “I understand there’s been a sign-off,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “But I don’t know what they agreed. I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he already said, and what he said was OK.”

Still, the president continued to voice his support for the anti-weaponization fund, echoing comments he made last week suggesting that he wanted to find a way to revive it.

Those remarks had appeared to validate the senators’ fears. In a social media post last week, Mr. Tillis wrote that Mr. Trump “clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against.”

Though Mr. Blanche promised lawmakers during his confirmation hearing that the fund was dead, Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis had urged him to take that position in writing. The memo he released on Sunday night said that the fund “shall have no force or effect” and that the memo “establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no fund.”

In a statement accompanying that memo, the Justice Department said that although Mr. Blanche had “repeatedly advised Congress” about the withdrawal of the fund, “today’s order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026, order.”

That statement also said that only Mr. Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization would be immune from audits, excluding a broader pool of Trump family members and their associates who appeared to be eligible for protection under the original Justice Department deal. Mr. Blanche also stipulated that their future tax returns could still be audited — another one of Mr. Cornyn’s demands.

Both the audit protections and the fund — which the Trump administration said was established to compensate those it says were victims of “weaponization” under Democratic administrations — have faced criticism since their inception.

Democrats have slammed both provisions as corrupt handouts to the president and his allies, and many Republican senators privately expressed outrage that the fund could be used to reimburse people who were charged in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, attack at the Capitol.

The new agreement failed to quiet Democratic critics, who argued that it did little to address their concerns about the fund or the audit immunity. Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, criticized Mr. Blanche’s agreement as insufficient, particularly given Mr. Trump’s continued support for the fund.

“There’s no guardrail preventing Trump and Blanche from using taxpayer dollars to give cash payouts to MAGA insurrectionists and billionaires,” Mr. Schumer said on the Senate floor on Monday.

Mr. Trump sued the I. R. S. in January, initially demanding $10 billion over the leak of his tax returns during his first term. The Justice Department, which represents the I. R. S. in federal court, never contested Mr. Trump’s suit, instead agreeing to settle, even though lawyers at the I. R. S. thought the government had a clear defense against the president’s claims.

Hari Raj contributed reporting.

I Helped Run Lululemon. Companies Need to Stop Kidding Themselves About A. I.

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Julie Averill

Ms. Averill is a former chief information officer of Lululemon.

I served as the chief information officer of the athletic apparel company Lululemon for eight years. Deploying new technologies, artificial intelligence included, was part of the job. But when I left, my successor was handed a new title: chief A. I. and technology officer.

I winced — not about the person but about the pattern. Companies these days are quick to stick “A. I.” in news releases, in earnings calls, in product names, in job postings and in titles at the top of their organizations. The real question is what strategy sits behind the abbreviation. A title costs nothing, but it doesn’t produce anything, either.

And that’s a problem. When companies mistake an announcement for a strategy, they spend real money — and sometimes cut real jobs — chasing a future that isn’t actually being built. And in doing so, they’re persuading Americans to reject a powerful innovation that could do so much good for all of us.

I have spent 30 years in technology, and like many of my peers, I used the newest tools to solve hard problems. In the internet era, my colleagues and I built a tool that let every customer check the inventory in each of Nordstrom’s stores. It increased sales significantly. When I was at Lululemon, we found a way to use A. I. to help executives better predict which products would sell in which stores. It took time, lots of people and big budgets.

Then ChatGPT arrived. This new technology was easy to understand for most nontechnologists — a chief executive, board member or investor — a healthy portion of whom began demanding their organizations immediately embed the technology throughout their operations. A. I. companies started popping up like food trucks at a street fair.

These A. I. companies arrived armed with demonstrations, and the demos were amazing. Talented technologists promised to crack business problems that were too complicated and expensive to solve before. Leaders across departments cleared their calendars to listen to the parades at their doorsteps.

This was the beginning of what I call A. I. wishing: the belief by company leaders that A. I. is magic, that you can wave its wand toward a hard problem and skip the work of solving it. It is sincere, and that is what makes it dangerous. I continued to meet with the stream of A. I. vendors, all promising their tools would be game changers. Collectively, the hordes introduced chaos into teams already stretched thin.

A few years ago an executive brought me an A. I. product and asked me to fast-track it. A board member had recommended it. The promises were bold: It could answer any question about the company. It could predict years and years of sales, tell which advertising was working and suggest what would work better, find and fix waste in how products were made and moved, and more.

I was skeptical. I know that even A. I. cannot tackle an issue it has never been taught to understand or accurately advise a business it knows nothing about. When we met with the company, it didn’t ask us a single question — not about our data, our systems or how we worked. We eventually said no, but it took longer than it should have. Even a room full of people who knew better wanted its promises to be true.

In the meantime, we continued to run pilots — small test versions of tools inside the business before committing to it. I wanted them to work as much as the next person, but the results were the same almost every time. The demo looked like magic. But the tool wanted clean, connected data and decisions made in consistent, repeatable ways. Ours lived in a dozen systems that did not agree, layered with decades of exceptions and workarounds.

This is not just my story. When I compare notes with other chief information officers, the details change, but the ending rarely does. One runs an insurer, another an airline, another a manufacturer. Each tried tools that dazzled in the demo and stalled the moment they hit the mess of a real, decades-old business. Last year a report from M. I. T.’s Project NANDA put a number on it, finding that 95 percent of enterprise generative A. I. pilots never delivered real results.

We are getting smarter from each round of pilots. The tools keep improving, and the gap keeps narrowing. But better A. I. tools are never going to close it on their own. What’s left is the part that was always ours: the slow, expensive work of cleaning up the messy data, complex human decisions and tangled systems.

This is how the A. I. revolution is actually going, at company after company.

Don’t mistake any of this for doubt about A. I.’s potential. It is the most powerful technology I’ve seen, and entire industries are already being remade by it. Pharmaceutical companies are rebuilding drug discovery around it. Banks run fraud and risk detection on it. Governments are treating the chips behind it as a matter of national security. This kind of work doesn’t happen in a quarter, and believing that it can is the trap.

This brings me to A. I. washing. The insidious cousin of A. I. wishing, it is when a company — under pressure to immediately show results — claims to be doing more with A. I. than it actually is.

The board wants to see progress. A leader who can’t show something starts to look like the problem. Seventy-five percent of executives admitted their A. I. strategy is “more for show,” according to a recent global survey by the A. I. company Writer and the research firm Workplace Intelligence. So a chatbot becomes the first step in an A. I. “transformation,” and a demo becomes proof of what’s coming. It isn’t lying, exactly. It’s describing what you hope will happen as if it already had taken place.

Perhaps the best-known version of A. I. washing is the most tragic one: the A. I. layoff. A company proclaims it needs fewer people because A. I. made its operations more efficient. Often the efficiency doesn’t exist yet. The cut is really about freeing up cash, sometimes to spend more on A. I.

In May, U. S. employers announced 97,000 job cuts, and according to one research firm, companies blamed 40 percent of them on A. I. A separate survey found that around one-third of hiring managers who had cut a role because of A. I. had already rehired for the same or a similar one.

Of course they did. They eliminated positions before redesigning the work, so the work shifted onto the people who remained. Then companies quietly hired back some of the capability they claimed A. I. had replaced. That cycle burns money and loses the talent and experience that was pushed out the door (not to mention the trust of the people asked to stay).

And there’s another cost. Behind all of those cuts are human beings who might have been falsely told a machine could do their jobs. Some had the demoralizing task of training the very tools meant to replace them. I know a few such individuals. One gave two decades to a company that told her, in a short meeting, that software could now do what she did. Truth was that it couldn’t, not really. She wasn’t a cost to be optimized. She was the person who knew why the numbers looked the way they did, the very context no tool could see. The ones who stayed absorbed her work and quietly wondered if they were next.

Every inflated announcement, every time a company blames A. I. for layoffs teaches people to distrust the technology itself. Distrust builds resistance. The Writer and Workplace Intelligence report found that 44 percent of Gen Z workers and roughly a third of the broader work force said they were actively sabotaging their company’s A. I. rollout. The fear is real, and it is spreading.

The way out of this is not more hype. It’s honesty. A vocal minority of people genuinely believe superintelligence is nearly here, ready to either remake the world or end it. Who knows if they’ll be proved right? I’m skeptical because the humans are still in charge and we have a habit of moving slower than the hype. But most companies aren’t living in that debate. In my experience, the useful truth is the plainer one in between: A. I. is a genuinely powerful technology that still needs people, and putting it to use is slow, human work. The sooner we are honest about that with our boards, our employees, our investors and the public, the sooner we can stop performing A. I. and start building something with it.

Today I often get asked what separates the companies where AI works from the ones where it stalls. My answer is never technical. It's how strong the culture is, whether people can speak the truth without consequences, take risks, and keep learning. Curious if that matches what others have seen.

Julie Averill is a former chief information officer of Lululemon and the author of “Chief Impact Officer: Real Transformation Comes From Human — Not Just Artificial — Intelligence.”

Documents Undercut Trump’s Claims About Utah National Monument

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump said recreation in Bears Ears National Monument was virtually impossible. Documents reviewed by The New York Times show officials knew otherwise.

By Maxine Joselow

Reporting from Washington

When President Trump sharply reduced the size of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah by more than 1.2 million acres, he claimed it was necessary because recreation was virtually impossible within the site’s boundaries.

“You can’t go hunting, you can’t go fishing, you can’t do anything, you can virtually not even walk on it,” Mr. Trump said during a ceremony in the Oval Office last month.

The No. 2 official at the Interior Department, Kate MacGregor, chimed in, saying, “That’s exactly right, sir, so you are remedying that today.”

But recreation has been allowed in Bears Ears since President Barack Obama designated the monument in 2016. And government documents reviewed by The New York Times show that Trump administration officials were briefed on recreational opportunities inside the monument about a month before the Oval Office event.

Utah officials, who pushed for shrinking the monument, told the Trump administration in June that there was “current recreational access” to Bears Ears, according to the documents, which The Times obtained via a public records request.

The state officials specifically cited two trails popular among hikers, backpackers and off-road vehicle drivers, the documents show. (Other trails attract scores of horseback riders, mountain bikers and rock climbers, as Mr. Obama noted when he designated the monument.)

The documents suggest that the administration was “lying or spreading misinformation about these fantastic public lands” when it justified cutting the protected areas, said Steve Bloch, the legal director at the nonprofit Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, who reviewed the records at the request of The Times.

National monuments are public lands that are legally protected from oil and gas drilling, mining and other industrial development. They have similar protections as national parks, but while national parks are created by Congress, national monuments can be created by presidents through the Antiquities Act of 1906.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, did not answer questions about the documents but said in an email that “the Obama and Biden administrations abused the Antiquities Act to lock up millions of acres of Utah’s public lands, impoverishing local communities and sharply restricting access for recreation, grazing, resource development and fire prevention."

Charlotte Taylor, a spokeswoman for the Interior Department, also did not address the documents but said in an email that previous administrations “shut hunters, anglers and other sportsmen out of land they had accessed for generations.”

Mr. Trump signed executive orders last month to cut Bears Ears and a second national monument in Utah, Grand Staircase-Escalante, by more than 90 percent. The orders opened both sites, which are known for their sandstone canyons and vast mesas, to oil drilling, uranium mining and other commercial activities.

During his first term, Mr. Trump shrank Bears Ears by 85 percent and cut Grand Staircase nearly in half. But tribes and environmentalists sued over the move, saying the Antiquities Act authorized presidents to designate monuments but not to abolish or shrink them. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. subsequently restored sweeping protections to both sites before a court could issue a final decision. Mr. Trump’s new second-term cuts are even bigger.

The documents reviewed by The Times show that Redge Johnson, the director of Utah’s Public Lands Policy Coordinating Office, sent a memo in June to Sam Crofts, a senior adviser at the Interior Department, detailing Bears Ears’ history, geology and recreational opportunities.

The memo said that a route called the Peavine Corridor was open to off-road vehicles and provided “motorized access deep into the area.” It added that “backpackers often use Rig Canyon as a junction point on massive wilderness loops,” including a popular 40-mile loop.

Mr. Crofts, a former policy director for Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah, did not respond to a request for comment. Representatives for Utah’s Public Lands Policy Coordinating Office also did not return a request for comment.

Bears Ears is the ancestral homeland of five tribes in the region: the Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, Ute Indian Tribe, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe and Pueblo of Zuni. It contains thousands of archaeological sites that tribes consider culturally significant, including the remains of burial grounds, cliff dwellings and rock art panels.

The monument also boasts “world class outdoor recreation opportunities,” Mr. Obama wrote in his proclamation designating Bears Ears, which cited “rock climbing, hunting, hiking, backpacking, canyoneering, whitewater rafting, mountain biking and horseback riding.”

Louis Williams, the founder and owner of Ancient Wayves River and Hiking Adventures, which provides tours of Bears Ears led by Indigenous guides, said he watched live as Mr. Trump signed the executive order to shrink the monument.

“I was shaking my head,” Mr. Williams said. “I was like, ‘I wonder if he’s ever been here to this region, because if he knew this region, he would find out this place is totally accessible.’”

But Ben Burr, the executive director of the BlueRibbon Coalition, a group that pushes to open public lands to off-road vehicles, said he supported Mr. Trump’s move. He noted that the Biden administration proposed a plan to prohibit off-road vehicles across 600,000 acres of the monument, though it never took effect.

“Nobody ever felt those restrictions because the plan was adopted in the final midnight hours of the Biden administration, and then it was never actually enforced,” Mr. Burr said. “So we think that the discussion around what was allowed and not allowed in these monuments has been kind of obfuscated by that.”

The documents did not mention hunting or fishing. But the Utah Department of Natural Resources, which houses the Public Lands Policy Coordinating Office, allows people to hunt and fish in Bears Ears if they have valid licenses and tags.

Maxine Joselow covers climate change and the environment for The Times from Washington.

After revelations that a botched renovation, not vandalism, had caused the pool’s recent problems, the U. S. attorney’s office has dropped several prosecutions.

By Clarence Williams

Reporting from Washington

Prosecutors in Washington are dropping charges against three more defendants who had been accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The motions to dismiss the three misdemeanor cases coincide with the decision last week to drop the most serious of the cases, the felony prosecution of a former Olympian who prosecutors had accused of damaging the pool.

The U. S. attorney, Jeanine Pirro, abruptly abandoned the four cases after investigators concluded that botched work by a contractor, not vandalism, was the primary cause of “widespread damage” to the pool’s new blue lining.

President Trump has been fixated for months on the condition of the Reflecting Pool, which has been plagued for years by water leaking out between its long concrete slabs. This year, the Interior Department, which oversees the site, gave a no-bid contract to fix the pool to Atlantic Industrial Coatings, a small Virginia firm.

After pieces of the pool’s new blue lining began to peel up, the president and administration officials blamed several people who had been arrested and charged with vandalizing the pool.

But the extraordinary motions filed in District of Columbia Superior Court over the last few days indicated that the problems that had drawn the president’s ire were caused by a faulty repair job, not vandals.

David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, was the one defendant who was facing a felony charge, and on Friday, it was his case that the U. S. attorney’s office moved first to dismiss.

Ms. Pirro’s filing on Friday said that prosecutors had determined “the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism.”

Along with Mr. Hearn, prosecutors moved to drop charges against three others: Justin Carreno, Sophie Dennison-Gibby and Cameron Thiers, who all were charged with destruction of property less than $1,000.

G. Allen Dale, who represents Mr. Thiers, said prosecutors had contacted him in an email to state their intent to drop the case.

“Mr. Thiers and I are both very happy this case is over. It probably shouldn’t have been brought in the first place,” Mr. Dale said in a phone interview Monday. “At least this nightmare is over for him.”

On Friday, Ms. Pirro said Interior Department officials initially misled prosecutors by blaming vandals for damage, when, in fact, the new blue coating installed by contractors had actually started to fail within two days of the project’s completion.

Ms. Pirro blamed Atlantic Industrial Coatings for a “flawed installation” and the administration’s rush to complete the project ahead of the America 250 celebration on July 4.

Earlier this summer, federal officials said at least seven people had been accused of vandalizing the pool. But the identity of the other people and the status of any cases against them could not be immediately determined.

Timothy Lauer, a spokesman for the U. S. attorney’s office, declined to comment.

Jamison Koehler, a lawyer who represents Ms. Dennison-Gibby, said his client was “relieved” the charges were being dropped after she had faced threats of jail time and had been “petrified to learn the President of the United States was threatening to bring full force of the U. S. criminal justice against her and others.”

Mr. Koehler added that while the case has been dropped for now, he considers a possibility a charge could resurface.

“This administration is so petty and manipulative, there is always the fear that they might,” he said.

For Trump, the Year Is Always 2020

The New York Times August 03, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Trump insists on revisiting and rewriting much of what happened six years ago, including the coronavirus pandemic and the election he lost. Many voters would rather he focus on 2026.

By Katie Rogers

Katie Rogers, a White House correspondent, covered President Trump’s response to the coronavirus pandemic and the aftermath of his election loss.

What year is it again?

Over the past few days, President Trump has been living in the year 2020, claiming that he defied his advisers to reopen the country during the coronavirus pandemic, saying that one of them, Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, was the one with all the “crazy ideas.”

He has revisited his near-daily falsehood that he won the 2020 election and that it was rigged, a belief held by a large swath of his political base. And, on Friday, he said that his supporters who ransacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, were simply on an “innocent journey.” Four people died that day.

Mr. Trump is not so much a student of history as a rewriter of it. In his second term, he is so set on avenging his election loss and pursuing retribution against his political enemies that he has Americans looking backward when many have signaled they would rather he explain why the country is at war with Iran, or help them afford groceries now, in the year 2026.

Neither his falling poll numbers nor the concerns among Republicans about the midterms seem to be modulating his insistence on revisiting much of what happened six years ago.

“I don’t think his ego allows him to accept the fact that someone he perceives as so weak as Joe Biden was able to beat him,” said Sarah Matthews, who was a deputy press secretary in the first Trump administration and resigned amid the Jan. 6 attacks.

“I witnessed it firsthand that he had advisers telling him he lost and there was no evidence of fraud,” said Ms. Matthews. “He stopped listening to those people and started surrounding himself with enablers and conspiracy theorists.”

Six years later, she said that Americans are still living with the consequences, “in the sense that he’s not focusing on the things that most Americans are focused on.”

In a statement, Abigail Jackson, a White House spokeswoman, suggested that Mr. Trump’s fixation on the 2020 election was part of an effort to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require voters to prove their citizenship to register, ban IDs without a photo at polling places and severely restrict voting by mail. Democrats have argued that the legislation would make it more difficult for eligible voters to make it to the polls.

“The president knows how critical this issue is for the American people, and he will not stop fighting until it is passed, but he can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. “The Trump administration continues to lower drug prices, restore American jobs, restore gold standard science and more.”

Last week, Senate Republicans joined Mr. Trump back in 2020. Revisiting a collective national trauma far more complicated than how they presented it, Senate Republicans trumpeted Dr. Fauci’s journal entries — recovered from a government server and shared with the public courtesy of Mr. Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In them, Dr. Fauci wrote of all the attention that he received from celebrities like Julia Roberts and Barbra Streisand.

Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times on Wednesday during a hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. To many, this was a tacit admission of guilt from the 85-year-old, who retired from public service in 2022. (Mr. Trump pleaded the Fifth hundreds of times during a 2022 fraud trial, according to publicly available documents.)

In his journals, Dr. Fauci detailed his deteriorating relationship with Mr. Trump as they disagreed over experimental treatments for the virus, mask guidance, testing availability and school closures. There was tension as far back as January 2020, when the president was downplaying the spread of the mysterious virus.

“I had to answer that we are taking this very seriously and that Americans should not be frightened or worry,” Dr. Fauci wrote of a television appearance he made at the time. “Let us see if this pits me against the POTUS.”

Turns out, he was right to be wary: Mr. Trump has lumped Dr. Fauci in with a long list of political enemies he believes he made during the last year of his first term.

That list includes Joseph R. Biden Jr. Last month, Mr. Trump veered off course during events that were supposed to be about U. S. nuclear capability and manufacturing and the environment to insult his successor. He also claimed on social media that he had warned Mr. Biden about Dr. Fauci, despite the fact that Mr. Trump gave the doctor a presidential commendation for his work to bring a Covid vaccine to the public.

“I called Biden to tell him Fauci was no good, either didn’t have a clue, or was dishonest. The call was well received, but sadly, not acted on,” Mr. Trump wrote. “He went on to give Fauci vast destructive power.”

Two people directly familiar with Mr. Biden’s conversations with Mr. Trump, who were granted anonymity because they did not want to get into a public back-and-forth with the president, say that call did not happen.

A former senior administration official who was part of the first-term White House coronavirus task force and was granted anonymity to avoid getting into a public spat with former colleagues, recalled that Mr. Trump and his advisers would frequently disagree with Dr. Fauci in Situation Room meetings about the virus.

Dr. Fauci’s refrain during tense moments was to tell members of that group that his job was to make science-based recommendations. The job of White House officials, he said, was to weigh those recommendations against potential economic harm.

Mr. Trump’s retellings have, at a minimum, stripped nuance from matters as complex as his handling of a virus outbreak that would kill over a million people. In Mr. Trump’s version of events, there is only good and bad, hero and villain, with him or against.

Thomas B. Pepinsky, a political scientist and a co-author of “Pandemic Politics: The Deadly Toll of Partisanship in the Age of COVID,” said that this binary approach was evident during the pandemic and may have cost Mr. Trump the election he cannot stop obsessing about.

“The main finding was that the Trump administration interpreted the pandemic as a political threat,” Mr. Pepinsky, who teaches at Cornell, said of his research. “It was a tactical error. He could have been re-elected if he had treated the pandemic differently.”

Mr. Trump’s constant, incorrect assertions about the 2020 election results have carried a cost for American democracy. A raft of polls have found deepening distrust in government institutions and election security, but a partisan split in the reasons why. According to a Politico poll published in May, a majority of Republicans are worried about ineligible people voting, while a majority of Democrats are worried about voter suppression.

Many Americans remain legitimately angry and upset about what happened to them and their families during the pandemic. And experts like Mr. Pepinsky see a missed opportunity to learn from mistakes made in 2020.

Americans now face a growing measles outbreak and fears about food supply contamination. Asked last week about an outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a diarrhea-causing illness whose recent spread has been linked to contaminated iceberg lettuce, Mr. Trump shrugged off concerns.

“I haven’t thought about it,” Mr. Trump said, before joking with the reporter who asked the question. “Are you eating lettuce recently?”

People who know how Mr. Trump operates believe he will persist with his focus on the events of 2020, given the main lesson he seems to have learned from that time period: Facts have not gotten in the way of his opinions, and he has been rewarded for it.

“If he says something enough times, he has the world’s largest megaphone,” Ms. Matthews said. “Of course, there are going to be millions of Americans who are going to believe him and take him at his word, even if he has no evidence to back it up.”

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.
