AI Slop Melodramas Are Taking Over X—and Their Creators Are Cashing In

Wired July 31, 2026

For 6 months, my husband convinced everyone that I had stolen millions from the company I built, including our own daughter. As I sat in federal court, certain I was about to lose my freedom, the doors suddenly opened. My 9-year-old son walked in carrying an old blue backpack, looked straight at the judge, and said, “Your Honor. I know who framed my mom. They’re sitting in this room.”

So begins a thread on X that appeared in my feed one day. I knew that the first-person narrator probably didn’t exist, and following this thread would draw me into a mawkish tale where good triumphs over evil. Indeed, the author is not a mother on trial for theft, but a self-identified 21-year-old stock trader in Nigeria, who uses AI to generate stories—and gets paid for it by X.

I found this out when I began wondering about the proliferation of these compact melodramas of redemption in my feed. It’s probably my own fault; I sometimes idly click on these cheesy stories—you know, just to see what happens next—and the algorithm took notice. In this case, the author is one of countless beneficiaries of X’s Creative Revenue Sharing program, which pays for posts that boost engagement on the platform. To join, a creator must become a Premium X user, have at least 500 verified followers, and have drawn a minimum of 5 million impressions in the last three-month period. The stated goal is to encourage “authentic, high-quality content,” and some of the money surely goes to creators doing just that.

But paying for posts that go viral makes the program ripe for exploitation. Some creators in the program engage in “rage baiting,” using outrageous content to draw comments and views. In May 2025, X sued 8 Vietnamese creators and 25 “John Does,” alleging that they fraudulently drew money from the program by posting phony AI-generated content and then boosting engagement by bot-driven comments. In April, X moved to cut the payments of “aggregators” who primarily posted news from other sources, and threatened sanctions against those who overused the BREAKING tag to draw eyeballs. On July 16 of this year, X revealed that it had removed millions of posts that purloined already-published content posted by others.

It’s not clear how X regards the AI-generated story slop that has infected my feed. (The company, now part of xAI—which is itself now part of SpaceX—would not answer my questions about this.) Most of the stories are falsely presented as true first-person narratives, though it’s pretty obvious that they are fabricated. In many cases, the creators describe themselves in their profile as storytellers. It’s hard to prove that the actual authors are AI models, but the vast majority bear the signs. The posts are manipulative and dumb and anything but authentic.

Rob Cover, a professor at Australia's RMIT Digital Ethnography Research Centre who studies AI-generated content, broke down the structure of these posts for me in an email. It’s as formalized as a sonnet. First comes a rage-baiting setup, “in which an innocent person is wrongfully fired, evicted, scammed, loses their rightful place on public transport, or is the subject of judicial overreach.” This is followed by a turnaround: “The underdog is redeemed while the adversary is defeated, humiliated, and shamed (often as a representation of a public shaming),” says Cover.

In many of these tales, narrators are in possession of sealed documents that turn the table on tormentors, often in divorce disputes or the execution of a relative’s estate. Or it could be something as simple as an airline passenger who fiercely retains their assigned seat when rude moochers lay claim to it—and the adversary suffers a walk of shame to the back of the plane.

These stories are shockingly popular, routinely garnering hundreds of thousands—sometimes millions—of views, and routinely get hundreds of likes and dozens of reposts. (Some of that might be bot traffic.) Those numbers reveal something about ourselves: a hunger for fairness, a lust for retribution. Reading them gives a jolt of dopamine as justice prevails. The AI knows it and reliably churns out content we can’t resist.

Jenna Russell, a PhD candidate at the University of Maryland who is studying AI writing, tells me that it’s blindingly simple to generate those mini-melodramas. “I think these spammers have simply optimized for the least effort and the most engagement, which means using easy, well-known tropes and prompting AI to write something that fits the bill,” she says.

That certainly is the case with the person who goes by the handle BIGBEN, who posted the climactic courtroom scene. He was the only person among the multiple storytellers I contacted who answered my DM invitation to tell me how they worked. At first he didn’t seem to understand how a journalistic exchange worked; he thought I was suggesting a partnership. If we uploaded his stories to Backchannel, he suggested, I could generate cash flow from my end. I explained that this scheme wouldn’t work for WIRED. I just wanted to hear how he worked, “Before I give out my leverage, what’s in it for me?” he asked.

Nonetheless, BIGBEN, who claimed he was a 21-year-old trader living in Nigeria, did share his process. Though he contended that some stories come from experiences that people shared with him, he fessed up to using AI to write for him. When it’s time to make up a new story, he says, he gives just Grok or ChatGPT a prompt. The first post in a story thread he posted earlier this week, presumably narrated by a second wife abused by her in-laws, notched 1.5 million views in two days. X pays him every two weeks as part of its Creative Revenue Sharing program. BIGBEN says the paychecks are usually between $500 and $700. Others report earning thousands of dollars in each cycle.

Compared to X posts involving rage, misinformation, porn, and stolen content, these stories of protagonist redemption and villain-shaming are fairly harmless. And if you’re curious what happened to the woman on trial in BIGBEN’s courtroom tale, I’ll save you from clicking. Her husband’s scheme to frame her was thwarted by her 9-year-old son, who had planted a digital recorder in dad’s office that exonerated the narrator and put hubby behind bars. A neat denouement, but a hollow one considering that it was a fabricated tale posted just for clicks. That hollow feeling may well become all too familiar as AI writing proliferates.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

This AI Assistant Wants to Make Up for Your Boyfriend’s Incompetence

Wired July 31, 2026

Over the past few years, the term “weaponized incompetence” has blown up in dating discourse online.

It’s used to describe someone—most often the guy, when it comes to heterosexual relationships—who acts like they are incapable of doing things like cooking, cleaning, scheduling, and just generally being thoughtful, in the hopes that their partner will simply take care of it.

A new AI agent, Orchid, was advertised this week as a way to fix relationship problems by simply doing all of those tasks for an inconsiderate partner instead.

In the promo, released on Wednesday, Sam, a boyfriend who is busy gaming and rifling through expired groceries, has forgotten his anniversary. “Ok ok, I can do this,” he types to Orchid, when the AI agent reminds him of the day’s significance. “You can’t. That’s why I’m here,” Orchid replies, as it goes about making a reservation and buying his girlfriend’s favorite flowers—lilies—another detail he didn’t remember. The girlfriend, who is also consulting Orchid throughout the day, is well aware that the AI assistant is doing all of this labor yet somehow allows Sam to take credit for the whole plan.

The rollout was blasted by users on X, for advertising to “adult babies uninterested in the world they live in” and “perpetuating … dead-end relationship[s] that both parties secretly hate.”

To state the obvious: Orchid will not fix long-simmering relationship resentments through task managing.

“Trying to outsource difficult but necessary communication will prevent couples from facing the messy but meaningful growing pains of their relationship,” says Lauren Maher, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Los Angeles. “An AI app will never be able to compensate for a lack of attention or genuine caring, and no amount of feigned attention will convince the nervous system that someone is there for you when they are not.”

Maher adds that “triangulation”—the term for when individuals do not speak to each other directly but communicate through a third party—is regularly advised against in couples therapy. Now we have the “bizarre option to triangulate the nonhuman entity of AI into our romantic relationships,” she says, but Orchid’s use case for couples is only a temporary mask for problems in the relationship that are likely to sprout later. “While this is being marketed as a solve, indirect communication is notorious for straining relationships.” Orchid did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The actual usefulness of AI assistants remains in doubt when it comes to matters of the heart.

According to one recent survey from astrology app Hint, which polled more than 13,000 adults across the US, Latin America, and Europe, AI assistants are actually making dating decisions harder, with 59 percent of the participants saying the advice left them more confused than before. Overburdened with too much machine-generated guidance, 47 percent said AI input influenced them to postpone decisions about their romantic relationships.

The company’s viral ad seems to be a bait-and-switch more than anything, as its larger ambitions are focused on workflow. Pitched as the ideal agent to “automate your life,” it offers to work across your connected apps without requiring you to switch between them.

But it’s unclear, beyond its texting feature, what makes it unique from other AI agents.

Rage-bait or not, the ad featuring the couple certainly generated a lot of chatter about the company, which, according to a blog post from June, wants to usher in a new vision for how people do, well, everything. But fixing a shitty relationship probably isn’t one of those things.

Review: Steelseries Arctis Nova Pro Omni

Wired July 31, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

The easiest way to describe the Steelseries Arctis Nova Pro Omni gaming headset is that it’s the middle child between the Nova Pro and the Nova Elite. It mixes elements from both, namely the plastic and steel build of the Pro and the newer tuning, ANC, microphones, and USB hub of the Elite to create something fresh. Does SteelSeries really need three different “Pro” gaming headsets above $300? I’m not so sure, but the Omni makes a convincing case as a great option for multisystem, multimedia power users.

As with its siblings, the two standout features here are battery swapping and multisystem mixing. You’re paying a premium for both, and if you don't need them, there are plenty of other great headsets that cost half as much (like the brand's own Arctis Nova 5, for example). But if you truly need three or even four different audio sources, the Omni can handle it much more seamlessly than the Pro (and for much less than the Elite).

The Nova Pro Omni may have the same 40-millimeter drivers as the Pro model, but changes to the tuning and processing have made a big difference in audio quality. The Steelseries software does a lot of heavy lifting here, with game-specific profiles that help pull the right sounds to the surface. Turning on the profile built for Marathon, the heady screeching and chirping sound effects and environmental noise was appropriately scalding, but I could still easily hear the crunching of enemies approaching from outside buildings. Combined with improved active noise canceling that's similar to the Elite model, the audio experience is truly excellent.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The headphones work just as well for music and movies, which is where I heard the biggest upgrade from the older Pro model. There's a nice richness, particularly with the EQ presets for music applied, that you don't get on most wireless gaming headsets. Like the fancier Elite, the Omni support hi-res audio wirelessly, another upgrade from the older Pro model. I still have doubts about whether it's actually useful for gaming, but I usually listen to music while I play games, so the benefits are there regardless.

Switching back and forth between the Omni and the much pricier Elite, I can definitely hear the difference, but it’s subtle. The Omni don’t have the same spacious soundstage or delicate details as the Elite. This stands out more with music than with gaming. But when I have two or three sources running at once, I don’t feel like I’m missing anything using the Omni over the more expensive Elite.

Multisystem mixing is the key selling point with the Omni. Like the other Nova Pro headsets, it comes with a dedicated USB hub for inputs. You can mix up to four inputs, up from two on the Pro model, but I struggle to come up with scenarios where it's truly needed. The most complex common situation I can think of would be a console for gameplay, a PC for Discord voice chat, and a phone or tablet for music over Bluetooth. The Pro can’t handle that setup, but the Omni can, so if that sounds like you, it’s worth the cost of the upgrade. The microphone will also output to multiple destinations at once, so if you need to pop into proximity chat while on a Discord call, you can do that.

SteelSeries also made a point to emphasize that this microphone, now omni-directional, is a big improvement over the old models, but that’s more of a gift for your friends and fellow raid members who have to hear you. The Omni, like the Nova Pro and Elite, sound significantly cleaner and crisper than most gaming headset mics, although I still think the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro is a bit sharper. Both do an excellent job of filtering out coughing, chair scooting, and the occasional dog bark.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The other big selling point is the swappable battery, a trick that I haven’t seen any other gaming headset makers attempt. The USB hub, which also hosts the 2.4-GHz wireless connection, has a slot in the side to charge up one of the two included batteries. When the headset starts to get low, you swap out the batteries, and the result is essentially infinite juice as long as you’re near your desk. If you do it fast enough, the headset will even turn back on and reconnect automatically. If you do find yourself away from the hub, there’s a sneaky USB-C port hidden under the ear cup cover for charging.

Like the entire Nova family, these are among the most comfortable gaming headsets I've tested. The “ski goggle” support strap on the headset helps keep pressure off the top of your dome during long sessions, and the ear cups are noticeably thicker and more padded than on the older Pro. While you can't get these in the very slick sage and gold color exclusive to the Elite, they do come in a nice dark blue that's different and not too gamer-coded.

I’m not sure what led SteelSeries to produce three different gaming headsets at $300 or above, particularly when most folks I talk to spend significantly less. As I write this, the older Nova Pro is available for $280 at Best Buy, and especially if you can get it for even cheaper, I think you’ll be more than happy with the sound, comfort, and two-source mixing. There’s certainly no reason to upgrade to the Omni if you are an existing Pro owner, unless you really need the extra inputs.

If both are at full price, the Nova Omni has some extra functionality, namely four inputs and improved wireless audio quality, but I only really noticed this while listening to music or watching movies. Still, you should only reach for the top-tier Nova Elite if you think spending an extra $200 is worth it for extra-premium materials (carbon fiber and brass) and that exclusive sage/gold color.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Ultimately, I like the Arctis Nova Omni just as much as I like the Nova Pro, and I don’t mean that to come off as dismissive: They're both excellent headphones. If you’re willing to spend more on your gaming headset, these are undoubtedly the most feature-rich and elegant sounding ones out there, at least for serious, mixed-use gamers. I had hoped for something a little more distinct from the brand's other headsets, but the subtle improvements and extra functionality make them worth the cost, assuming your setup is complex enough to warrant it.

The Best Dyson Vacuums

Wired July 31, 2026

Amazon

Dyson

Amazon

Best Buy

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Shopping for the best Dyson vacuum can feel like you’ve been sucked into one. Between Dyson's massive new lineup and the dizzying array of models you can find on sale, it feels exhausting to keep up with which model is worth the price tag. But as someone who tests vacuums for a living, I can tell you getting a Dyson is well worth the splurge for several homes and use cases.

I've tested all the latest Dyson models side by side to find out which ones are worth investing in. After all the new models arrived earlier this year, the best vacuum turns out to be the Dyson Gen5Detect ($949) followed by the Dyson V16 Piston Animal ($850). If you're looking for the best bang for your buck, the Dyson V10 Konical ($500) has less power but scored above other models with similar or more power in my tests.

Read on to find out how each Dyson vacuum did in tests against sand on my rug, piles of litter on my hard floors, and overall results of vacuuming the three stories of my home. Don't miss my other vacuum guides if you don't find the best one for you here: I also cover cordless vacuums, robot vacuums, car vacuums, and the best vacuums ever.

Updated July 2026: I've updated this guide with a new top pick, the Dyson Gen5Detect, and the V10 Konical and V16 Piston Animal as additional picks. There are also new notes on the V8 Cyclone and the V15 Detect after the latest round of testing.

Dyson

Amazon

Wayfair

Dyson's most powerful stick vacuum is the Dyson Gen5Detect. It's been our top pick for pet hair since it does a fantastic job deep cleaning and has a HEPA filter that Dyson says traps 99.99 percent of particles down to 0.1 microns. After side-by-side testing against Dyson's new vacuums and our longtime favorite, the V15 Detect, the Gen5Detect came out with the best score.

The Gen5Detect scored the highest out of all five Dyson vacuums I tested it with (the V16 Piston Animal, V15 Detect, V10 Konical, and V8 Cyclone) in vacuuming up Cheerios on carpet, cat litter on hard floors, and general vacuuming in both vacuum mode and handheld mode. It didn't do as well vacuuming sand on a thin rug, but when I moved to a thicker rug, it got all of the sand in a single sweep. You can really feel the suction in action on this vacuum—it packs 262 air watts (AW) and has a motor that reaches 35,000 revolutions per minute (rpm).

It comes with the Digital Motorbar cleaner head for carpets, and you can use it on hard floors too, but Gen5Detect also comes with the Fluffy Optic cleaner head that has fluffy roller bars made to pick up dust and debris off wood and similar flooring. The Fluffy Optic head has a bright laser, too, making it easy to spot debris you need to vacuum over. Gen5's laser is twice as bright, so it's easier to spot dust and debris. Overall, it's a fantastic, powerful vacuum and worth investing in if you've got pets or want to get the overall best experience when shopping for a new Dyson vacuum.

The only thing it doesn't have that Dyson's newer models will is compatibility with the new docking station, nor compatibility with a Submarine wet roller head, which newer models will have.

Dyson

Dyson

Best Buy

If you want to spend less but still get a great Dyson vacuum, the V10 Konical did much better than I expected. It has 150 air watts of power, three cleaning modes, a HEPA filter, and a new cleaner head called the All Floor Cones head. It's similar to the new head you'll find on the V16 Piston Animal, though without the sensing technology. Still, it's designed for both hard floors and soft carpet, and uses dual rotating conical brush bars to keep hair from getting tangled in it as it vacuums. There's a built-in light, which is nice for vacuuming hard floors to spot dust you might miss, though the green laser on the Fluffy Optic head is better for that.

The V10 Konical did a good job in my overall testing of Dyson vacuums. It did slightly better than the more powerful V15 Detect when vacuuming sand on a rug, and it did a good job picking up Cheerios. It felt similar on rugs and carpets to the V15 Detect, though it has a lower power level and cheaper price point. It didn't impress me as much on hard floors, but since it doesn't have the Fluffy Optic head option, this vacuum is at a disadvantage. The V10 can still get it clean, it just needs a couple passes to clean up particularly dirty areas (e. g., areas where I have intentionally dumped a handful of cat litter).

Overall, if you're set on a Dyson but don't want to spend close to a grand, this is a great option. It's on sale for the same price as the cheaper V8 Cyclone, but it did better in all my side-by-side tests than the V8. It also works with the new Auto-empty Dok, a self-emptying docking station that doubles as a charger and accessory storage. The V10 is available with the Dok for $650.

Dyson

Amazon

Amazon (Submarine)

Dyson

Dyson (Submarine)

The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson's new top-of-the-line vacuum, with 315 air watts of suction, 70 minutes of run time, a new cleaner head (plus the Fluffy Optic head for hard floors), and some quality-of-life design upgrades. There are two built-in crevice tools (one on the motor, one on the end of the long wand) so you can do targeted cleans without needing to grab an accessory, and there's a release on the top of the wand you can pull to switch out the vacuum cleaner head without bending over. A compressor in the dust bin helps get the dust and hair out, though I usually still need to manually remove some stragglers.

The suction on the V16 works fantastically on carpet and rugs alike, and it did well in all of my tests except for vacuuming on a thin rug. The V16 Piston Animal scored right behind the Gen5Detect after vacuuming sand, Cheerios, cat litter, and general vacuuming and handheld mode around my three-story townhouse. The suction is excellent at getting cat hair and debris out of my carpets, and the HEPA filtration will keep pet dander from circulating back into the air.

But the biggest gain is this vacuum's compatibility with not just two great vacuum heads, but a third. The V16 has a Submarine variant ($1,100) to let you use it as a wet floor cleaner and is eventually slated to get its own self-emptying docking station like the V10 has. But you'll have to spend a pretty penny to get that third vacuum head, and the docking station price is a mystery (as is its arrival timing). Still, if your home is full of hard floors, it might be worth it for you.

Dyson

Best Buy

Amazon (Plus)

Dyson

If you're looking to spend less but still get two vacuum heads, the V15 Detect is often on sale for around $600 these days and comes with both the Digital Motorbar and Fluffy Optic cleaner head. That's more than you'll get with the new cheaper Dyson vacuums like the V10 and V8, but I also wouldn't buy this vacuum at full price anymore since it's five years old and didn't perform better than the cheaper V10 Konical in my side-by-side tests.

Still, it's a good vacuum. The Fluffy Optic head has the green laser light to spot dust, but it's a weaker light than newer models have. There are other versions you might spot, like the V15 Detect Plus, which just means there are different attachments (the Plus has a dusting brush instead of a combination tool, but everything else is the same), or the Submarine version that comes with the Submarine wet mop roller head.

You don't get a power button with this model; instead, you have a trigger control you have to hold down while you're using it. It's fine, but I don't love it for longer vacuuming sessions. There is an LCD screen that tells you the number of particles the V15 is sucking up, and it tells you the particle sizes. It's fun if you love data, but not a feature I look at often; I usually just use the screen to check battery life and which mode I'm on.

Dyson

Best Buy

Dyson

The name of Dyson's latest robot vacuum, the Spot+Scrub AI, makes it easy to guess its marquee feature: artificial intelligence that promises to identify stains and scrub them away. More interesting, in my opinion, is the fact this is Dyson's first robot vacuum that can also mop. I'm not sure what took Dyson so long, but if you're going to get a Dyson robot vacuum, I'd recommend this model that can both vacuum and mop over one that vacuums only. It does a good job both vacuuming and mopping, and has solid suction that left my carpet and rugs feeling great after a run of the vacuum.

The navigation could use a little work, particularly in the height department. While the Spot+Scrub didn't struggle on rugs or around chair legs like the older Vis Nav did for WIRED reviewer Chris Haslam, it did struggle to notice when it was too tall and would bump into my cabinets or even wedge itself under spots it then couldn't get itself out of. It struggled the most with the builder-grade lower kitchen cabinets and IKEA pieces around my house, so if your home is full of low furniture (particularly if it's from IKEA, which seems to be at the perfect height to thwart this vacuum), I'd consider a different model so that you don't have to watch it run into furniture over and over.

The Spot+Scrub comes with a massive base station that has a distinctly Dyson look and features a translucent dry debris canister. Because of this, I do like that I never had to wonder when to empty it, and it'll remind you to empty both the dry and wet debris regularly.

Dyson

Amazon

Dyson

If you already have a stick vacuum, then you don't need a handheld vacuum like this one. But if you're looking for a handheld vacuum to complement your upright vacuum or a robot vacuum, then the best Dyson handheld is the Car+Boat. It's small but mighty, with a spin speed of 110,000 RPM, and works particularly great for vehicles like cars and boats, as the name suggests.

It's an affordable way to get into the Dyson ecosystem and a good way to expand your home vacuum options if you currently have a bulky upright and nothing else. It comes with a couple of tools and features a trigger-power design like the V15. There's no display on this handheld, but instead just a switch for the two modes (standard and max) and the trigger to activate the vacuum. The dustbin is small compared to most of Dyson's lineup, but actually larger than the cheap Digital Slim. It's much larger than most other handheld vacuums you'll try, and has a great long battery life.

We've tested a variety of Dyson vacuums, both corded and cordless. The vacs below are still worth buying, as long as you don't pay full price.

Dyson Ball Animal 3 for $420: If you really, really, want an upright vacuum instead of a cordless stick vacuum from Dyson, the Dyson Ball Animal 3 is the way to go. We've tested the Ball Animal 3 Extra, which has more attachments, but the regular is just as powerful. Former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey found it performed well against the rabbit hair in her home. The downside is that it's loud and heavy.

Dyson Clean+Wash Hygiene Wet and Dry Floor Cleaner for $500: This wet-dry cleaner’s claim to fame is its lack of an “unhygienic” filter, and WIRED reviewer Kat Merck has experienced no off smells in her three months of consistent use. The device is similar to the previous Wash G1, with a self-propelled design that's easy to push. It has a screen to show battery life and mode and a dock for self-cleaning. Dyson’s new probiotic floor cleaner ($24) is also a nice product on its own that's odorless and does an impressive job on Merck's Coretec LVP floors, leaving them both feeling and looking cleaner than when she sanitizes them with a steam mop. The Clean+Wash is not great for detritus like hair and leaves, though, since it has no suction and just a microfiber roller. She found it best for spot-cleaning stains and spills, but at that point, you might prefer to get a cheaper wet mop with more suction power.

Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones for $600: I liked this vacuum a lot more than I expected I would. It's easy to maneuver, and packs both its motor and the dustbin into the handle, so it's much lighter and easier to use than classic cordless vacuums. But it's pricey for only being good for hard floors. That being said, if your home is hard floor only, this is a fun one to choose. It's also nice for anyone with strength or mobility challenges who struggles with a top-heavy cordless vacuum, since it feels closer to pushing a Swiffer mop than a vacuum. The original price of $600 is a little steep for its limited capability, but when it's on sale or listed for under $500 (like it is right now!) it's a much better buy.

Dyson V12 Detect Slim for $650: Dyson's V12 Detect Slim is excellent for small spaces like a studio or a one-bedroom apartment since it's compact, lightweight, and a great size for hard-to-reach spots and minimal storage. There's an LCD screen, 150 air watts of power, a run time of up to 60 minutes, and a charging time of up to 4.5 hours. But for $650, you could get one of Dyson's newer vacuum with HEPA filtration and newer heads, though only the PencilVac is slimmer than this model.

There are a lot of Dyson models out there, even if they're on the older side.

Dyson 360 Nav Vis for $1,000: The 360 Vis Nav isn't Dyson's previous robot vacuum that had a powerful spin speed, but it can only vacuum and needs some work on its navigation. WIRED reviewer Chris Haslam found that it struggled around chair legs and on rugs, something similar vacuums didn't have a problem with. It doesn't have a base station, either, but it is pretty cheap now that it's an older Dyson model.

Dyson Big Ball Multi Floor Vacuum for $339: This was originally one of our top picks for tight spaces. But Dyson no longer sells it, and it's often out of stock at third-party retailers—unless you're OK with purchasing a used model (however, you shouldn't spend more than $250 to $300 on it). It's a good option if you're looking for more maneuverability than a stick can offer. You only have to wield a thin suction tube, as long as you don't mind periodically repositioning the canister. Dyson's Cinetic technology means there are no filters to wash or replace, and it still has HEPA-grade filtration for capturing allergens and most particulates. If you find a new model, I suggest waiting until it's on sale between $300 and $400.

Dyson V11 for $550: When WIRED reviewer Adrienne So reviewed the V11, she called it the “dream vac.” However, that was in 2019, and many updated models have come out since then, though it does have 185 air watts, making it stronger than some of the new, similarly priced models. If you can find a V11 for under $350, it’s worth it; otherwise, I recommend going with a later (or cheaper) model. If you're looking into the latest V11 Dyson offers, it's important to note it doesn't come with Dynamic Load Sensor technology (a feature that allows it to automatically adjust suction across different floor types).

Dyson V8 Cyclone for $400: I wanted to love this vacuum, but the V10 Konical costs only a little more (or already seems to be on sale for the same price) and cleans better, has HEPA filtration, and a new cleaner head that has a built-in light. It's an affordable option with 150 air watts of power, but I'd recommend the V10 Konical over it any day.

Dyson WashG1 for $399: The WashG1 is Dyson's first dedicated wet floor cleaner. It comes equipped with two very absorbent microfiber rollers that rotate counter to each other and a pump that distributes water evenly from a 27-ounce tank via 26 pulse-modulated water outlets. It's fantastic for cleaning floors, but the tray is gross and messy to clean, and mine grew mold at one point. I'd recommend checking out the newer Clean+Wash Hygiene, above, if you want a cleaner like this.

What Does Dyson’s Terminology Mean?

Dyson doesn't stick to chronological order when naming its stick models. Sometimes it skips numbers, and sometimes it'll introduce a lower number as a later model than a higher number. For example, Dyson introduced the V15 immediately after the V11, and then the V12 after the V15. In the broadest sense, the numbers seem to loosely grow larger with each passing release—the V11 is newer than the V10, and the V10 is newer than the V8. But Dyson's naming system is cryptic enough that even I can't predict what the subsequent model will be.

Dyson also has a lot of sub-models, because its naming scheme isn't confusing enough. Each one has a different number of included tool attachments and accessories. Every model (V7, V8, V10, V11, V15, etc.) seems to introduce new sub-models, so the list just keeps growing, and then there are discontinued sub-models that show up as old stock on websites, typically on sale.

Detect isn't exactly a sub-model, but rather part of the name of the V15 Detect and V12 Detect Slim. It refers to the laser detection system that measures particle size and count to customize suction power.

Absolute is usually the king-of-the-hill version with the most attachments. I can't list them all, because they vary based on parent model, but expect a variety of brush nozzles, crevice attachments, and motorized roller heads to scrub tough grit off hard floors and out of deep-pile carpets.

Allergy used to mean that it came with an upgraded filter that traps 99.99 percent of bacteria and dust, so it expels cleaner air than regular models, but after the V7, all Dyson stick vacs started including the upgraded filters. It's largely a legacy designation now, and it hasn't been used on newer models.

Motorhead sounds fancy, but it's the low-end sub-model that comes with a motorized head, a couple of basic brush and crevice tools, and that's about it. It's mostly a holdover from the V7 days. Dyson has found other names for basic sub-models.

Origin, Fluffy, and Animal come with relatively few attachments. The Fluffy and Animal don't come with any unique attachments particular to usefulness in cleaning up after pets; it's just become shorthand for "base model with fewer attachments." The same is true for the Origin, although its name makes more sense.

Fluffycones is a new variation introduced by the PencilVac that describes the unique cone-shaped fluffy rollers in the head. So far it's only in that vacuum, but I'm curious if Dyson will include it in future models.

Outsize is a larger version of a Dyson model. There's a Gen5Detect and a Gen5Detect Outsize, for example, and the Outsize version has bigger bin, wider vacuum head and weighs more. There's no Outsize version so far of any of Dyson's newer models after the Gen5Detect.

Dyson isn't above combining sub-model names. The more names Dyson slaps onto a model, the more attachments it comes with. For example, the V8 Animal Pro comes with more stuff than the Animal, but the Animal Pro+ comes with even more than that.

What Are the Dyson Accessory Bundles?

You will also notice that we mention the different accessories in each model, which vary depending on the model you buy. These make your vacuum more versatile, making it easier to tackle specific parts of the house. If your vac doesn't come with an accessory you want, you can always purchase it separately. But it can be tough to discern which one does what, especially if this is your first Dyson. (Save on top Dyson vacuums and accessory bundles with our exclusive Dyson promo codes.)

What About Replacement Parts?

When unboxing your new vacuum, I recommend downloading Dyson's companion app—MyDyson (iOS, Android)—and registering your device to activate your warranty, which is two years for cordless models and five years for corded. The coverage goes into effect on the day you buy it, so long as you have proof of purchase. If you don't, the warranty will kick in 90 days after the manufacture date. The warranty covers replacement parts (including batteries and certain parts), repairs (Dyson will collect the machine free of charge, or you can visit one of its Service Centers), and replacements. If the repairs can't be done, Dyson will fully replace it for you. You can check here for a full list of what it does and doesn't cover.

When your warranty is up, you'll have to buy the replacement parts. Dyson offers spare filters, batteries, chargers, specific parts (V-ball wheels, axles and rollers, and rear edges), and accessories for purchase. You can go directly through Dyson's site (which is accessible via the app), but stock fluctuates depending on the specific part you're looking for. You can also purchase them through authorized sellers like Amazon and Walmart. If you're looking elsewhere, it's important to make sure these parts are genuine Dyson parts (you can do this by checking that Dyson is the retailer through the third-party seller you're purchasing from). Dyson offers a 12-month warranty on its genuine parts, and those sold by other brands may not be covered. Inauthentic parts may not fit or work properly either—regardless of whether the seller claims they're compatible—and could damage the vacuum entirely. I made the mistake of ordering new filters through a third-party seller for the Dyson V15 I was testing at the time, only to find they were too small.

How Do You Clean a Dyson Vacuum?

Dyson vacuums are expensive, so it's important to maintain yours—this helps to increase its longevity and maintain its powerful suction. If you have a cordless model, the company suggests cleaning the filter once a month (at least).

You can clean the filter (on both cordless and upright models) by removing it, tapping lightly on the side of your garbage bin or sink, and rinsing it with cold tap water (Dyson says not to use any detergents). Then, fill the filter with warm tap water, cover the open sides with your hands, and shake it firmly to remove dirt. You should repeat these steps until the water runs clear, at which point you can then shake the filter to get rid of any excess water. You should then let the filter dry for at least 24 hours in an area that has airflow (like near a fan or open window). Once it's fully dry, you can place it back into the body. To clean the canister, use a damp microfiber cloth.

You can also clean the roller cleaner head by cutting away any hair using scissors (depending on the Dyson you have, you might need to use a screwdriver to remove the plate on the cleaner head). If your model comes with a soft brush bar, you can clean that too. Remove it from the cleaner head (take the end cap off too), hold it under running water while gently rubbing it to remove dirt and lint, and let it dry for 24 hours. If you're using an upright vac, you can also clean the hose by running it under warm water. As with the rest of the parts, you should let it dry for 24 hours before reattaching it.

How Do You Set Up a Dyson Wall Mount?

Some of Dyson's cordless vacs, like the V15 Detect and Gen5Detect, don't stand upright. The battery has a flat back so that you can rest it against a wall, but it's not the most stable. The company includes a wall dock with these models, and there's also a spot to place the charging cable so the device stays charged on the dock. It's simple to install (you may need a drill), but it's the ideal storage solution.

Dyson is launching more and more models with freestanding docks, including the PencilVac and the Clean+Wash, and the Dyson Piston Animal is due to have a docking station that it can self-empty into. If you'd be more interested in a freestanding dock instead of a wall-mounted stand, check out Dyson's newest vacuums.

Does Dyson Come Out With New Models Every Year?

Not always. There's no cycle to when Dyson will release new products or whether a new model will replace something in the lineup or just add to the existing one. Some of Dyson's newest vacuums don't launch in every market right away, either—the Digital Slim and PencilVac, for example, were available only in Asia at first. This year has had several new Dyson launches, including the Spot+Scrub AI robot vacuum and PencilVac, which came to North America, and there are a couple more new models still due to arrive.

What's the Cheapest Dyson Vacuum?

If you're looking for even more of a budget buy, Dyson moves older models down the product lineup, so the top model from three years ago might be today's value option. You can even usually find discontinued Dyson vacs at a steep discount as old stock sells out. Dyson's official eBay outlet occasionally has exclusive deals on outgoing models, too.

How Does WIRED Test Vacuums?

WIRED tests vacuums within home environments to see how they'd work for day-to-day messes and buildup. We test them on carpets, rugs, staircases, and hard floors like hardwood, vinyl, and tile to see how well they do at picking up dust, dirt, and debris. We also make sure to test every attachment for its intended use, but the main focus is using the vacuum itself like a normal person would to see if it's worth investing in.

How Does WIRED Acquire Its Review Samples? What Happens to Them After Testing?

WIRED acquires review samples in a handful of ways: they can be provided by a company (though if provided, WIRED doesn't promise coverage or what that coverage will be) or purchased by WIRED. Writers can also write about items they've purchased themselves. For this guide, all of these picks were all provided as review samples for WIRED staffers to test.

After we're done testing, samples are either returned, donated, or held onto for long-term testing. Dyson vacuums are a category I like to long-term test since there isn't very much turnover in the lineup, making it possible for us to spend longer testing a Dyson without needing to move on to the model that replaced it.
